title: Revisiting Classic Thought Experiments to Measure Consciousness for Artificial Intelligence Safety
summary: This research note revisits Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, and Searle's Chinese Room through the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework. It formalises a toy symbolic setting in which successful behaviour is measured by task performance ($W_{causal,T}$), while the efficiency with which preserved internal structure supports that behaviour is measured by operational consciousness ($κ_T$). Within this setup, an uncompressed lookup system and a compact generative system can in principle achieve comparable behavioural success, yet diverge sharply in $κ_T$: the former relies on an expanding standing store of unreused mappings, whereas the latter reuses compact internal structure. The note therefore reframes classic disputes about understanding by separating outward performance from the organisation that sustains it, and motivates why this distinction may matter for later AI-safety analysis.

AI.tldr: This research note reframes classic philosophical debates (Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, Searle's Chinese Room) using the Conservation-Congruent Encoding (CCE) framework, introducing a formal distinction between outward task performance (W_causal,T) and operational consciousness (κ_T), showing that uncompressed lookup systems and compact generative systems may achieve equivalent behavioural success yet diverge fundamentally in the efficiency with which internal structure supports that behaviour.
AI.motivation: To resolve long-standing philosophical disputes about machine understanding — where behaviourally equivalent systems provoke conflicting intuitions — by providing a formal apparatus that separates mere outward performance from the organisational efficiency of internal structure, thereby motivating why this distinction carries implications for AI safety.
AI.method: The authors construct a toy symbolic setting formalised within the CCE framework, defining two metrics: (1) W_{causal,T} for task performance, and (2) κ_T for operational consciousness, which measures the efficiency with which conserved internal structure supports behaviour. They then compare an uncompressed lookup system (expanding store of unreused mappings) against a compact generative system (reusing compact internal structure), demonstrating how κ_T exposes a divergence invisible to behavioural metrics alone.
AI.result: Both system types can achieve comparable behavioural success (W_{causal,T}), yet diverge sharply in operational consciousness (κ_T). The lookup system exhibits low κ_T due to its expanding, non-reused storage, while the generative system achieves high κ_T through compact structural reuse. This demonstrates that behavioural equivalence masks fundamentally different organisational properties.
AI.conclusion: Classic disputes about understanding — Leibniz's mill, Turing's imitation game, and Searle's Chinese Room — can be reframed productively by separating outward performance from the organisational structure that sustains it. The κ_T metric captures this structural dimension, and the authors argue this distinction is not merely philosophical but may prove relevant for future AI-safety analysis.

title: AutoFOAM: The Self-Refining Autonomous OpenFOAM Agent
summary: Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) plays an important role in modern engineering, but using open-source solvers such as OpenFOAM requires considerable knowledge and skills, as well as time-consuming configuration file setup. To reduce this burden, we propose AutoFOAM - a self-evolving large language model (LLM) agent that creates, evaluates, runs, and evolves its own OpenFOAM simulations based solely on natural-language instructions. Our model is pre-trained on the Qwen-coder 2.5-14B, which is then fine-tuned on 252 text prompts targeting 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 parametrized mesh templates, and a y plus-aware numerical policy. The crucial element of the algorithm is a sophisticated evolution loop composed of 7 stages. To prevent model degeneration under repeated self-training, the agent employs three complementary anti-collapse streams: RAG-augmented retry context, surgical dictionary-level patching, and prompt-diversity paraphrasing. By bridging generative artificial intelligence with rigorous fluid simulations, AutoFOAM accelerates rapid prototyping and democratizes advanced CFD workflows.

AI.tldr: AutoFOAM is a self-evolving LLM agent based on Qwen-coder 2.5-14B that automates OpenFOAM CFD simulation setup, execution, and refinement from natural-language prompts, using a 7-stage evolution loop with three anti-collapse mechanisms to prevent model degeneration.
AI.motivation: Using open-source CFD solvers like OpenFOAM demands substantial domain expertise and labor-intensive configuration file preparation, creating a high barrier to entry. The authors aim to reduce this burden by enabling natural-language-driven simulation workflows, thereby democratizing advanced CFD and accelerating rapid prototyping.
AI.method: The approach fine-tunes Qwen-coder 2.5-14B on 252 text prompts covering 7 OpenFOAM solvers, 13 parameterized mesh templates, and a y-plus-aware numerical policy. A 7-stage self-evolution loop iteratively creates, evaluates, runs, and refines simulations. To combat model collapse during repeated self-training, three complementary anti-collapse streams are employed: (1) RAG-augmented retry context, (2) surgical dictionary-level patching, and (3) prompt-diversity paraphrasing.
AI.result: The paper presents AutoFOAM as a functional LLM-agent framework capable of automating OpenFOAM workflows. Specific quantitative benchmarks (e.g., success rates, mesh quality metrics, solver accuracy comparisons) are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: By bridging generative AI with rigorous fluid simulations, AutoFOAM demonstrates a viable path toward lowering the expertise threshold for CFD, enabling faster design iteration and broader accessibility to advanced simulation tools.

title: Enhancing LLMs with Context-Specific Knowledge for Mitigating Misinformation in SMEs: A RAG-based Modeling and Analysis
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs), a part of artificial intelligence (AI), are increasingly being adopted by Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to enhance question-answering capabilities and support business decision-making processes. However, hallucinations in LLM-generated outputs can serve as a source of misinformation, reducing user confidence in their reliability and trustworthiness within SMEs. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge by incorporating external knowledge sources into the modeling process. In this paper, we present VectorRAG and GraphRAG modeling approaches to mitigate hallucinations and misinformation risks and evaluate their effectiveness in SME environments. Our experimental evaluation is conducted on multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, including LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen, to assess performance in terms of useful response generation, risk of hallucination, contextual relevance, as well as human-interpretation. The results demonstrate that RAG-enhanced LLMs can significantly improve response quality by reducing hallucinations and misinformation, thereby supporting more reliable, trustworthy, and context-aware decision-making in SME environments.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates VectorRAG and GraphRAG as retrieval-augmented generation approaches to reduce LLM hallucinations in SME contexts, testing on LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen models, and finds RAG significantly improves response quality, reliability, and decision-making support.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly adopted by SMEs for question-answering and decision support, but hallucinations produce misinformation that erodes user trust. RAG offers a potential solution, yet its effectiveness in SME-specific environments requires systematic evaluation.
AI.method: The authors propose and compare two RAG modeling approaches — VectorRAG (dense vector retrieval) and GraphRAG (graph-structured knowledge retrieval) — integrating external knowledge into SOTA LLMs (LLaMA, Mistral, Qwen). Evaluation metrics include response usefulness, hallucination risk, contextual relevance, and human interpretability.
AI.result: RAG-enhanced LLMs significantly improve response quality across all metrics: reduced hallucinations and misinformation, higher contextual relevance, and better human-interpretable outputs, thereby supporting more trustworthy SME decision-making.
AI.conclusion: RAG, in both vector and graph-based forms, is an effective strategy for mitigating LLM hallucinations in SME settings, enhancing reliability and trustworthiness for business-critical applications.

title: Energy Efficiency of Locally Deployed LLMs: A Preliminary Quantitative GPU Power Benchmark on Consumer Hardware
summary: The local deployment of large language models (LLMs) is gaining traction due to privacy concerns and the desire for on-premise inference. However, the energy costs on consumer hardware remain poorly characterized, as most benchmarks focus solely on accuracy. This paper presents a reproducible, hardware-level energy benchmark of nine open-source LLMs (1B to 7B parameters) executed on a single consumer GPU (RTX 4060Ti 16GB). Using the Ollama inference engine, GPU power draw was sampled at 2Hz via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. We evaluate mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tok/s). Our findings suggest that factors beyond raw parameter count, including model architecture and quantization strategy, drive energy efficiency. Specifically, gemma3:1b and llama3.2:1b achieve the lowest energy cost (0.56 J/token and 0.65 J/token) and the highest throughput (>170 tok/s). In contrast, the 7B-Mistral model consumes up to 4.4x more energy per token than the most efficient model. Notably, qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning, highlighting the need to distinguish between token generation modes in efficiency metrics.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks energy consumption of nine open-source LLMs (1B–7B parameters) on a consumer GPU (RTX 4060Ti). Gemma3:1b and Llama3.2:1b are most energy-efficient (~0.56 J/token); Mistral 7B consumes up to 4.4× more. Qwen3.5:2b shows anomalously high energy due to extended reasoning, underscoring the need to distinguish generation modes in efficiency metrics.
AI.motivation: Local LLM deployment is rising due to privacy and on-premise needs, yet energy costs on consumer hardware are poorly characterized—most benchmarks focus only on accuracy, neglecting power consumption.
AI.method: Nine open-source LLMs (1B–7B parameters) were evaluated on a single RTX 4060Ti 16GB GPU using the Ollama inference engine. GPU power draw was sampled at 2 Hz via nvidia-smi across a fixed prompt set. Metrics: mean/peak power, total energy per prompt (J/prompt), energy per output token (J/token), and throughput (tokens/s).
AI.result: Gemma3:1b and Llama3.2:1b achieve lowest energy (~0.56 and 0.65 J/token) and highest throughput (>170 tok/s). Mistral 7B consumes up to 4.4× more energy per token than the most efficient model. Qwen3.5:2b exhibits anomalously high per-prompt energy due to extended internal reasoning, revealing that token generation mode affects efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Energy efficiency is driven by factors beyond parameter count—including architecture and quantization strategy. Efficiency benchmarks must distinguish between token generation modes (e.g., direct generation vs. internal reasoning chains) to provide meaningful comparisons.

title: Hierarchical BM25: Lexical Search at Billion-Document Scale
summary:
A flat BM25 index over one billion documents occupies about 400 GB. Holding it in memory requires DRAM proportional to corpus size. Serving it from disk takes 4-12 seconds per query. Exact top-k lexical retrieval at this scale is therefore impractical within an interactive latency budget.
  Hierarchical BM25 gives up exact ranking in exchange for fixed bounds on memory and latency. A resident coarse index selects which of ~1K topical, size-balanced document groups a query visits, using two signals: the total frequency of each query term within a group, and, for informative terms spread too thinly across groups for frequency totals to reflect, whether several of them appear together in one document. Selected groups are then searched exhaustively and scored against ~100 KB of global statistics. Every returned score therefore equals the flat index's score, and the approximation is confined to selection alone. The resident footprint is ~4.4 GB, independent of corpus size. Sixteen-term queries over one billion documents return in ~300 ms (4.7x to 5.6x the throughput of a flat multi-threaded index), and a warmed cache sustains ~32 queries per second versus under 3 for flat indexing. At a 500K-document configuration, visiting 5-10% of clusters recovers 0.83-0.92 of the exhaustive result score. Billion-scale recall and a direct comparison against document-reordered BlockMax-WAND remain open.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Hierarchical BM25, a two-stage lexical retrieval system that approximates exact BM25 ranking over billion-scale document collections while maintaining a fixed, small memory footprint (~4.4 GB) and interactive latency (~300 ms per query). It uses a coarse resident index to select a subset of document groups before exhaustive scoring.
AI.motivation: Flat BM25 indexing over one billion documents requires ~400 GB of DRAM, which is proportional to corpus size, and disk-based serving incurs 4–12 seconds per query. Exact top-k lexical retrieval at this scale is therefore infeasible within interactive latency budgets. The authors seek a solution with fixed, corpus-independent memory bounds and sub-second query latency while sacrificing as little ranking quality as possible.
AI.method: The system, called Hierarchical BM25, operates in two stages. First, a lightweight resident coarse index partitions the corpus into approximately 1,000 topical, size-balanced document groups. Two selection signals determine which groups a query visits: (1) the total frequency of each query term within a group, and (2) for informative but thinly spread terms, whether multiple such terms co-occur in a single document within the group. Selected groups are then exhaustively searched and scored against ~100 KB of global statistics. Every returned score is exactly equal to the flat BM25 score; approximation is confined entirely to group selection. The resident footprint is ~4.4 GB, independent of corpus size.
AI.result: Sixteen-term queries over one billion documents return in approximately 300 ms, achieving 4.7x to 5.6x the throughput of a flat multi-threaded index. A warmed cache sustains ~32 queries per second versus under 3 for flat indexing. At a 500K-document configuration, visiting 5–10% of clusters recovers 0.83–0.92 of the exhaustive result score.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical BM25 enables practical interactive lexical retrieval at billion-document scale by trading exact ranking for a bounded-memory, bounded-latency approximation. The method confines approximation to group selection while preserving exact BM25 scoring within selected groups. Open questions remain regarding billion-scale recall and direct comparison against document-reordered BlockMax-WAND.

title: Width, Memory, and Delay: A Resource Accounting for the Limits of Flat Multi-Agent Systems
summary: A recurring question in the design of scalable multi-agent systems -- from robot swarms to collectives of large-language-model (LLM) agents -- is whether adding more agents can, on its own, overcome performance limits, or whether a qualitatively \emph{deeper} organization is required. A recent preprint argues that flat, homogeneous multi-agent systems face an irreducible, population-independent ``causal floor'' on achievable error, removable only by hierarchical (nested-loop) organization. Using a controlled disturbance-rejection testbed with an exactly computable optimum, we show this conclusion is too strong and replace it with a quantitative resource model built on three resources: population \emph{width} $N$, per-agent internal-model \emph{memory} $d$, and prediction across the observation \emph{delay} $τ$. We establish three claims. (i) The achievable floor is governed not by architectural hierarchy but by per-agent internal-model content: a flat, homogeneous swarm whose agents carry a matched internal model of the disturbance matches or beats a designed two-loop hierarchy at equal per-agent memory -- so temporal depth can be dynamical (recurrent memory), not architectural (nesting). (ii) The three resources are \emph{not mutually interchangeable}; we chart the exchange rates and the hard non-exchange boundaries on an explicit width$\times$memory map, including a strict equal-total-state-budget comparison. (iii) A residual floor is set by the observation delay and the environment's unpredictability over that horizon, which we verify against the optimal controller. We quantify the price of replacing oracle knowledge of the disturbance spectrum with online learning, provide a preliminary robustness check against a mild bounded nonlinearity and a spatially-extended plant, and distill four design rules for practitioners.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the claim that hierarchical (nested-loop) architecture is necessary to overcome an irreducible error floor in multi-agent systems. Instead, it introduces a quantitative resource model based on population width, per-agent memory, and observation delay, showing that flat swarms with matched internal models can match or outperform hierarchies, and maps the trade-offs among these three resources.
AI.motivation: A recent preprint argued that flat, homogeneous multi-agent systems face an irreducible, population-independent "causal floor" on achievable error that can only be removed by hierarchical organization. This paper tests and challenges that strong claim, seeking to determine whether architectural hierarchy is truly necessary or whether alternative resource allocations (internal model capacity, memory, population size) can achieve equivalent or better performance.
AI.method: The authors use a controlled disturbance-rejection testbed with an exactly computable optimum (optimal controller). They systematically compare flat homogeneous swarms against a designed two-loop hierarchy under equal per-agent memory constraints, varying three resources: population width N, per-agent internal-model memory d, and observation delay τ. They construct an explicit width×memory map charting exchange rates and non-exchange boundaries, verify the residual delay-induced floor against the optimal controller, and provide robustness checks against bounded nonlinearity and a spatially-extended plant.
AI.result: Three main results: (i) The achievable error floor is governed by per-agent internal-model content, not architectural hierarchy — a flat swarm with matched internal models matches or beats a two-loop hierarchy at equal per-agent memory. (ii) The three resources (width, memory, delay) are not mutually interchangeable; the paper charts hard non-exchange boundaries and exchange rates. (iii) A residual error floor is set by observation delay and environmental unpredictability over that horizon, verified against the optimal controller. The paper also quantifies the cost of replacing oracle disturbance-spectrum knowledge with online learning.
AI.conclusion: The conclusion that hierarchy is strictly necessary to break an error floor is too strong. Temporal depth achieved through dynamical (recurrent) memory in flat architectures can substitute for architectural (nesting) depth. The paper distills four design rules for practitioners based on the three-resource model of width, memory, and delay.

title: CoT-Core: Accelerating LLM Evaluation via CoT-Aware Coreset Selection
summary: Evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) incurs prohibitive computational overhead during continuous development processes. While coreset selection accelerates evaluation, existing methods either suffer from a severe ``cold start'' bottleneck requiring massive historical logs (e.g., Item Response Theory) or exhibit a surface lexical bias that misses the underlying reasoning manifold of tasks. We propose CoT-Core, a novel training-free core question selection framework. Recognizing that lexically disparate questions can share equivalent underlying logic, CoT-Core prompts LLMs to unroll zero-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning trajectories. Projecting these paths into a latent space effectively clusters questions by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than superficial text similarity. Extensive experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA demonstrate that CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation, and delineate the boundary conditions of reasoning-aware pruning, revealing that its efficacy is intrinsically gated by task complexity.

AI.tldr: CoT-Core selects representative questions for efficient LLM evaluation by clustering based on Chain-of-Thought reasoning trajectories rather than surface text, achieving high-fidelity score estimation with drastically reduced costs.
AI.motivation: LLM evaluation is computationally prohibitive during iterative development. Existing coreset methods suffer from cold-start problems requiring historical data (e.g., IRT) or rely on lexical similarity, missing the underlying reasoning structure of tasks. A training-free method that captures logical equivalence is needed.
AI.method: CoT-Core prompts LLMs to generate zero-shot Chain-of-Thought reasoning trajectories for each question, then projects these trajectories into a latent space where questions cluster by intrinsic logical equivalence rather than surface-level lexical similarity. Core questions are selected from these clusters to form a representative evaluation subset.
AI.result: Experiments on GSM8K, MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA show CoT-Core drastically reduces evaluation costs while maintaining high-fidelity score estimation. The method's effectiveness is gated by task complexity, with stronger benefits on reasoning-intensive tasks.
AI.conclusion: CoT-Core provides a training-free, reasoning-aware solution to evaluation coreset selection, overcoming cold-start limitations and lexical bias. Its efficacy is contingent on task complexity, establishing boundary conditions for reasoning-aware pruning in LLM evaluation.

title: CeQe: Grounding Lexical Retrieval in Semantic Evidence
summary: Lexical retrieval (BM25) captures exact keyword matches and weights terms by corpus-wide significance, but it is blind to the semantic vocabulary gap: when a relevant document phrases an answer differently from the query, BM25 never retrieves it, and no amount of downstream reranking or fusion can recover a document that was never in the candidate set. We present Cross-Encoder Query Expansion (CE-QE), which reads the per-token relevance attributions of a cross-encoder applied to top semantic search results, selects the terms the cross-encoder treats as decisive, and appends them to the BM25 query. Unlike classical pseudo-relevance feedback, which reuses BM25's own (possibly wrong) top results, CE-QE seeds expansion from the semantic retriever's results, avoiding self-reinforcing query drift. Unlike recent generative query expansion (HyDE, Query2doc), which prompts a large language model to hallucinate text from its parametric knowledge, every CE-QE expansion term is copied verbatim from a retrieved passage, so it cannot introduce vocabulary the corpus does not contain, and its only added cost is attribution extraction on a cross-encoder a hybrid pipeline already runs for reranking. On seven BEIR datasets, CE-QE improves lexical recall substantially where query and answer vocabulary diverge (e.g., NQ Recall@100 from 0.32 to 0.47), and its score-fusion variant (SESF) beats cross-encoder score fusion by 2.5% on Recall@100 and beats SPLADEv2 and ColBERTv2 by 5.3% and 4.6% on nDCG@10, while leaving the underlying BM25 index completely unmodified.

AI.tldr: CE-QE improves lexical retrieval by extracting decisive terms from a cross-encoder's token-level relevance attributions on semantic search results, appending them to BM25 queries. This bridges the semantic-lexical gap without hallucination, self-reinforcing drift, or index modification, achieving significant gains in recall and nDCG across BEIR datasets.
AI.motivation: BM25 captures exact keyword matches but misses semantically relevant documents phrased differently. If a document is never retrieved, no downstream reranking or fusion can recover it. Existing solutions like pseudo-relevance feedback risk query drift, while generative expansion (HyDE, Query2doc) can hallucinate out-of-corpus terms. The authors aim to expand BM25 queries with corpus-grounded, semantically decisive terms without modifying the index.
AI.method: CE-QE works in three steps: (1) a semantic retriever fetches top-k results, (2) a cross-encoder scores each candidate and extracts per-token relevance attributions (identifying which tokens most influenced the relevance decision), and (3) the top decisive tokens are appended to the original BM25 query. A score-fusion variant (SESF) combines BM25 scores from the expanded query with cross-encoder scores. Since attribution extraction runs on a cross-encoder already used for reranking, the added cost is minimal.
AI.result: On seven BEIR datasets, CE-QE substantially improved BM25 recall where vocabulary mismatch is severe (e.g., NQ Recall@100 from 0.32 to 0.47). The SESF variant outperformed cross-encoder score fusion by 2.5% on Recall@100 and beat SPLADEv2 and ColBERTv2 by 5.3% and 4.6% on nDCG@10, respectively—all without modifying the BM25 index.
AI.conclusion: CE-QE provides a lightweight, principled method for bridging semantic and lexical retrieval by grounding query expansion in cross-encoder attributions over real passages. It avoids the pitfalls of pseudo-relevance feedback and generative expansion while delivering state-of-the-art hybrid retrieval performance with zero index modification.

title: MAPLE-Guard: Memory-Aware Link Enforcement Against Memory-Link Poisoning in Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables. Includes examples that may be misleading or harmful. Code: https://github.com/xiong-wenjun/MAPLE-Guard
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) increasingly rely on persistent private and shared memories for long-horizon coordination. This memory layer improves continuity, but it also gives attackers a durable channel: a poisoned memory can be written once, continuously retrieved in later tasks, promoted into shared memory, and reused by other agents. A single poisoned write can therefore steer many later decisions and contaminate agents that never saw the original attack, all while no malicious message crosses a visible communication edge at the moment of harm. Further, because existing safeguards mainly inspect prompts, actions, or communication edges, they can miss attacks whose content appears benign at write time but becomes harmful after retrieval. We introduce Memory-Aware Propagation and Link Enforcement Guard, MAPLE-Guard, a memory-link guard for memory-enabled MAS. MAPLE-Guard monitors the memory lifecycle and places gates at write, retrieval, promotion, and cross-agent reuse, so risky memories can be quarantined, unsafe retrievals filtered, and poisoned private memories blocked before they enter shared memory. In the main evaluation, MAPLE-Guard lowers attack success rate (ASR) from 38.2% to 0.9% on LongMemEval and from 34.7% to 0.2% on AppWorld; it also raises multi-agent defense success rate (MDSR) from 54.0% to 74.3% and from 42.5% to 99.8% on the same benchmarks. These results suggest that memory-aware link enforcement covers a gap left by prompt-level and topology-level defenses. Code is available at the link: https://github.com/xiong-wenjun/MAPLE-Guard.

AI.tldr: MAPLE-Guard is a memory-link defense for LLM-based multi-agent systems that monitors the full memory lifecycle (write, retrieval, promotion, cross-agent reuse) to block poisoned memories. It reduces attack success rates from 38.2%→0.9% on LongMemEval and 34.7%→0.2% on AppWorld, while significantly improving multi-agent defense success rates.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems increasingly depend on persistent private and shared memories for long-horizon coordination. This memory layer introduces a durable attack surface: a poisoned memory can be written once, silently persist, be retrieved repeatedly, promoted into shared memory, and contaminate other agents—all without any malicious message crossing a visible communication edge at the moment of harm. Existing defenses that inspect prompts, actions, or communication edges miss attacks whose content appears benign at write time but becomes harmful upon later retrieval.
AI.method: MAPLE-Guard (Memory-Aware Propagation and Link Enforcement Guard) monitors the memory lifecycle and inserts security gates at four critical points: (1) write time, (2) retrieval time, (3) promotion to shared memory, and (4) cross-agent reuse. This allows risky memories to be quarantined, unsafe retrievals to be filtered, and poisoned private memories to be blocked before they propagate into shared memory.
AI.result: On LongMemEval, MAPLE-Guard reduces ASR from 38.2% to 0.9% and improves MDSR from 54.0% to 74.3%. On AppWorld, ASR drops from 34.7% to 0.2% and MDSR rises from 42.5% to 99.8%.
AI.conclusion: Memory-aware link enforcement effectively addresses a critical gap left by prompt-level and topology-level defenses in multi-agent systems. By guarding the memory lifecycle rather than just communication channels or individual prompts, MAPLE-Guard substantially mitigates durable, cross-agent memory poisoning attacks.

title: Optimization and Constraint Modeling using LLMs with a Retrieval Augmented Generation Process
summary: Both optimization modeling and constraint modeling are non-trivial problems requiring deep domain expertise and proficiency in modeling formalism languages. Despite their importance across logistics, healthcare, and supply chain management, current large language models regularly produce structurally inconsistent or incomplete optimization formulations, particularly in combinatorial settings. This paper evaluates whether a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline built on a curated synthetic dataset can meaningfully improve LLM optimization modeling performance. A total of 500 optimization problems were synthesized using seed descriptions from the Text2Zinc dataset and professional personas created using an LLM, specified in JSON and associated with validated Python solver scripts. These problems were encoded in a Chroma vector database. For each inference problem, semantically similar problems were retrieved and used as contextual guidance for a LangChain LLM agent. Three benchmark testbeds were used to evaluate the proposed pipeline under the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model. Accuracy rose from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. The use of semantically validated synthetic examples greatly improves both solution accuracy and structure. The combination of synthetic dataset generation with retrieval augmentation provides an effective alternative to fine-tuning, suggesting that domain-specific synthetic corpora paired with retrieval augmentation can serve as a practical pathway for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts without costly model retraining.

AI.tldr: A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using a curated synthetic dataset of 500 optimization problems significantly boosts LLM performance on optimization modeling, improving accuracy from 40%→72% (NL4OPT), 40%→56% (MAMO Easy), and 32%→56% (MAMO Complex) with Qwen 3 30B, offering a cost-effective alternative to fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Current LLMs struggle to produce structurally consistent and complete optimization formulations, especially for combinatorial problems, despite optimization modeling's critical importance across industries. The authors aim to address this gap without resorting to expensive model fine-tuning.
AI.method: The authors synthesized 500 optimization problems (seeded from Text2Zinc descriptions and LLM-generated professional personas), specified them in JSON with validated Python solver scripts, and embedded them in a Chroma vector database. At inference, semantically similar problems are retrieved and fed as contextual guidance to a LangChain LLM agent. Evaluation uses three benchmarks (NL4OPT, MAMO Easy, MAMO Complex) under the Qwen 3 30B Instruct model.
AI.result: The RAG pipeline improved accuracy from 40% to 72% on NL4OPT, 40% to 56% on MAMO Easy, and 32% to 56% on MAMO Complex. Both solution accuracy and structural consistency improved substantially.
AI.conclusion: Semantically validated synthetic examples combined with retrieval augmentation provide a practical, effective alternative to fine-tuning for deploying LLM-based optimization tools in real-world decision-support contexts, avoiding costly model retraining while achieving meaningful accuracy gains.

title: A Context-Aware Cultural Heritage Guide Powered by LLMs
summary: We present an extension of Triangolazioni (a Cultural Heritage webapp) to enrich curated content with context-dependent, external information provided by Large Language Models (LLMs) within a loosely-coupled architecture agnostic to the LLM. The system supports context-dependent information search and presentation within an architecture agnostic to the exploited LLM.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an extension of the Triangolazioni Cultural Heritage webapp that integrates LLM-generated external information into curated content through a loosely-coupled, LLM-agnostic architecture supporting context-dependent search and presentation.
AI.motivation: To enrich curated cultural heritage content with dynamically retrieved, context-dependent external information without tightly binding the system to any specific Large Language Model.
AI.method: A loosely-coupled architectural extension is employed, decoupling the LLM component from the core Triangolazioni webapp. This enables context-dependent information retrieval and presentation while remaining agnostic to the underlying LLM provider or model.
AI.result: The extended system successfully supports context-dependent information search and presentation within an LLM-agnostic architecture, demonstrating the feasibility of enriching curated cultural heritage content with external, dynamically generated information.
AI.conclusion: Loosely-coupled, LLM-agnostic integration offers a flexible and sustainable approach for augmenting curated Cultural Heritage applications with contextually relevant external knowledge from Large Language Models.

title: BANDMAS: Causality-Inspired Semantic Packet Scheduling for Bandwidth-Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems make decisions based on the aggregated information via exchanging messages across specialized agents. Forwarding every generated message among agents increases application-layer traffic. Yet, it introduces tremendous input tokens for agent processing, potentially raising inference latency and computational overhead. Existing approaches attempt to address the above issues by pruning agents or discarding redundant messages. Nevertheless, such agent-level or message-level optimization results in insufficient evidence supporting for final decisions or still containing redundant message transmissions. To address these challenges, we propose BANDMAS, a multi-agent collaboration framework that models inter-agent communications as task-oriented traffic, which enables efficient transmission via causality-inspired replay valuation. Specifically, we decompose messages into several data packets by analyzing their semantic features such as evidence and requests. The system only transmits these packets if their predicted replay-derived contribution exceeds their resource cost. Consequently, BANDMAS is able to adaptively schedule communication packets while adhering to bandwidth, latency, deadline, and receiver context constraints. On frozen Qwen3-4B traffic across SciFact, HotpotQA, and FanOutQA, our framework reduces application-layer bytes by 53.2\% to 77.3\% at selected caps and attains the highest mean task metric among constrained methods on all three workloads.

AI.tldr: BANDMAS is a multi-agent collaboration framework that treats inter-agent communication as task-oriented traffic, decomposing messages into semantic data packets and transmitting only those whose predicted replay-derived contribution exceeds their resource cost, achieving 53–77% reduction in application-layer bytes while maintaining top task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems forward every generated message among agents, causing excessive application-layer traffic and input token overhead that increases inference latency and computational cost. Prior solutions that prune entire agents or discard messages result in either insufficient evidence for decisions or residual redundancy. A more fine-grained, packet-level optimization is needed.
AI.method: BANDMAS models inter-agent communications as task-oriented traffic. Messages are decomposed into data packets based on semantic features (e.g., evidence, requests). A causality-inspired replay valuation mechanism predicts each packet's contribution to downstream task performance. Packets are transmitted only if their predicted contribution exceeds resource cost, subject to bandwidth, latency, deadline, and receiver context constraints, enabling adaptive communication scheduling.
AI.result: On frozen Qwen3-4B with SciFact, HotpotQA, and FanOutQA workloads, BANDMAS reduces application-layer bytes by 53.2% to 77.3% at selected caps and achieves the highest mean task metric among all constrained methods across all three benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: BANDMAS demonstrates that fine-grained, packet-level semantic scheduling with causality-inspired valuation can substantially reduce multi-agent communication overhead without sacrificing — and even improving — task performance, offering a principled alternative to agent-level or message-level pruning.

title: Memory Reward Inflation in Self-Improving LLM Agents
summary: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly learn from experience without updating any weights. Each episode is stored in an external memory, scored, and retrieved for similar future tasks to shape later behavior. Viewed through a reward lens, the stored score is a proxy reward for an implicit, non-parametric policy. Each retrieved episode then becomes a policy-improvement step whose reliability hinges on how that score is produced. In deployment, ground-truth labels are unavailable, so the stored reward is at best an LLM assessment. This substitution creates a failure mode, the *Echo Gap*, across the memory-based self-improving agents and model families studied. Incorrect episodes receive inflated rewards; thus, the agent preferentially reuses the very mistakes it has most confident in. Because the error compounds through memory rather than averaging out and the confirming judge's errors remain correlated with the original self-grading bias, so it cannot identify which memories are overvalued. The missing property is formalized as the *Error-Independence Assumption* (EIA), which we prove is a *necessary* condition for correcting the inflation, not merely a description of a good verifier: a usable signal must track truth *and* decorrelate its error from the memory bias, and the recoverable payoff is a closed-form function of exactly those two quantities. We further show the inflation compounds not only when retrieval ranks by the stored score but also under plain similarity retrieval which is the regime the deployed agent uses. Finally, the answer-free de-inflation algorithm LUCID delivers a consistent end-to-end gain on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark. It raises execution accuracy to $56.9\%$, above both a Memento-style self-graded agent ($54.0\%$, a $+2.9$-point mean gain across seeds) and a memory-less agent of identical architecture ($52.4\%$).

AI.tldr: Self-improving LLM agents that store scored experiences in memory suffer from an "Echo Gap": erroneous episodes get inflated scores, leading to compounding reuse of mistakes. The authors formalize the necessary Error-Independence Assumption (EIA) for correcting this inflation and propose LUCID, a de-inflation algorithm that yields consistent gains on the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark.
AI.motivation: Memory-based self-improving LLM agents rely on stored scores as proxy rewards, but in deployment, ground-truth labels are absent, forcing reliance on LLM self-assessment. This introduces systematic score inflation for incorrect episodes, causing agents to preferentially retrieve and repeat their most confident mistakes. The authors aim to formally characterize and mitigate this failure mode.
AI.method: The paper formalizes the Echo Gap failure mode, where self-grading bias inflates stored rewards, and proves the Error-Independence Assumption (EIA) as a necessary condition for correction. They derive the recoverable payoff as a closed-form function of truth-tracking and error decorrelation. They further demonstrate that inflation compounds under both score-based and similarity-based retrieval. The proposed algorithm, LUCID, performs answer-free de-inflation by decorrelating judge error from memory bias.
AI.result: On the BIRD text-to-SQL benchmark, LUCID achieves 56.9% execution accuracy, outperforming a Memento-style self-graded agent (54.0%, +2.9-point mean gain across seeds) and an identical memory-less agent (52.4%).
AI.conclusion: The Echo Gap is a fundamental failure mode in memory-based self-improving agents caused by correlated self-grading errors. The EIA is necessary for correction, and LUCID provides a practical, answer-free de-inflation method that yields consistent end-to-end improvements.

title: PHA-Net: Prototype-based Hierarchical Alignment Network for Text-Video Retrieval
summary: With the emergence of large-scale image-text pre-training models, e.g., CLIP, text-video retrieval has experienced substantial advances in recent years. Existing best-performing methods involve aligning cross-modal semantics at individual, local, and global levels simultaneously, raising concerns about the intrinsic semantic mismatch between concise texts and rich videos. A canonical approach is to integrate multiple language-video attention modules into the hierarchical framework while this paradigm only optimizes visual representations with prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a new prototype-based hierarchical alignment network (PHA-Net) to align individual/local/global level representations across modalities. Concretely, we introduce multiple modality-shared prototypes as the bridge to efficiently optimize text and video representations for cross-modal alignment. Then, we argue that the imbalanced semantic distribution in clustered tokens may undermine retrieval performance, as tokens with weak semantics are of little interest. To reduce the impact of these tokens, a proposed prototype-supported token merge module is responsible for enhancing tokens with strong semantics and suppressing others with weak semantics via prototype semantics guidance. Moreover, we devise a prototype contrastive loss to encourage textual and visual prototypes to focus on different semantic information. The idea of this auxiliary loss is to ensure higher similarity between textual and visual prototypes from the same prototype than those from different prototypes. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our PHA-Net, which achieves significant improvements in the sum of all recalls on MSR-VTT (8.8%), ActivityNet (19.2%), VATEX (0.7%), and Charades (4.9%). Code is available at https://github.com/JingXiaolun/PHA-Net.

AI.tldr: PHA-Net introduces modality-shared prototypes to efficiently align text and video representations at individual, local, and global levels, addressing semantic mismatch and computational inefficiency in text-video retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing text-video retrieval methods align cross-modal semantics at multiple granularities but suffer from (1) intrinsic semantic mismatch between concise text and rich video, (2) prohibitive computational costs from multiple attention modules, and (3) imbalanced semantic distributions where weak-semantic tokens degrade retrieval performance.
AI.method: PHA-Net uses modality-shared prototypes as bridges for efficient cross-modal alignment at individual/local/global levels. A prototype-supported token merge module enhances strong-semantic tokens and suppresses weak ones via prototype guidance. A prototype contrastive loss enforces higher similarity between textual and visual prototypes from the same prototype than from different ones.
AI.result: PHA-Net achieves significant sum-of-recalls improvements: MSR-VTT (+8.8%), ActivityNet (+19.2%), VATEX (+0.7%), and Charades (+4.9%) across four benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The prototype-based hierarchical alignment framework effectively and efficiently bridges the text-video semantic gap, outperforming prior methods while reducing computational overhead.

title: MDGAM-Based Cooperative Task Scheduling for Communication-Constrained Distributed Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Cooperative task scheduling in communication-constrained distributed multi-agent systems is challenging because each agent must make decisions from partial and dynamic observations while satisfying complex practical constraints. Existing heuristics rely on handcrafted bidding rules and repeated consensus, whereas many learning-based methods assume global observations and lack explicit communication-based coordination. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a neural scheduling framework for distributed multi-robot task allocation (MRTA), consisting of a multi-decoder graph attention model (MDGAM) policy model and a critic-free group relative multi-agent policy gradient (GRMAPG) training algorithm. MDGAM uses an extended graph attention mechanism to jointly update node and edge features, and employs multiple decoders to generate task-selection decisions and communication messages. GRMAPG constructs group-relative advantages from equivalent task-planning instances to replace the critic network used in conventional MARL algorithms, thereby reducing training difficulty and improving convergence performance. Experiments under different problem scales and communication ranges show that the proposed method improves task-completion performance over existing heuristic and learning-based methods, while ablation, complexity, and generalization tests further validate the proposed innovations.

AI.tldr: A neural scheduling framework for distributed multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) that uses a multi-decoder graph attention model (MDGAM) with a critic-free training algorithm (GRMAPG), achieving superior performance over existing heuristic and learning-based methods under communication constraints.
AI.motivation: Cooperative task scheduling in communication-constrained distributed multi-agent systems is difficult because agents operate on partial, dynamic observations under complex constraints. Existing heuristic methods rely on handcrafted bidding rules and repeated consensus, while learning-based methods often assume global observations and lack explicit communication-based coordination.
AI.method: The paper proposes (1) MDGAM: a multi-decoder graph attention model that uses an extended graph attention mechanism to jointly update node and edge features, with multiple decoders generating both task-selection decisions and communication messages; and (2) GRMAPG: a critic-free group relative multi-agent policy gradient algorithm that constructs group-relative advantages from equivalent task-planning instances, replacing the critic network to reduce training difficulty and improve convergence.
AI.result: The proposed method improves task-completion performance over existing heuristic and learning-based methods across different problem scales and communication ranges. Ablation, complexity, and generalization tests further validate the proposed innovations.
AI.conclusion: The MDGAM-GRMAPG framework effectively addresses distributed MRTA under communication constraints by combining graph-based joint node-edge attention with a critic-free multi-agent policy gradient approach, demonstrating both superior performance and robust generalization.

title: Request-Level Energy Attribution for Batched LLM Serving
summary: Batched LLM serving improves throughput but complicates energy accounting. GPU power telemetry is aggregate, whereas sustainability reporting, chargeback, and workload analysis often require request-level energy charges. Existing inference-energy benchmarks report model-, phase-, or token-level energy, and recent carbon-accounting work motivates Shapley fairness conceptually. Neither provides measured request-level ground truth, so how far the accounting rules used in practice deviate from a fair allocation has remained unknown. We present JouleShare, an attribution framework with two components. An offline harness establishes this ground truth by replaying request subsets under vLLM with a reproducible protocol, integrating GPU power telemetry, and computing exact Shapley energy for each request. A lightweight calibration model, JCalib, then learns to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features for use at serving time. Across 16 model/workload runs, token-proportional attribution differs from exact Shapley by 0.440 normalized L1 on average under static batching and by 0.458 under continuous batching, a gap that reproduces across three data-center GPUs. JCalib reduces this error to 0.116 under static batching and 0.177 under continuous batching, below even a standalone-measurement baseline that is unavailable online, while preserving exact batch-energy efficiency. Sampled Shapley extends the measured reference to larger group sizes, where the gap persists and a single offline calibration remains the most accurate deployable rule. The results show that token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution, and that measured Shapley ground truth can calibrate low-cost request features toward fairer attribution.

AI.tldr: JouleShare establishes ground-truth Shapley-value energy attribution for batched LLM requests and shows that token-proportional accounting deviates significantly from fairness; a learned calibration model (JCalib) significantly reduces this error using cheap request features at serving time.
AI.motivation: Batched LLM serving aggregates GPU power telemetry, making per-request energy attribution opaque. Existing methods rely on token-proportional heuristics without measured ground truth, so the fairness gap between practical accounting rules and a theoretically fair allocation (Shapley) has been unknown.
AI.method: JouleShare comprises: (1) an offline harness that replays request subsets under vLLM with reproducible protocols, collects GPU power telemetry, and computes exact Shapley energy per request; (2) JCalib, a lightweight calibration model trained to predict Shapley shares from cheap request features (e.g., token counts, latency) for online use. Sampled Shapley extends the measured reference to larger group sizes.
AI.result: Token-proportional attribution deviates from exact Shapley by 0.440 normalized L1 (static batching) and 0.458 (continuous batching) across 16 model/workload runs and three GPU types. JCalib reduces error to 0.116 (static) and 0.177 (continuous), outperforming even an offline-only standalone-measurement baseline while preserving batch-energy efficiency. The gap persists at larger group sizes where sampled Shapley reference and offline calibration remain most accurate.
AI.conclusion: Token attribution is not a reliable proxy for marginal energy under batched execution. Measured Shapley ground truth can effectively calibrate low-cost request features to achieve fairer and deployable request-level energy attribution.

title: GARDRec: Decision-Level Graph Grounding for Large Language Model Recommendation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for recommendation by interpreting item descriptions, user instructions, and external knowledge through natural-language prompts. However, existing graph-augmented LLM recommenders often use knowledge graphs mainly as prompt-level evidence, leaving ranking decisions weakly constrained by structured user-item relations. This is problematic for next-item recommendation, where the model must compare candidates under the same user context while preserving temporal preference, collaborative signals, and attribute matches. To address this issue, we propose \emph{GARDRec}, a Graph-grounded Adaptive Reasoning and Decision-aware Recommendation framework for LLM-based next-item ranking. GARDRec constructs semantic-structural item representations from textual node features and graph propagation, derives personalized graph contexts from temporally weighted histories and first-order neighborhoods, and aligns graph-derived representations with a frozen LLM through continuous multimodal prompts. Explicit interaction and matching features are injected through late-stage decision branches, while inter-candidate attention and restricted generative likelihood support final ranking. Experiments on three public benchmarks with multiple LLM backbones show that GARDRec generally improves candidate-ranking performance over representative baselines. Ablation and diagnostic analyses verify the contributions of graph projection, neighborhood retrieval, explicit decision features, ranking loss, and generative calibration.

AI.tldr: GARDRec is an LLM-based next-item recommendation framework that grounds recommendations in graph-derived user-item relations through continuous multimodal prompts and explicit decision branches, improving ranking over prompt-only graph LLM methods.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-augmented LLM recommenders use knowledge graphs only as prompt-level evidence, leaving ranking weakly constrained by structured user-item relations. This is problematic for next-item recommendation, which requires comparing candidates under the same user context while preserving temporal preferences, collaborative signals, and attribute matches.
AI.method: GARDRec constructs semantic-structural item representations via textual node features and graph propagation, derives personalized graph contexts from temporally weighted histories and first-order neighborhoods, aligns graph representations with a frozen LLM through continuous multimodal prompts, and injects explicit interaction/matching features via late-stage decision branches. Inter-candidate attention and restricted generative likelihood support final ranking.
AI.result: Experiments on three public benchmarks with multiple LLM backbones show GARDRec generally improves candidate-ranking performance over representative baselines. Ablation and diagnostic analyses verify contributions of graph projection, neighborhood retrieval, explicit decision features, ranking loss, and generative calibration.
AI.conclusion: GARDRec demonstrates that structurally grounding LLM-based recommenders with graph-derived representations, rather than using graphs merely as prompts, yields consistent ranking improvements for next-item recommendation.

title: HIERA: Hierarchical Multi-Agent Relevance Assessment for Content Discovery Systems
summary: Content discovery systems depend on relevance judgment for search quality evaluation, but human annotation faces inter-annotator disagreement and scaling costs. While Large Language Models show promise as automated assessors, current approaches rely on flat aggregation strategies: single-step prompting, voting ensembles, or uncoordinated multi-agent pipelines that aggregate independent outputs without integration. We propose HIERA, a hierarchical multi-agent relevance assessment framework with four specialized agents: a Relevance Judge, Query Analyzer, Item Analyzer, and Relation Analyzer. The Judge determines when specialist analysis is needed; the Relation Analyzer then coordinates query and item analyses with external knowledge to establish relevance relationships for final judgment. Ablation studies show that the same agents and external knowledge without hierarchical coordination degrade performance, confirming that the coordination structure itself accounts for the improvement. Evaluation across five datasets (EVS, MSRD, ESCI, WANDS, Home Depot) shows improvements over 11 baselines: 10.2\% on Home Depot, 4.8\% on ESCI, and up to 38\% on EVS ($p < 0.05$). Hierarchical coordination yields 12.7\% improvement over uncoordinated collaboration using identical agents.

AI.tldr: HIERA proposes a hierarchical multi-agent framework for automated relevance assessment, where a Relevance Judge dynamically delegates to specialized analyzers coordinated by a Relation Analyzer, outperforming flat aggregation baselines by 4.8–38% across five datasets.
AI.motivation: Human relevance annotation for search evaluation suffers from inter-annotator disagreement and scalability issues. Existing LLM-based approaches use flat aggregation (single-step prompting, voting, uncoordinated multi-agent pipelines) that lack structured integration of specialized analyses, limiting assessment quality.
AI.method: HIERA employs four specialized agents: (1) Relevance Judge that decides when specialist analysis is needed, (2) Query Analyzer, (3) Item Analyzer, and (4) Relation Analyzer that coordinates query and item analyses with external knowledge to establish relevance relationships for the final judgment. The key innovation is the hierarchical coordination structure rather than flat aggregation.
AI.result: HIERA achieves improvements over 11 baselines across five datasets: 10.2% on Home Depot, 4.8% on ESCI, and up to 38% on EVS (p < 0.05). Hierarchical coordination yields a 12.7% improvement over uncoordinated collaboration using identical agents, confirmed by ablation studies.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical coordination structure, rather than the agents or external knowledge alone, drives the performance gains. Structured, coordinated multi-agent collaboration is a superior paradigm for automated relevance assessment compared to flat aggregation strategies.

title: Skillsets on the Chain: A Blockchain-based Zero-Trust Framework for Agentic AI Networking
comment: Accepted at IEEE Transactions on Cognitive Communications and Networking
summary: Agentic AI networking (AgentNet) systems rely heavily on third-party skillset implementations and distributed multi-agent collaboration, yet they face major claim-to-capability inconsistencies and security vulnerabilities under trust-by-declaration assumptions. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes TrustAgentNet, a dual-tier blockchain-secured zero-trust framework. Specifically, a global Chain of Skillsets (CoS) governs the lifecycle of skillset metadata with protocols empowered by specialized agents to enforce off-chain auditing while maintaining lightweight on-chain cryptographic consensus. Furthermore, transient, task-oriented Chains of Collaboration (CoC) are dynamically established to enable trustless distributed multi-agent collaboration. Theoretical analysis of the three-way trade-off among security level, task performance, and resource overhead is provided and empirically validated. Experimental results on a hardware prototype demonstrate that compared with no-blockchain trust-by-default baselines, the zero-trust overhead of TrustAgentNet is dominated by off-chain inference, while the blockchain layer incurs minor ledger costs via the ledger-IPFS storage and on/off-chain integration design. Crucially, the proposed verification pipeline achieves a flawless 100% accuracy across 50 AI models, correctly validating 40 honest skillsets and intercepting 10 adversarial ones, and generalizes to non-AI domains with an 83.91% accuracy and a 0.85 F1-score across 1478 features from 171 ClawHub skills. Adversarial experiments further show that TrustAgentNet enables autonomous skillset self-recovery against various malicious attacks.

AI.tldr: TrustAgentNet proposes a dual-tier blockchain framework to enforce zero-trust security in agentic AI networking, combining a global Chain of Skillsets for lifecycle governance and transient Chains of Collaboration for trustless multi-agent coordination, achieving 100% adversarial detection accuracy on AI models.
AI.motivation: Existing Agentic AI networking (AgentNet) systems suffer from claim-to-capability inconsistencies and security vulnerabilities due to trust-by-declaration assumptions, where third-party skillsets are implicitly trusted without verification, creating risks in distributed multi-agent collaboration.
AI.method: A dual-tier blockchain framework: (1) Chain of Skillsets (CoS) — a global blockchain layer governing skillset metadata lifecycle with specialized agents performing off-chain auditing and on-chain cryptographic consensus; (2) Chains of Collaboration (CoC) — transient, task-oriented blockchains dynamically established for trustless distributed multi-agent collaboration. The design integrates ledger-IPFS storage and on/off-chain integration to minimize blockchain overhead. A three-way trade-off analysis among security, task performance, and resource overhead is provided.
AI.result: The verification pipeline achieves 100% accuracy across 50 AI models (40 honest, 10 adversarial correctly classified). On non-AI domains, it attains 83.91% accuracy and 0.85 F1-score across 1478 features from 171 ClawHub skills. Blockchain overhead is minor due to ledger-IPFS and on/off-chain integration, with zero-trust overhead dominated by off-chain inference. The system demonstrates autonomous skillset self-recovery against malicious attacks.
AI.conclusion: TrustAgentNet effectively bridges the security gap in AgentNet systems by replacing trust-by-declaration with cryptographically enforced zero-trust verification, achieving high detection accuracy with acceptable resource overhead, and generalizing beyond AI-specific domains.

title: Textro: A Prototyping Toolkit for Solderless and Chipless Smart Textile Interfaces
summary: In this paper, we present Textro, a prototyping toolkit for designing, fabricating, and testing solderless and chipless smart textile interfaces. Unlike prior approaches that rely on rigid components or soldered connections, Textro enables users to build functional textile interfaces using only readily available materials and tools. The toolkit integrates three parts: (1) a web-based design environment for importing sewing patterns, defining sensing elements, and automatically generating optimized component and circuit designs based on empirical experiments; (2) a fabrication pipeline that generates fabrication files for embroidery and cutting machines, with embroidery optimized for one-stroke continuous stitching paths and components assembled through glue-based attachment methods via capacitive coupling; and (3) a reader device and software for wirelessly retrieving sensor data and visualizing real-time sensor signals. We demonstrate Textro through four application examples and conduct a user study with fashion experts, makers, and novices, highlighting its usability and potential for smart textile prototyping.

AI.tldr: Textro is a prototyping toolkit for designing, fabricating, and testing solderless, chipless smart textile interfaces using only common materials and tools, integrating a web-based design tool, optimized embroidery fabrication, and wireless sensor data retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing smart textile interfaces depend on rigid electronic components or soldered connections, which limit flexibility, accessibility, and ease of prototyping. Textro aims to democratize smart textile creation by eliminating these constraints.
AI.method: The toolkit comprises three integrated parts: (1) a web-based design environment for importing sewing patterns, defining sensors, and auto-generating optimized circuit/component designs grounded in empirical experiments; (2) a fabrication pipeline producing embroidery and cutting machine files, featuring one-stroke continuous stitching optimization and glue-based component attachment via capacitive coupling; (3) a reader device and companion software for wireless sensor data retrieval and real-time visualization. Evaluated through four application examples and a user study with fashion experts, makers, and novices.
AI.result: The system successfully produced functional smart textile interfaces across four application examples. A user study with fashion experts, makers, and novices demonstrated the toolkit's usability and highlighted its potential for accessible smart textile prototyping.
AI.conclusion: Textro lowers the barrier to smart textile prototyping by enabling solderless, chipless fabrication using commonly available materials. The toolkit's integrated design-to-fabrication pipeline shows strong potential for adoption among diverse user groups, from novices to domain experts.

title: Motif-Mamba: network motif improved mamba for long-range sequence modeling
comment: 9 pages of main text, 8 pages of appendix, 6 figures. Submitted to NeurIPS 2026
summary: Efficient long-sequence modeling remains a central challenge for large language models, as self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length. Mamba offers a linear-time alternative through selective state space recurrence, but its predominantly diagonal state transitions restrict explicit interactions among state dimensions. We propose Motif-Mamba, a structured state space model that augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway. Inspired by the dynamics of three-node network motifs, the proposed pathway projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace, imposes motif-guided interactions, and maps the resulting dynamics back to the original state space. This design enhances cross-dimensional communication while preserving the linear-time recurrent structure of Mamba. Experiments on long-sequence extrapolation, language modeling benchmarks, and brain--computer interface decoding show consistent improvements over Mamba backbones, suggesting that motif-guided low-rank dynamics provide an effective structural prior for long-range sequence modeling.

AI.tldr: Motif-Mamba augments Mamba with a motif-constrained low-rank recurrent pathway inspired by three-node network motifs, improving cross-dimensional state interactions while preserving linear-time complexity. It shows consistent gains on long-sequence modeling, language benchmarks, and brain-computer interface decoding.
AI.motivation: Mamba's selective state space recurrence enables linear-time sequence modeling, but its predominantly diagonal state transition matrices restrict explicit interactions across state dimensions, limiting representational capacity for long-range dependencies.
AI.method: Motif-Mamba introduces a low-rank recurrent pathway that projects hidden states into a compact dynamical subspace, applies motif-guided interactions derived from three-node network motifs, and maps the resulting dynamics back to the original state space, all while maintaining Mamba's linear-time recurrent structure.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over Mamba backbones are demonstrated on long-sequence extrapolation tasks, standard language modeling benchmarks, and brain-computer interface decoding applications.
AI.conclusion: Motif-guided low-rank dynamics serve as an effective structural prior for enhancing long-range sequence modeling, suggesting that incorporating biologically-inspired network motifs into state space models is a promising direction.

title: A Triple-Robustness Analysis of Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-Hop Requirements Traceability
summary: Reported verdicts on GraphRAG versus vector RAG disagree, and the evidence is typically tied to a single corpus, embedder, and judge -- and, we show, to where citation quality is measured. We present a triple-robustness analysis that holds a five-pipeline architecture matrix fixed and varies embedder (local e5-small vs. Azure text-embedding-3-small), corpus (DO-178C typed-edge requirements vs. Wikipedia paragraph chains via MuSiQue), and judge (paired GPT-5.4 x GPT-4.1 on both corpora), over 2x4,440 main-matrix runs, 600 cross-corpus runs, and over 5,000 faithfulness judgments. (C2a) GraphRAG's graph walk floods the context window at precision 0.12-0.23, but the synthesizer cites selectively at precision 0.48-0.65; scoring the retrieved set as the attribution set inverts the architecture ranking, which reconciles part of the disagreement in prior reports. (C1) Answer-level citation winners are corpus- and stratum-conditional but embedder-robust: GraphRAG ties vanilla on short-hop DO-178C queries and wins every MuSiQue stratum, while agentic pipelines lead only on 3+-hop requirements queries. (C2b) Faithfulness is corpus-conditional: on DO-178C it declines with hop distance (trend p<0.05 in three of four judge x embedder combinations); on Wikipedia chains neither judge shows a collapse. (C3) Single-judge LLM faithfulness is fragile to retrieval state: GPT-5.4's self-kappa across embedders is 0.137 (41% verdict change) against a same-day test-retest floor of 0.76, and re-judging frozen inputs eleven weeks later gives kappa <= 0.14 for both judges. A learned router on dense embeddings alone reaches macro-F1 0.86 on hop classification (C4). We argue that RAG architecture claims should be tested at this level of robustness -- including robustness to the citation-measurement point -- before they are trusted.

AI.tldr: A triple-robustness analysis comparing GraphRAG vs. vector RAG across multiple embedders, corpora, and judges reveals that citation quality depends heavily on where it is measured (retrieved set vs. synthesizer output), that GraphRAG's advantage is corpus- and query-stratum-conditional but embedder-robust, and that single-judge LLM faithfulness evaluations are fragile, with low self-consistency over time and across embedders.
AI.motivation: Prior comparisons of GraphRAG versus vector RAG yield conflicting verdicts, but these studies typically vary only one component at a time (single corpus, single embedder, single judge) and fail to account for where citation quality is measured. The authors aim to reconcile these disagreements through a rigorous, multi-factor robustness analysis.
AI.method: The authors fix a five-pipeline architecture matrix and systematically vary (1) embedder: local e5-small vs. Azure text-embedding-3-small, (2) corpus: DO-178C typed-edge requirements vs. Wikipedia paragraph chains (MuSiQue), and (3) judge: paired GPT-5.4 × GPT-4.1. They run 2×4,440 main-matrix experiments, 600 cross-corpus runs, and over 5,000 faithfulness judgments. They also introduce a learned router on dense embeddings for hop classification and assess judge reliability via same-day test-retest and eleven-week re-judging of frozen inputs.
AI.result: Key findings: (C2a) GraphRAG's graph walk retrieves at precision 0.12–0.23 but the synthesizer cites selectively at 0.48–0.65; measuring attribution at the retrieved set reverses architecture rankings, reconciling prior disagreements. (C1) Answer-level citation winners are conditionally dependent on corpus and query stratum but robust to embedder choice: GraphRAG ties vanilla RAG on short-hop DO-178C queries, wins every MuSiQue stratum, while agentic pipelines lead only on 3+-hop requirements queries. (C2b) Faithfulness declines with hop distance on DO-178C (trend p<0.05 in 3/4 judge×embedder combinations) but not on Wikipedia chains. (C3) Judge reliability is poor: GPT-5.4 self-kappa across embedders is 0.137 (41% verdict change) vs. 0.76 test-retest floor; eleven-week re-judging yields κ ≤ 0.14 for both judges. (C4) A learned router on dense embeddings achieves macro-F1 0.86 on hop classification.
AI.conclusion: RAG architecture claims should be validated through multi-dimensional robustness testing — including robustness to the citation-measurement point — before being considered trustworthy. Single-judge LLM faithfulness evaluations are insufficiently reliable for drawing definitive conclusions.

title: Stress-Relief Annealing: Polynomial-Time Simulation-Free Layout Optimization for Automated Warehouses
summary:
We study the problem of optimizing physical layouts for automated warehouses, where hundreds to thousands of robots are coordinated to transport packages. Previous works have shown that optimizing the warehouse layout (e.g., the physical location of the storage shelves) significantly improves throughput. However, state-of-the-art layout optimization approaches are based on evolutionary optimization methods, which treat the entire warehouse as a black box and rely on random mutation to search for high-quality layouts. While the optimization outcomes are promising, these methods require a massive number of simulations to evaluate candidate solutions, making them sample-inefficient. In this paper, we present Stress-Relief Annealing (SRA), a polynomial-time simulation-free layout optimization algorithm. SRA turns the task demand into a per-vertex \emph{stress field} that predicts where traffic will concentrate in the warehouse; the field's peak provably caps the throughput.
  Our experimental results show that (1) SRA improves both the throughput and the scalability of a human-designed warehouse, roughly doubling the number of robots it can sustain, (2) it matches or exceeds the throughput of the evolutionary baselines while taking only $19$ minutes on one CPU core, against their $25{,}000$ simulations and $25$ hours on a $64$-core machine, and (3) the gain generalizes across different Multi-Agent Path Finding algorithms, non-uniform task demands, and a warehouse with doubled dimensions.

AI.tldr: SRA is a polynomial-time, simulation-free algorithm for optimizing warehouse layouts. It uses a per-vertex stress field derived from task demand to predict traffic bottlenecks, achieving throughput matching or exceeding evolutionary methods in minutes rather than thousands of simulations.
AI.motivation: Current layout optimization for automated warehouses relies on evolutionary algorithms that treat the warehouse as a black box, requiring massive numbers of simulations (tens of thousands) and heavy compute (e.g., 25 hours on 64 cores). This sample inefficiency makes them impractical for rapid design iteration and large-scale deployment.
AI.method: Stress-Relief Annealing (SRA) converts task demand into a per-vertex stress field that predicts traffic concentration. The field's peak provably bounds throughput, allowing SRA to optimize layouts in polynomial time without running any simulations. It uses annealing to iteratively relieve stress hotspots.
AI.result: SRA doubles the sustainable robot count of a human-designed warehouse. It matches or exceeds evolutionary baselines in throughput while taking only 19 minutes on a single CPU core, versus 25,000 simulations over 25 hours on 64 cores. Gains generalize across different MAPF algorithms, non-uniform demand, and doubled warehouse dimensions.
AI.conclusion: SRA provides a principled, simulation-free alternative to black-box evolutionary layout optimization, offering dramatic improvements in both computational efficiency and layout quality for automated warehouses.

title: Deep Learning for Cyber Threat Detection and Mitigation in Healthcare-IoT
comment: PhD thesis, University of Limerick, 2026. 357 pages. Supervisors: Dr. Lubna Luxmi Dhirani and Prof. Ciarán Eising
summary: Cybersecurity is a fundamental requirement for protecting wearable devices used in healthcare Internet of Things (H-IoT) systems. Security failures in these resource-constrained systems directly compromise patient safety. Physiological data and network traffic are frequent targets of cyberattacks in H-IoT environments. To address these risks, deep learning-based cybersecurity mechanisms for H-IoT often involve complex architectures with large parameter counts. Existing datasets are also rarely assessed for quality, limiting their applicability. However, this research addresses these challenges by developing multiple realistic datasets and proposing lightweight deep learning models, namely the Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and Residual TCN (Res-TCN), for H-IoT. It includes two binary classification datasets for Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks and a multiclass dataset representing Selective Forwarding (SF), Man-in-the-Middle (MITM), and DDoS attacks. The datasets UL-ECE-MQTT-DDoS-H-IoT2025 and UL-ECE-UDP-DDoS-H-IoT2025 are generated in Cooja and ns-3 to capture transmission behaviours and protocol variations. The third dataset, UL-ECE-MultiAttack-H-IoT2025, integrates physiological and network features to represent multiple cyber threats in H-IoT. Building on this, the TCN model is designed to detect and mitigate DDoS attacks over the MQTT and UDP-based datasets. It incorporates a monitoring frequency-based detection mechanism and a dynamic threshold-based mitigation strategy. To enable edge deployment, the model is quantised and converted into TensorFlow Lite (TFLite) for real-time DDoS detection on Raspberry Pi 4, achieving low latency and power-efficient operation in H-IoT. This thesis establishes a deep learning-based cybersecurity defence mechanism encompassing realistic dataset generation, lightweight model design, and edge deployment for securing H-IoT systems.

AI.tldr: This thesis proposes lightweight Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and Residual TCN (Res-TCN) models for cybersecurity in healthcare IoT, supported by three newly developed realistic datasets (two binary DDoS, one multiclass multi-attack). It further demonstrates edge deployment on Raspberry Pi 4 via quantised TFLite models, achieving real-time, low-latency, power-efficient attack detection and mitigation.
AI.motivation: Healthcare IoT (H-IoT) wearable devices are resource-constrained and highly vulnerable to cyberattacks (e.g., DDoS, SF, MITM) that directly threaten patient safety. Existing deep learning-based defences use overly complex architectures with large parameter counts and rely on datasets of unverified quality, limiting practical deployment and generalisability.
AI.method: The work (1) generates three realistic H-IoT datasets — UL-ECE-MQTT-DDoS-H-IoT2025 (Cooja), UL-ECE-UDP-DDoS-H-IoT2025 (ns-3), and UL-ECE-MultiAttack-H-IoT2025 (combining physiological and network features) — covering DDoS, Selective Forwarding, and MITM attacks. (2) It designs lightweight TCN and Res-TCN models for DDoS detection with a monitoring frequency-based detection mechanism and a dynamic threshold-based mitigation strategy. (3) The models are quantised and converted to TensorFlow Lite for real-time edge deployment on Raspberry Pi 4.
