AI.result: The TCN and Res-TCN models achieve effective detection and mitigation of DDoS attacks over both MQTT and UDP datasets. Edge deployment on Raspberry Pi 4 demonstrates low latency and power-efficient operation suitable for real-time H-IoT environments.
AI.conclusion: The thesis establishes a complete deep learning-based cybersecurity defence framework for H-IoT, spanning realistic dataset generation, lightweight model design, and practical edge deployment — addressing critical gaps in dataset quality, model complexity, and real-world applicability.

title: ReVoicer: Conversational Voice Annotation for Human-Centered, LLM-Assisted Peer Review
summary: We present ReVoicer, a prototype system that supports peer reviewers by letting them converse with a paper as they read it. The reviewer highlights a passage and speaks (or types) a train-of-thought comment. A large language model then cleans the comment using the surrounding prose as context, tags it by comment type, and anchors it to the passage. After the reviewer finishes reading, ReVoicer checks the accumulated notes against a venue-specific rubric, reports coverage gaps, and drafts a review composed only from the reviewer's own comments, written to a style guide distilled from the reviewer's past reviews. The system introduces no critiques of its own. We describe the system's design rationale and implementation, and we outline plans for future evaluations. With the ISMAR community, we will gather feedback and discuss the system design and ideas for additional features and evaluations.

AI.tldr: ReVoicer is a prototype review-support system that lets peer reviewers annotate papers conversationally via voice or text, then auto-generates a structured review from their comments while flagging coverage gaps against a venue-specific rubric.
AI.motivation: Peer reviewing is cognitively demanding and time-consuming. Reviewers often produce unstructured notes while reading and must later reconstruct a coherent review, which can lead to incomplete coverage, inconsistency, and inefficiency. The authors aim to reduce this friction without introducing AI-generated critiques.
AI.method: ReVoicer integrates three stages: (1) During reading, the reviewer highlights passages and speaks/typing train-of-thought comments; an LLM cleans each comment using surrounding text as context, classifies it by type, and anchors it to the passage. (2) After reading, the system checks accumulated comments against a venue-specific rubric and reports coverage gaps. (3) It drafts a review composed solely from the reviewer's own comments, styled according to a guide distilled from the reviewer's prior reviews.
AI.result: The paper describes the system's design rationale and implementation, with plans for future evaluations. No empirical results are reported; the contribution is a system prototype and design framework.
AI.conclusion: ReVoicer demonstrates a novel approach to AI-assisted peer review that preserves reviewer agency by never introducing its own critiques. The authors plan to gather feedback from the ISMAR community to refine features and evaluation strategies.

title: Nova: An End-to-End MLIR Compiler for Deep Learning
summary: The performance of deep learning models at scale relies heavily on how effectively high-level mathematical operations are mapped to underlying physical hardware. While high-level tensor frameworks provide flexible abstractions for model design, their eager execution models inherently lack the whole-graph visibility and granular control over hardware and memory required to maximize physical hardware utilization natively. To bridge this gap, we designed Nova, an automated end-to-end JIT compiler whose defining purpose is to achieve absolute control over this hardware mapping: fusing operations across operation boundaries, optimizing complex memory hierarchies, and tuning execution down to the register level. By capturing eager executions and unifying forward and backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect, Nova unlocks aggressive whole-graph optimizations. It then utilizes an Analytic Configurator to deterministically derive optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity, dropping search time to zero. Backed by a structural hashing runtime, Nova synthesizes fine-grained kernels directly from the computation's structure. In our evaluations on an RTX 3060, Nova matches or modestly exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matmuls on most shapes, maintaining a stringent < 5e-4 relative error. At the model level, Nova achieves up to 10.6% greater throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% greater than XLA on a 42-million parameter model, without compromising on numerical fidelity. Crucially, by reducing the memory footprint by up to 29% relative to PyTorch, Nova successfully trains a 144-million parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch encounters Out-Of-Memory (OOM) failures on the same 12 GB consumer GPU.

AI.tldr: Nova is an end-to-end JIT compiler that captures eager executions, unifies forward/backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect, and uses an Analytic Configurator for zero-search-time optimal scheduling. It matches or exceeds cuBLAS/XLA on matmuls, achieves up to 10.6% higher throughput than PyTorch, reduces memory footprint by up to 29%, and trains a 144M-parameter model where PyTorch runs out of memory on a 12 GB GPU.
AI.motivation: High-level tensor frameworks like PyTorch use eager execution, which lacks whole-graph visibility and fine-grained hardware/memory control. This leads to suboptimal hardware utilization, excessive memory consumption, and missed opportunities for cross-operation fusion. The authors aim to bridge the gap between flexible high-level abstractions and peak physical hardware efficiency through a compiler that achieves absolute control over hardware mapping.
AI.method: Nova operates as an automated end-to-end JIT compiler with four key components: (1) capturing eager executions and unifying forward/backward passes into a single value-semantic dialect for whole-graph optimization; (2) fusing operations across boundaries and optimizing memory hierarchies down to the register level; (3) an Analytic Configurator that deterministically derives optimal execution schedules based on arithmetic intensity, eliminating search time; and (4) a structural hashing runtime that synthesizes fine-grained kernels directly from computation structure.
AI.result: On an RTX 3060: Nova matches or modestly exceeds cuBLAS and XLA on TF32 matrix multiplications across most shapes with <5e-4 relative error. At the model level, Nova delivers up to 10.6% higher throughput than PyTorch and 4.4% higher than XLA on a 42M-parameter model. Memory footprint is reduced by up to 29% vs. PyTorch, enabling training of a 144M-parameter model at 17,900 tokens/s where PyTorch suffers OOM failures on the same 12 GB consumer GPU.
AI.conclusion: Nova demonstrates that whole-graph compilation with analytic (non-search-based) scheduling can achieve competitive or superior performance to hand-tuned libraries and existing compilers while significantly reducing memory pressure, enabling larger model training on resource-constrained hardware without sacrificing numerical fidelity.

title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Optimization for Generative Recommendations
comment: 12 pages, 6 figures, 10 tables. Accepted at KDD 2026 Research Track
summary: Generative recommenders select items by autoregressively decoding semantic identifiers (SIDs), whose token positions induce a coarse-to-fine hierarchy over the item space. In practice, SID decoders are trained via supervised next-token prediction, which imitates logged trajectories rather than directly optimizing downstream utility. This motivates post-training with outcome feedback to guide decoding toward higher utility. However, logged feedback is only observed for the final exposed item, causing most post-training methods to operate at the item level and broadcast the same terminal signal across all SID tokens. As a result, token-level credit assignment becomes sparse, high-variance, and layer-dependent. To this end, we propose Hierarchical Residual Policy Optimization (HRPO), a post-training framework that converts item-level outcomes into dense, token-aligned learning signals for conservative token-wise improvement. Specifically, HRPO first estimates SID prefix-level utilities via group-wise reward smoothing over feature-based user clusters. It then decomposes these utilities into residual token credits and accumulates them into credit-to-go signals. Finally, Residual-Return Policy Optimization (RRPO) optimizes the residual credits using clipped updates, group-normalized advantages, and KL regularization to preserve stability. Experiments on a public dataset and an online A/B test in a large-scale commercial system show consistent gains in session-level utility and key business metrics. Source code and the archived artifact are available for reproduction.

AI.tldr: HRPO converts sparse item-level feedback into dense, token-aligned signals for generative recommenders by estimating prefix utilities via cluster-based reward smoothing, decomposing them into residual token credits, and optimizing with clipped updates and KL regularization.
AI.motivation: Generative recommenders using SID decoding suffer from sparse, high-variance token-level credit assignment because logged feedback is only available for the final item, not intermediate tokens. Existing post-training methods naively broadcast the terminal signal, failing to account for the coarse-to-fine hierarchy.
AI.method: HRPO operates in three stages: (1) Group-wise reward smoothing over feature-based user clusters to estimate SID prefix-level utilities; (2) Decomposition of prefix utilities into residual token credits, accumulated into credit-to-go signals; (3) Residual-Return Policy Optimization (RRPO) with clipped surrogate updates, group-normalized advantages, and KL regularization for stable, conservative token-wise improvement.
AI.result: Experiments on a public dataset and an online A/B test in a large-scale commercial system demonstrate consistent gains in session-level utility and key business metrics.
AI.conclusion: HRPO effectively addresses the credit assignment problem in generative recommenders by converting sparse item-level feedback into dense, hierarchical token-level signals, enabling stable post-training that improves both offline and online recommendation performance.

title: When Collaboration Becomes a Trigger: Collective Evidence-Threshold Backdoors in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) extend LLM capabilities through iterative communication and shared contexts. However, this collaboration introduces a vulnerability: backdoor behavior can be activated when peer evidence reaches a hidden threshold, rather than being determined by any single message. We introduce a collective evidence-threshold backdoor paradigm for MAS and Boundary-Conditioned Backdoor Injection (BCBI), which constructs counterfactual boundary pairs to separate benign behavior before the threshold from the adversarial objective after it, and learns latent progression aligned with evidence. To mitigate this threat, we propose LAtent Transition Test-time Evaluation (LATTE), a clean-only latent-transition defense that learns benign communication dynamics and quarantines anomalous agent updates before their responses propagate. Across several benchmarks, BCBI yields selective activation with little premature activation; without knowing the attack target or trigger, LATTE limits propagation with minimal disruption.

AI.tldr: Proposes BCBI, a backdoor attack on LLM multi-agent systems that activates only when collective peer evidence hits a threshold, and LATTE, a defense that detects anomalous latent transitions at test time without needing attack knowledge.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems rely on iterative communication and shared context, creating a new attack surface where backdoor behavior can depend on cumulative evidence across messages rather than any single trigger. Existing backdoor defenses fall short against this collective, threshold-based activation paradigm.
AI.method: BCBI constructs counterfactual boundary pairs to separate benign behavior (pre-threshold) from adversarial behavior (post-threshold), learning a latent progression aligned with accumulating evidence. LATTE, the defense, models benign communication dynamics in latent space and quarantines anomalous agent updates at test time by detecting deviations from expected latent transitions, all without access to attack targets or triggers.
AI.result: BCBI achieves selective activation with minimal premature triggering across several benchmarks. LATTE effectively limits backdoor propagation with little disruption to normal multi-agent communication, operating without knowledge of the attack target or trigger.
AI.conclusion: Collective evidence-threshold backdoors pose a realistic threat to LLM-based MAS, and latent-transition monitoring at test time offers a viable, clean-only defense against such hidden, threshold-dependent attacks.

title: Enforcing Access Control in Distributed Version Control Systems
summary: Version control systems (VCS), including central VCS (CVCS) and distributed VCS (DVCS), are widely adopted to manage the changes to various types of data. Unlike the CVCS where all the entities obtain the data from the server and the access control is enforced with the cooperation of the server, each entity in the DVCS stores the entire repository, obtains the repository shared by any entity and is free to share its own repository. Therefore, existing access control schemes for CVCS are not suitable for DVCS. In this paper, we present a distributed access control scheme (Disac) for DVCS. Disac makes each entity have full control over its data, while the access control is enforced at each entity independently. We adopt Attribute-based Encryption (ABE) and Attribute-based Signature (ABS) to achieve the read and write permission control. The analysis of the Git client demonstrates that Disac can be integrated easily.

AI.tldr: Disac is a distributed access control scheme for Distributed Version Control Systems (DVCS) that uses Attribute-based Encryption (ABE) for read control and Attribute-based Signature (ABS) for write control, enabling each entity to independently enforce access control while maintaining full ownership of its data.
AI.motivation: In DVCS, every entity stores the entire repository and can freely share it with any other entity, unlike CVCS where a central server mediates access. Existing CVCS access control schemes fail in this decentralized setting because there is no trusted central authority to enforce policies. A new access control mechanism tailored for DVCS is therefore needed.
AI.method: The authors propose Disac, which leverages Attribute-based Encryption (ABE) to enforce read permissions (only entities possessing the required attributes can decrypt data) and Attribute-based Signature (ABS) to enforce write permissions (only entities with the required attributes can produce valid signatures). Access control is enforced independently at each entity without relying on a central server. Integration feasibility is demonstrated through analysis of the Git client.
AI.result: The scheme enables each entity in a DVCS to retain full control over its own data while independently enforcing read and write access policies. Analysis of Git client integration shows that Disac can be incorporated with relative ease.
AI.conclusion: Disac provides a viable distributed access control solution for DVCS by combining ABE and ABS, addressing the fundamental mismatch between centralized access control models and the decentralized nature of DVCS.

title: Theory, Experience, and Instinct: A Glimpse Into AAA Game Processes and How UX Leaders Navigate Pre-Production
summary: Foundational decisions shape a project's long-term trajectory, a dynamic that becomes especially evident in the inherent complexity of game pre-production. However, academic frameworks often see limited uptake at this stage, as they do not readily map onto industry contexts, production constraints, and cross-functional workflows. To better understand how design decisions are made in practice, we conducted interviews with 15 UX leaders from the AAA (triple-A) games industry. Our findings show that early UX decisions emerge from a dynamic blend of theory, experience, and intuition. In cross-functional structures (such as strike and competency teams), UX leaders collaboratively align player needs, technical feasibility, and creative vision. These decision-making processes involve translating academic concepts into production-ready insights, codifying experiential knowledge into reusable practices, and relying on informed intuition amid uncertainty. We argue that meaningful impact requires academia to develop malleable conceptual tools that integrate with practitioners' highly adaptive design processes. We conclude by discussing how existing frameworks might be adapted to connect academic insights with AAA workflows. Rather than prescriptive directives, we offer these as starting points for discussion that support strike and competency teams through shared language, reusable design systems, and strategies for collaborative, context-sensitive decision-making.

AI.tldr: Interviews with 15 AAA UX leaders reveal that early design decisions blend theory, experience, and intuition within cross-functional teams. The paper argues academia should develop malleable, production-ready conceptual tools that integrate with practitioners' adaptive workflows, rather than prescriptive frameworks.
AI.motivation: Academic frameworks for game design see limited uptake during pre-production because they fail to map onto industry constraints, production realities, and cross-functional workflows. There is a gap between academic theory and how UX decisions are actually made in AAA game development.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 15 UX leaders from the AAA games industry, focusing on understanding how early design decisions are made in practice within cross-functional team structures such as strike teams and competency teams.
AI.result: Early UX decisions emerge from a dynamic blend of three sources: (1) academic concepts translated into production-ready insights, (2) experiential knowledge codified into reusable practices, and (3) informed intuition used amid uncertainty. UX leaders collaboratively align player needs, technical feasibility, and creative vision within cross-functional structures.
AI.conclusion: Academia should develop malleable conceptual tools that integrate with practitioners' adaptive design processes. The authors propose adapting existing frameworks to connect with AAA workflows through shared language, reusable design systems, and strategies for collaborative, context-sensitive decision-making — offered as discussion starters rather than prescriptive directives.

title: Cross-Benchmark Generalization in Long-Horizon Agents
comment: Accepted at the COLM 2026 Workshop on Agent Behavior. 11 pages, 4 tables
summary: For reinforcement learning (RL) in self-contained environments, a policy can get rewards by exploiting environment-specific regularities (tool schemas, grader parsing, task templates) rather than by acquiring transferable skill, and an in-distribution holdout shares those regularities. We argue that the discriminating question is behavioral, namely how a trained agent acts, and that cross-benchmark transfer is the right place to look for it. We post-train an open-weight mixture-of-experts model (Qwen3.5-122B-A10B) on 363 long-horizon Model Context Protocol (MCP) tasks across 27 categories, using a two-stage SFT-then-RL pipeline. Toolathlon performance informed the initial base-family and SFT-teacher choices, but no external-benchmark task or grader entered training and no external score informed the reward, training hyperparameters, trained-checkpoint selection, or stopping. At greedy pass@1, the trained model improves over the base on five reported external evaluations: Toolathlon (+9.6 pp), $τ^2$-Bench (+5.3 pp), BFCL-V4 (+3.5 pp), SWE-Bench Pro (+5.8 pp), and Terminal-Bench 2 (+2.8 pp). Both software-engineering benchmarks improve despite the training collection containing no software-engineering tasks. An exploratory paired-trajectory analysis identifies four recurring behavioral differences (more careful local-goal formation, building goal-relevant working state, keeping parent goals stable through local repairs, and verifying completion) that appear in analogous forms across office workflows and code. These results provide descriptive evidence that long-horizon multi-tool post-training can change ways of working that transfer beyond its training domain.

AI.tldr: Post-training a Qwen3.5 MoE model on 363 long-horizon MCP tasks via SFT+RL yields consistent cross-benchmark transfer gains (Toolathlon, τ²-Bench, BFCL, SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench) — including on software engineering despite no such training tasks. The transfer is attributed to four behavioral changes in how the agent forms goals, maintains state, repairs plans, and verifies completion.
AI.motivation: Standard RL evaluation conflates exploiting environment-specific regularities (tool schemas, grader parsing) with acquiring genuinely transferable skill. The authors argue that cross-benchmark transfer constitutes the proper behavioral litmus test for whether training produces reusable capabilities rather than benchmark overfitting.
AI.method: A two-stage SFT-then-RL pipeline post-trains Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (a mixture-of-experts model) on 363 long-horizon MCP tasks spanning 27 categories. Crucially, no external-benchmark task, grader, or score enters training, hyperparameter selection, checkpoint selection, or early stopping. Paired-trajectory analysis of base vs. trained model rollouts is used to identify emergent behavioral differences.
AI.result: At greedy pass@1, the trained model improves over base on five held-out benchmarks: Toolathlon (+9.6 pp), τ²-Bench (+5.3 pp), BFCL-V4 (+3.5 pp), SWE-Bench Pro (+5.8 pp), and Terminal-Bench 2 (+2.8 pp). SWE-Bench Pro and Terminal-Bench improvements occur despite zero software-engineering tasks in training. Four recurring behavioral patterns are identified: more careful local-goal formation, building goal-relevant working state, maintaining parent goals through local repairs, and verifying completion — manifesting analogously across office workflows and code.
AI.conclusion: Long-horizon multi-tool post-training can induce transferable ways of working that generalize beyond the training domain. The behavioral patterns observed provide descriptive evidence that the model acquires meta-level strategies rather than narrow environment-specific heuristics.

title: SIRIN: A Unified Toolkit for Detecting Contextual Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented and Memory-Grounded LLM Systems
summary:
SIRIN (Semantic Inconsistency Recognition and Inspection Nexus) is a unified toolkit and interactive web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations (fluent, plausible responses unsupported by the provided evidence) in retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems. SIRIN unifies three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, and judge-style verification) and the complementary task of pre-generation query answerability under one interface, configuration system, and evaluation pipeline, supporting response- and span-level inspection in both white-box and black-box settings. The web UI enables live analysis of user-supplied context-query-answer triples through hallucination scores, unsupported-span highlighting, and side-by-side detector comparison, with a lightweight plug-in design for adding new detectors. We demonstrate SIRIN on hallucination detection, query answerability, and as a faithfulness gate within long-term memory systems.
  The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/sb-ai-lab/SIRIN.

AI.tldr: SIRIN is a unified toolkit and interactive web UI for detecting contextual hallucinations in LLM systems, integrating three detector paradigms (representation probing, uncertainty estimation, judge-style verification) plus query answerability assessment, with support for both white-box and black-box settings and span-level inspection.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented, agentic, and memory-grounded LLM systems suffer from contextual hallucinations — fluent but unsupported responses. Existing detection approaches are fragmented across different paradigms, lacking a unified interface for evaluation, comparison, and practical deployment. SIRIN addresses this gap by consolidating multiple detection methods into one cohesive toolkit.
AI.method: SIRIN unifies three detector paradigms under a single configuration system and evaluation pipeline: (1) representation probing, (2) uncertainty estimation, and (3) judge-style verification. It also integrates the complementary task of pre-generation query answerability. The toolkit supports both response-level and span-level hallucination detection, works in white-box and black-box settings, and provides an interactive web UI with hallucination scores, unsupported-span highlighting, and side-by-side detector comparison. A lightweight plug-in design facilitates adding new detectors.
AI.result: SIRIN is demonstrated on three use cases: hallucination detection, query answerability assessment, and serving as a faithfulness gate within long-term memory systems. The web UI enables live analysis of user-supplied context-query-answer triples.
AI.conclusion: SIRIN provides a practical, extensible, and unified framework for detecting and inspecting contextual hallucinations in grounded LLM systems, with publicly available source code to facilitate adoption and further research.

title: Exponential Reward Weighting for Fine-Tuning Generative Recommenders under Sparse and Noisy Feedback
summary: In recommendation systems, users interact with only a small fraction of a vast item catalog, producing feedback that is both sparse and noisy. This challenges post-training generative recommenders: reward models trained from logged interactions often fail to generalize, while directly optimizing imperfect rewards can lead to reward over-optimization. We propose Exponential reward-weighted fine-tuning (Exp-RSFT), where each logged interaction is weighted by $\exp(r/λ)$, avoids this failure by optimizing directly on the logged rewards, with the temperature $λ$ regularizing against their noise. We theoretically show that Exp-RSFT's suboptimality decomposes into two costs: a coverage cost arising from limitations of the logging policy and a noise cost from imperfect feedback. The temperature $λ$ balances these competing effects, yielding an optimal tradeoff between exploiting high-reward behavior and robustness to noise. Across three public benchmarks and a large-scale industrial dataset, we verify this theoretical prediction: performance follows an inverted-U trend as a function of $λ$, while PPO and DPO often over-optimize unreliable reward models and degrade recommendation quality. Exp-RSFT consistently improves ranking performance without requiring online exploration or preference data.

AI.tldr: Exp-RSFT is a post-training method for generative recommenders that weights logged interactions exponentially by reward, using a temperature parameter λ to balance coverage and noise costs, outperforming PPO/DPO without needing online exploration.
AI.motivation: Post-training generative recommenders face two challenges: reward models trained on sparse, noisy logged feedback generalize poorly, and directly optimizing imperfect rewards leads to reward over-optimization (Goodhart's law). Existing RLHF methods like PPO and DPO are prone to exploiting unreliable reward signals.
AI.method: Exp-RSFT (Exponential Reward-weighted Supervised Fine-Tuning) weights each logged interaction by exp(r/λ), where r is the logged reward and λ is a temperature parameter. The method is purely offline — it requires no online exploration or pairwise preference data. The authors provide a theoretical decomposition of suboptimality into a coverage cost (from logging policy limitations) and a noise cost (from imperfect feedback), showing λ trades off between them.
AI.result: Exp-RSFT's performance follows an inverted-U curve as λ varies, confirming the theoretical tradeoff. On three public benchmarks and one large-scale industrial dataset, Exp-RSFT consistently improves ranking performance, while PPO and DPO degrade quality due to reward over-optimization.
AI.conclusion: Exp-RSFT provides a simple, theoretically grounded alternative to RLHF for post-training recommenders, achieving robust improvements by directly optimizing logged rewards with temperature-based noise regularization, without requiring online exploration or preference annotations.

title: Asking Questions the Right Way: A Multi-Agent Conversational System for Prompt Formulation in Complex Task Resolution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are integral to complex intellectual tasks, yet output quality remains constrained by user-provided prompts. Iterative multi-turn prompting often leads to context degradation and diminishing cognitive returns. We present PAWNI (Prompt Architecture Wizard using Neural Intelligence), an agentic conversational interface of eight agents that transforms unstructured queries into structured prompts through guided question-and-answer dialogue informed by a self-evolving knowledge base. Rather than optimizing the models response, PAWNI optimizes the question itself by front-loading intent clarification. We also propose a three-tier framework of 18 prompt elements across Essential, Enhancement, and Elevation categories.To evaluate system behavior and validate a measurement protocol, we conducted an exploratory within-subjects study (N=4) across four complex tasks, integrating 32-channel EEG, NASA-TLX workload, and behavioral metrics. Participants produced more structurally complete prompts with PAWNI (42% to 91% of assessed elements), rated LLM outputs higher across all quality dimensions, and reported lower workload (39.6 vs. 21.7 NASA-TLX). Every participant reached satisfactory output in a single turn, compared to 1-12 turns unaided. While effect sizes are unstable due to sample size, direction consistency supports the hypothesis that optimizing prompt formulation front-end is a critical lever for human-AI collaboration.

AI.tldr: PAWNI is an eight-agent conversational system that transforms unstructured user queries into optimized prompts through guided dialogue, supported by a self-evolving knowledge base and a three-tier framework of 18 prompt elements. A small exploratory study (N=4) with EEG, NASA-TLX, and behavioral metrics suggests improved prompt completeness, output quality, reduced workload, and fewer turns to satisfactory results.
AI.motivation: Iterative multi-turn prompting with LLMs causes context degradation and diminishing returns. Rather than optimizing model responses, the authors argue that optimizing the prompt formulation itself — specifically through front-loaded intent clarification — is a critical yet underexplored lever for improving human-AI collaboration quality.
AI.method: PAWNI (Prompt Architecture Wizard using Neural Intelligence) is an agentic interface comprising eight agents that engage users in guided Q&A dialogue to structure prompts. It draws on a self-evolving knowledge base and a three-tier taxonomy of 18 prompt elements (Essential, Enhancement, Elevation). Evaluation was conducted via an exploratory within-subjects study (N=4) across four complex tasks, measuring 32-channel EEG, NASA-TLX workload, and behavioral metrics (prompt completeness, output quality ratings, turns to satisfaction).
AI.result: With PAWNI, prompt structural completeness rose from 42% to 91% of assessed elements. LLM outputs were rated higher across all quality dimensions. NASA-TLX workload dropped from 39.6 to 21.7. Every participant achieved satisfactory output in a single turn, versus 1–12 turns unaided. Effect sizes were unstable due to small sample size, but directional consistency supported the hypothesis.
AI.conclusion: Front-end optimization of prompt formulation via guided intent clarification significantly improves human-AI collaboration outcomes. Despite limitations in sample size, the convergent behavioral, subjective, and neurophysiological evidence suggests PAWNI's approach is a promising direction for enhancing LLM interaction quality.

title: Stateful Cooperative Agents Safeguarding LLMs Against Evolving Multi-Turn Attacks
summary: As LLMs become increasingly integrated into complex applications, their vulnerability to adversarial attacks has raised significant concerns. However, existing defenses remain reactive in nature. This limitation makes it difficult for them to counter sophisticated threats, as adversaries continuously adjust their strategies across multi-turn interactions. In this paper, we present a proactive defense framework for securing LLMs against evolving multi-turn adversarial attacks that combines disruption, misdirection, and adaptation across successive interaction turns. In particular, it employs a cooperative multi-agent architecture in which specialized agents execute complementary defense strategies. These strategies include controlled response pacing to increase attack costs, strategically ambiguous outputs to mislead adversaries into ineffective strategies, and forensic analysis of interaction logs to identify attack patterns and refine defenses. These agents are coordinated by an adaptive mechanism that dynamically adjusts the defense strategy in response to escalating threats. To facilitate comprehensive evaluation, we present the EMRA dataset designed to simulate evolving strategies across multi-turn attacks, including 5,200 adversarial samples across eight attack types. Experimental results on EMRA across multiple LLM backbones show that the proposed framework reduces ASR by 69% on average relative to evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. Beyond suppressing harmful outputs, it sustains deceptive engagement, achieving an average DR more than six times that of the strongest baselines and increasing attacker-token consumption by 198.83% on average relative to evaluated baselines. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/SiyuanLi00/CoopGuard.

AI.tldr: A proactive, multi-agent defense framework for LLMs against multi-turn adversarial attacks, using disruption, misdirection, and adaptive coordination to reduce attack success rates by 69% while increasing attacker token consumption by ~199%.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM defenses are reactive and struggle against adversaries who adapt strategies across multi-turn interactions. A proactive, adaptive defense is needed to counter evolving threats.
AI.method: A cooperative multi-agent architecture with specialized agents for controlled response pacing, strategically ambiguous outputs, and forensic interaction log analysis, coordinated by an adaptive mechanism that dynamically adjusts strategy. Also introduces the EMRA dataset (5,200 samples, 8 attack types) for multi-turn attack evaluation.
AI.result: The framework reduces ASR by 69% on average vs. SOTA baselines, achieves >6× higher deception rate (DR), and increases attacker token consumption by 198.83% on average across multiple LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Proactive, multi-agent cooperative defense with adaptive coordination effectively counters evolving multi-turn adversarial attacks on LLMs, outperforming reactive baselines in safety, deception, and resource deterrence.

title: Read, Critique, or Sketch? Investigating Alternative Visualization Literacy Assessment Modalities
summary: Visualization literacy is a multifaceted construct encompassing skills and competencies, such as decoding data, constructing charts, and identifying design flaws. Yet, assessments of these competencies has been primarily constrained to multiple choice assessments that target lower-order skills, such as chart comprehension. As a result, they often exhibit ceiling effects (i.e., even modestly skilled individuals commonly score near the top of the scale), and do not provide enough information about an individual's higher-order skills (e.g., applying external knowledge, formulating critiques, and designing visualizations). To close these gaps, we develop and investigate two web-based qualitative assessments for testing the critique and design aspects of visualization literacy through online think-aloud critique and sketching of visualization designs based on data and a prompt. We compare performance on our assessments to two established visualization literacy assessments, CALVI and Mini-VLAT, by administering them to three groups that represent three experience levels: crowdworkers, students who have taken a relevant course, and researchers. We find that our critique and sketching assessments capture skills distinct from existing measures and that they differentiate between experienced individuals better than multiple choice-based alternatives. Although administering and grading qualitative assessments can be challenging, our findings suggest qualitative, multimodal assessments are a promising complement to existing visualization literacy assessments, in particular when high visualization skills need to be distinguished.

AI.tldr: Existing visualization literacy assessments rely on multiple-choice tests that target lower-order skills and suffer from ceiling effects. The authors develop two qualitative, web-based assessments—critique (think-aloud) and design (sketching)—and show they capture distinct, higher-order skills and better differentiate experienced individuals than established measures like CALVI and Mini-VLAT.
AI.motivation: Current visualization literacy assessments (e.g., CALVI, Mini-VLAT) are limited to multiple-choice formats that measure lower-order comprehension skills, leading to ceiling effects where even moderately skilled individuals score near the top. These tests fail to assess higher-order competencies such as applying external knowledge, formulating critiques, and designing visualizations, creating a need for assessments that capture these advanced skills and discriminate among experienced users.
AI.method: The authors developed two web-based qualitative assessments: (1) an online think-aloud critique task where participants evaluate visualization designs, and (2) a sketching task where participants design visualizations based on given data and prompts. They administered these alongside CALVI and Mini-VLAT to three groups representing distinct experience levels: crowdworkers (low experience), students who completed a relevant course (intermediate), and visualization researchers (high experience). Performance was compared across all four assessments to evaluate construct validity and discriminatory power.
AI.result: The critique and sketching assessments capture skills that are distinct from those measured by existing multiple-choice tests. Crucially, the qualitative assessments differentiate between experienced individuals (students vs. researchers) far better than CALVI and Mini-VLAT, which suffer from ceiling effects at higher skill levels. The qualitative measures reveal variance in higher-order skills that conventional assessments mask.
AI.conclusion: Qualitative, multimodal assessments—specifically critique and design sketching tasks—are a promising and valid complement to existing visualization literacy measures. Despite the practical challenges of administration and grading, they are particularly valuable when fine-grained discrimination among individuals with high visualization skills is needed.

title: Source Code Authorship Attribution Does Not Generalize from Competitions to Classrooms
summary: Source code authorship attribution aims to identify the author of a program fragment from its writing style. We fine-tune the pre-trained transformer CodeBERT on three sources of data: publicly available Google Code Jam (GCJ) submissions from an open Kaggle repository, a curated GCJ archive, and institutional coursework datasets collected at a technical university. On multi-round GCJ data, CodeBERT reaches 92.6% Top-1 accuracy for 10 authors and retains 70.7% Top-1 (88.2% Top-10) for 1000 authors. On the examined coursework datasets, the same pipeline performs at or below the corresponding chance baselines: 0.2% Top-1 on a closed-assignment dataset of 690 authors and 0.06% Top-1 on open-ended assignments evaluated over 812 authors. A companion multi-model benchmark provides consistent cross-model evidence across additional dataset configurations, indicating that the observed performance gap is not specific to CodeBERT and persists across the evaluated model families. We analyze dataset and task properties that plausibly explain this gap and argue that GCJ-based benchmarks overestimate the practical applicability of authorship attribution in educational settings unless they are validated on the target coursework context.

AI.tldr: CodeBERT fine-tuned for authorship attribution achieves 92.6% Top-1 accuracy on Google Code Jam data but drops to near chance levels (~0.2%) on coursework datasets, revealing that GCJ benchmarks overestimate real-world applicability in educational settings.
AI.motivation: Existing authorship attribution benchmarks rely heavily on competitive programming data (Google Code Jam), but their performance on real-world educational contexts remains unexamined. The authors aim to assess whether GCJ-based results generalize to institutional coursework, where practical applications like plagiarism detection matter most.
AI.method: Fine-tuning CodeBERT on three data sources: (1) public Kaggle GCJ submissions, (2) a curated GCJ archive, and (3) institutional coursework datasets (closed-assignment and open-ended). A multi-model benchmark across additional architectures tests whether performance gaps are model-specific.
AI.result: On multi-round GCJ: 92.6% Top-1 (10 authors), 70.7% Top-1 (1000 authors). On coursework: 0.2% Top-1 (690 authors, closed-assignment) and 0.06% Top-1 (812 authors, open-ended) — both at or below chance. The performance gap persists across all evaluated model families.
AI.conclusion: GCJ-based benchmarks systematically overestimate authorship attribution performance in educational contexts. Dataset properties (task homogeneity, author pool characteristics, stylistic constraints) likely explain the gap. Validation on target-context data is essential before deploying such systems in practice.

title: Linguistic Context Recodes Visual Representations in Vision-Language Models
summary: Goal-directed visual processing is a hallmark of human visual intelligence, resulting in representations that support downstream tasks such as categorization or search. Though vision-language models (VLMs) are often faced with these same tasks, their ability to recode visual representations when presented with goal-directed language remains poorly characterized. Indeed, prior work largely treats visual representations in VLMs as static repositories of visual information that are manipulated by language representations. In the present work, we provide evidence for two concrete instances of language-induced recoding of visual representations. First, we identify an abstract reference representation that denotes which objects are goal-relevant under a natural language prompt. We extract contrastive steering vectors corresponding to this reference representation and demonstrate that they are causally implicated in model predictions. These reference representations are abstract in that they generalize to different objects, different task contexts, and even from synthetic to naturalistic images. Second, we demonstrate language-induced attribute modulation: later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes in visual representations of objects. We demonstrate this phenomenon across a range of different prompts. Finally, we provide a causal intervention that demonstrates that attribute modulation mediates a VLM's response distribution. Together, our results support a more dynamic account of cross-modality processing in VLMs -- rather than vision tokens serving as static repositories of information, they are modulated to support queries articulated in language.

AI.tldr: Vision-language models dynamically recode visual representations in response to language prompts through two mechanisms: an abstract reference representation that marks goal-relevant objects, and attribute modulation that amplifies task-relevant features in later layers. Both are causally implicated in model predictions.
AI.motivation: Prior work treats visual representations in VLMs as static repositories manipulated by language, but the authors argue this view is incomplete. The paper aims to characterize whether and how language prompts actively recode visual representations to support goal-directed tasks like categorization and search.
AI.method: The authors extract contrastive steering vectors to identify an abstract reference representation denoting goal-relevant objects under natural language prompts. They test causal involvement via interventions. For attribute modulation, they analyze how later layers selectively amplify goal-relevant attributes in visual representations across diverse prompts, and perform causal interventions to show this modulation mediates the VLM's response distribution.
AI.result: Two concrete forms of language-induced recoding were found: (1) abstract reference representations that generalize across objects, task contexts, and from synthetic to naturalistic images, causally implicated in predictions; (2) attribute modulation in later layers that selectively amplifies goal-relevant attributes, causally mediating the response distribution.
AI.conclusion: Visual representations in VLMs are not static but are dynamically modulated to support language-articulated queries. This supports a more dynamic account of cross-modal processing in VLMs.

title: Tevatron Meets Megatron: Expert-Parallel LLM Reranker Training on an Academic Budget
summary: Modern reranking recipes---billion-scale cross-encoders, mixture-of-experts (MoE) backbones, and distillation against strong teachers---have outpaced the training infrastructure available to most academic groups. Existing Tevatron reranker training relies on the Hugging Face Trainer with DeepSpeed or PyTorch FSDP1, but these backends lack efficient support for large-scale MoE training. We present Tevatron 3.0, which integrates a Megatron-Core training backend into Tevatron while preserving its data pipeline, evaluation workflow, and Hugging Face-compatible checkpoints. We benchmark existing distributed training configurations against the new backend, showing that Megatron matches FSDP reranker quality and training efficiency under comparable data-parallel settings, is up to 22% faster in the recommended single-node configuration, and supports both LoRA and full-parameter fine-tuning. Crucially, expert parallelism enables training a 30B-parameter Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE reranker, which is infeasible with PyTorch FSDP1. Using this framework, we conduct a controlled comparison of MoE versus dense models, LoRA versus full-parameter tuning, and distillation versus contrastive training on BEIR-15 with three first-stage retrievers, and report serving throughput for Hugging Face and vLLM. We find that the MoE reranker matches dense 8B quality while activating less than half as many parameters and achieving substantially higher inference throughput. We will release the framework and trained checkpoints.

AI.tldr: Tevatron 3.0 integrates a Megatron-Core backend to enable efficient large-scale MoE reranker training (including a 30B-parameter model), showing MoE matches dense 8B quality with fewer activated parameters and higher inference throughput.
AI.motivation: Modern reranking approaches (billion-scale cross-encoders, MoE backbones, distillation) have outpaced the training infrastructure accessible to academic groups. Existing Tevatron backends (DeepSpeed, PyTorch FSDP1) lack efficient support for large-scale mixture-of-experts training.
AI.method: Integration of a Megatron-Core training backend into Tevatron, preserving the existing data pipeline, evaluation workflow, and Hugging Face-compatible checkpoints. Supports expert parallelism, LoRA, and full-parameter fine-tuning. A controlled comparison is conducted on BEIR-15: MoE vs. dense models, LoRA vs. full-parameter tuning, and distillation vs. contrastive training across three first-stage retrievers.
AI.result: Megatron matches FSDP quality and training efficiency under comparable settings, is up to 22% faster in single-node configuration. Expert parallelism enables training a 30B-parameter Qwen3-30B-A3B MoE reranker (infeasible with FSDP1). The MoE reranker matches dense 8B quality while activating under half as many parameters with substantially higher inference throughput.
AI.conclusion: Tevatron 3.0 makes large-scale MoE reranker training accessible to academic groups. MoE architectures offer a compelling efficiency-quality trade-off for reranking, matching dense model quality with lower activation cost and higher throughput. The framework and checkpoints will be open-sourced.

title: Imprecise Belief Fusion Improves Multi-agent Social Learning
summary: In social learning, agents learn not only from direct evidence but also through interactions with their peers. We investigate the role of imprecision in such interactions and ask whether it can improve the effectiveness of the collective learning process. To that end we propose a model of social learning where beliefs are equivalent to formulas in a propositional language, and where agents learn from each other by combining their beliefs according to a fusion operator. The latter is parametrised so as to allow for different levels of imprecision, where a more imprecise fusion operator tends to generates a more imprecise fused belief when the two combined beliefs differ. In this context we describe both difference equation models and agent-based simulations of social learning under a variety of conditions and with different initial biases. The results presented suggest that for populations with a strong initial bias towards incorrect beliefs some level of imprecision in fusion can improve learning accuracy across a range of learning conditions. Furthermore, such benefits of imprecision are consistent with a stability analysis of the fixed points of the proposed difference equation models.

AI.tldr: Agents in social networks learn by fusing beliefs via propositional logic. Introducing controlled imprecision into the fusion operator improves collective learning accuracy, especially when the population starts with a strong bias toward incorrect beliefs. Stability analysis of fixed points corroborates the simulation findings.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether imprecision in peer-to-peer belief exchange can enhance—rather than degrade—the effectiveness of social learning, particularly under conditions where the population holds strong initial biases toward incorrect beliefs.
AI.method: The authors propose a model where agent beliefs are propositional formulas and learning occurs through a parametrised fusion operator with tunable imprecision levels. They analyze the system using both difference equation models (macroscopic dynamics) and agent-based simulations across varying conditions and initial biases, supplemented by fixed-point stability analysis.
AI.result: Moderate imprecision in belief fusion improves learning accuracy when populations are strongly biased toward incorrect beliefs. This benefit holds across diverse learning conditions and is consistent with the fixed-point stability analysis of the difference equation models.
AI.conclusion: Imprecision in social belief fusion is not necessarily detrimental; under certain conditions—particularly strong initial incorrect biases—it can serve as a beneficial mechanism that enhances collective learning accuracy.

title: Symbolic Attack Chain Generation from Atomic Red Team Techniques: An Empirical Study of Predicate Representation Granularity
summary: Automated attack chain generation is critical for modern cybersecurity, yet manual construction fails to scale as adversary behaviors expand. While classical AI planning using PDDL offers a formal method to automate this process, it relies on the accurate translation of techniques into symbolic predicates. Current state-of-the-art systems like AURORA employ a nine-category Attack Action Linking Model (AALM), but the necessity of this specific granularity remains unvalidated. This work investigates the impact of predicate representation granularity on plan validity, cost, and fidelity. Utilizing a pipeline where a Large Language Model (LLM) performs translation and the Fast Downward engine performs deterministic reasoning, the study compares the full nine-category AALM against a reduced five-category scheme derived empirically from Atomic Red Team (ART) execution evidence. Results from a sixteen-technique corpus demonstrate that plan validity and cost are largely insensitive to granularity, with 81.3% identical outcomes across both schemes. The findings suggest that higher granularity primarily enhances the internal structural resolution of a plan's justification rather than the viability of the generated attack chain itself.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether the granularity of predicate representations in PDDL-based automated attack chain generation affects plan validity, cost, and fidelity. Testing a nine-category versus a five-category scheme on 16 ART techniques, it finds 81.3% identical outcomes and concludes that granularity impacts plan justification structure more than chain viability.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art systems like AURORA use a nine-category Attack Action Linking Model (AALM) to translate adversary techniques into PDDL predicates for AI planning. However, the necessity of this specific level of granularity has never been empirically validated, raising the question of whether a simpler representation could achieve comparable results.
AI.method: The authors construct a pipeline combining an LLM for translating technique descriptions into PDDL predicates with the Fast Downward planner for deterministic plan generation. They compare two predicate granularity schemes: the full nine-category AALM (used by AURORA) and a reduced five-category scheme derived empirically from Atomic Red Team (ART) execution evidence. Evaluation uses a corpus of 16 adversary techniques, measuring plan validity, cost, and outcome identity across both schemes.
AI.result: Plan validity and cost are largely insensitive to predicate granularity, with 81.3% of generated plans being identical across both representation schemes. Differences, where they occur, reflect changes in the internal structural resolution of the plan's justification rather than affecting whether a viable attack chain is produced.
AI.conclusion: Higher predicate granularity does not significantly improve the viability of automatically generated attack chains. Its primary benefit lies in enriching the explanatory depth and structural detail of the plan's rationale, suggesting that simpler predicate schemes may suffice for many practical automated planning tasks in cybersecurity.

title: Dynamic Surveys: Using LLMs to Blend Qualitative Depth,Quantitative Structure, and Collaborative Interaction
summary: Surveys are a powerful tool for collecting data and eliciting insights on social phenomena, and are critical in product design, marketing, scientific research. However, traditional open-ended and closed-ended question formats limit researchers' ability to capture data that combines both the richness of qualitative insights and the analytical rigor of quantitative data. To address these problems, we propose Dynamic Surveys, a survey platform that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to dynamically cluster qualitative responses in real time and to elicit quantitative ratings and rankings on those clusters and qualitative reflections on how their views compare to broader respondent trends, especially helpful in early-stage or exploratory research settings. This process generates a report showing survey creators and respondents the clustered responses as well as each cluster's rank, rating distribution, and follow-up reflections. To evaluate Dynamic Surveys, we conducted two field studies with 93 participants over a 2-month period. In the first study, 52 students provided input for a career workshop, while in the second, 41 students gave feedback on gaps in their academic curriculum. Of these, 44 respondents filled out a survey on their experience using Dynamic Surveys. We also shared the generated report with 4 individuals who were interested in the insights for their work, and interviewed them to understand their perspectives on the results and any contextual risks they saw in the platform design. Our findings suggest that Dynamic Surveys not only provide richer and deeper insights into responses compared with traditional survey tools, but also increase engagement and foster a sense of community. We discuss broader implications for the design of survey platforms that blend qualitative depth with quantitative structure, facilitating richer insights and offering more collaborative interactions.

AI.tldr: Dynamic Surveys is an LLM-powered platform that clusters open-ended survey responses in real time, generates quantitative ratings/rankings on those clusters, and enables respondents to reflect on how their views compare to others. Field studies with 93 participants show it yields richer insights and higher engagement than traditional surveys.
AI.motivation: Traditional surveys force a trade-off between open-ended (qualitatively rich but hard to analyze at scale) and closed-ended (quantitatively rigorous but shallow) formats. Researchers lack tools that blend qualitative depth with quantitative structure, particularly in exploratory research settings.
AI.method: The authors built Dynamic Surveys, a platform where LLMs cluster qualitative responses in real time. Respondents then rate/rank these clusters and provide reflections on how their views align with broader trends. The system produces an auto-generated report. Evaluation involved two field studies (career workshop feedback, curriculum gap feedback) with 93 total participants over two months, plus a user experience survey (n=44) and stakeholder interviews (n=4).
AI.result: Dynamic Surveys produced richer, deeper insights than traditional tools, increased respondent engagement, and fostered a sense of community among participants. Stakeholder interviews validated the practical utility of the generated reports while surfacing contextual risks in the platform design.
AI.conclusion: Blending qualitative depth with quantitative structure via LLM-mediated real-time clustering creates a new survey paradigm that enhances insight quality and respondent collaboration. The authors call for further exploration of survey platforms that integrate both modalities.

title: Modelling Android applications through static analysis and systematic exploratory testing
summary:
Mobile application development is a fast paced industry with frequent releases. While the development pace increases, so too does the need for automated test generation. Model-based test generation is one of the most common and successful approaches to support this need. Understanding and modelling the application under test is integral to producing comprehensive, dependable and effective tests. Unfortunately, mobile platforms such as Android, introduce a host of difficulties. Static analysis struggles with Android's event-based nature and the growing variety of mechanisms available for developers to implement different features. Additionally, dynamic analysis, implemented by popular random test generators, is slow, inefficient, and limited by a lack of application knowledge.
  This paper introduces DroidGraph, a framework to generate a comprehensive control flow model of Android applications using traditional static analysis and efficient systematic exploratory tests. DroidGraph provides a detailed model of an Android application, from low level method statements to high level user interface structures. This model can be used to support automated test generation. We apply DroidGraph to 19 diverse apps and show that our efficient exploratory tests, on average, interact with 18% more of the app than commonly used random exploration in 345 less interactions. Integrating the dynamic analysis results provided by these tests complements our static analysis, and uncovers on average 51 more components and 49% more interface callback links in the application code.

AI.tldr: DroidGraph combines static analysis with efficient systematic exploratory testing to build comprehensive control flow models of Android apps, outperforming random testing by covering 18% more app functionality in 345 fewer interactions while uncovering 51 more components and 49% more interface callback links.
AI.motivation: Android's event-driven architecture and diverse implementation mechanisms make static analysis alone insufficient for modeling apps. Dynamic analysis via random testing is slow, inefficient, and lacks application knowledge. A unified approach combining both is needed for effective automated test generation.
AI.method: DroidGraph integrates traditional static analysis with systematic exploratory tests to construct a hierarchical control flow model spanning low-level method statements to high-level UI structures. The exploratory tests are designed to be efficient and targeted, complementing static analysis findings.
AI.result: Evaluated on 19 diverse apps, DroidGraph's exploratory tests interact with 18% more of the app than random exploration while using 345 fewer interactions. The combined static-dynamic analysis uncovers, on average, 51 more components and 49% more interface callback links.
AI.conclusion: Combining static analysis with systematic exploratory testing produces significantly more comprehensive Android application models than either approach alone, enabling more effective automated test generation for the fast-paced mobile development industry.

title: RAG-TESTER: Automated End-to-End Testing of Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to use external and domain-specific knowledge, but its reliability depends on the interaction between the generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, and prompt construction strategy. We present RagTester, an automated end-to-end testing approach for RAG systems. RagTester generates retrieval documents, test inputs, and expected outputs; executes the tests; and evaluates the resulting answers using an LLM as a judge. Its test-generation strategy targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and document-coverage criteria. We evaluate RagTester using eight LLMs and six embedding models, yielding 24 compatible configurations, and compare it with a baseline test-input generator. Across 72,000 test executions, RagTester detected 21,633 failures, 6.6% more than the baseline, and outperformed it in 20 of the 24 configurations. The detected failures include inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete use of retrieved context, and difficulties interpreting complex passages. These results show that coverage-oriented test generation can effectively expose failures caused by the interaction between retrieval and generation components and support the assessment of RAG configurations before deployment.

AI.tldr: RagTester is an automated end-to-end testing framework for RAG systems that uses coverage-oriented test generation to expose failures at the retrieval-generation interface, detecting 6.6% more failures than baselines across 72,000 test executions involving 24 LLM/embedding-model configurations.
AI.motivation: RAG systems integrate multiple interacting components (generative model, embedding model, retrieval mechanism, prompt construction), making reliability assessment challenging. Existing testing approaches lack systematic, automated, end-to-end coverage of failure modes arising specifically from the interaction between retrieval and generation components.
AI.method: RagTester automatically generates (1) retrieval documents designed around complex passages, (2) test inputs including unsupported queries, and (3) expected outputs guided by document-coverage criteria. It then executes tests and employs an LLM-as-judge to evaluate answer quality. Its test-generation strategy deliberately targets complex passages, unsupported queries, and coverage-oriented document selection.
AI.result: Across 72,000 test executions using eight LLMs and six embedding models (24 configurations), RagTester detected 21,633 failures — 6.6% more than the baseline — and outperformed it in 20 of 24 configurations. Failures spanned inaccurate retrieval, unsupported answers, incomplete context use, and difficulty with complex passages.
AI.conclusion: Coverage-oriented test generation effectively exposes interaction-driven failures between retrieval and generation components, providing a practical means to assess RAG configuration reliability before deployment.

title: GRACE: Generative Recommender Acceleration Engine for Real-Time Ads Retrieval
summary: Productionizing generative recommenders for high-volume, real-time ads retrieval creates two serving challenges: eligibility, ensuring that each generated ad is eligible for the request under the advertiser's audience targeting rules, and compute, which requires meeting strict latency and GPU cost requirements while remaining capable of generating thousands of ads per request with wide-beam decoding. This paper presents GRACE, a serving system for ads generative retrieval that addresses both challenges. For eligibility, GRACE introduces Generative Target Matching (GTM), which extends catalog-valid constrained decoding with personalized filtering over Semantic ID (SID) prefixes using bitmask and Bloom filter matchers derived from targeting rules. SID-level GTM improves final ad-level target matching pass rate from 23.55% to 40.42% over constrained decoding alone. For compute-cost and latency, GRACE targets encoder-decoder Transformers, which are more lightweight than LLMs. It redesigns the decoder around the wide-beam, short-sequence regime, covering attention kernels, KV cache, and beam search optimizations. On NVIDIA GH200, compared with the faster of FlashAttention-2 and FlashAttention-3 baselines, GRACE improves cross-attention latency by 68.0 times and self-attention latency by 23.4-25.8 times across decode steps. Together, these changes reduce decoder latency by 11.1 times, keeping ads generative retrieval within latency and compute requirements.

AI.tldr: GRACE is a serving system for real-time ads generative retrieval that addresses eligibility (via Generative Target Matching with SID-level bitmask/Bloom filters, improving target matching from 23.55% to 40.42%) and compute challenges (via optimized encoder-decoder Transformers achieving 11.1× decoder latency reduction on NVIDIA GH200).
AI.motivation: Deploying generative recommenders for high-volume, real-time ads retrieval faces two critical serving challenges: (1) ensuring each generated ad complies with advertisers' audience targeting rules (eligibility), and (2) meeting strict latency and GPU cost constraints while generating thousands of ads per request with wide-beam decoding (compute).
AI.method: For eligibility, GRACE introduces Generative Target Matching (GTM), which extends catalog-valid constrained decoding with personalized filtering over Semantic ID (SID) prefixes using bitmask and Bloom filter matchers derived from targeting rules. For compute, GRACE uses encoder-decoder Transformers (more lightweight than LLMs) and redesigns the decoder for the wide-beam, short-sequence regime, optimizing attention kernels, KV cache, and beam search.
AI.result: SID-level GTM improves final ad-level target matching pass rate from 23.55% to 40.42% over constrained decoding alone. On NVIDIA GH200, GRACE improves cross-attention latency by 68.0× and self-attention latency by 23.4–25.8× over FlashAttention-2/3 baselines, yielding an 11.1× overall decoder latency reduction.
AI.conclusion: GRACE successfully enables production-grade ads generative retrieval by jointly solving eligibility and compute challenges, keeping the system within latency and compute requirements for real-time serving.

title: Training Small LLMs as Spatial Multi-Agent Policies
summary: Training LLM-based multi-agent systems with multi-agent reinforcement learning is rapidly gaining traction, and a parallel line of work argues that such systems should be judged by their behavior, not only their reward. We take up both threads in spatial cooperative games, where small frozen LLMs prompted with low-level actions fail outright, earning zero reward. Guided by the options/semi-MDP framework---and, because option execution is asynchronous across agents, its multi-agent extension in macro-action Dec-POMDPs---we equip each game with a library of symbolic \emph{options}: typed, state-feasible, short-horizon behaviors executed by a symbolic planner. Each library is drafted by a frontier coding model from the game's source code; the feasibility guards that filter each menu are then synthesized mechanically from cheap random-policy burn-in rollouts---a guard is adopted only if it explains repeated execution failures while hiding no logged success---so no guard is authored, selected, or reward-tuned by hand. Each agent's LLM acts as its policy over options, with a private per-agent LoRA adapter trained by a per-agent variant of multi-agent GRPO (PA-MAGRPO); this lifts frozen bases from zero reward to competent play across three games and four small backbones. Behavioral audits then reveal that reward and cooperation decouple: a rising reward curve may simply mean that one agent has learned to run the entire task alone while its partner idles---cooperation emerges only when the task makes it necessary. Reward alone is thus an unreliable readout of cooperation; behavioral evaluation must sit alongside it.

AI.tldr: Small frozen LLMs fail outright in spatial cooperative games when given low-level actions. The authors solve this by introducing symbolic option libraries (auto-generated by a coding model, with feasibility guards learned from random rollouts) and training per-agent LoRA adapters with a multi-agent GRPO variant. This lifts zero-reward frozen models to competent play, and behavioral audits reveal that reward and cooperation can decouple—reward alone is an unreliable proxy for cooperative behavior.
AI.motivation: Small frozen LLMs prompted with low-level actions earn zero reward in spatial cooperative games. Meanwhile, the multi-agent RL community increasingly argues that agent behavior—not just reward—should be the basis for evaluation. The paper aims to (1) make small frozen LLMs viable in spatial cooperative games via hierarchical action abstraction and (2) demonstrate empirically that reward curves can mask whether genuine cooperation is occurring.
AI.method: The authors adopt the options/semi-MDP framework and its multi-agent extension, macro-action Dec-POMDPs. For each game, a frontier coding model drafts a library of symbolic options (typed, state-feasible, short-horizon behaviors) from the game source code. Feasibility guards are synthesized mechanically from cheap random-policy burn-in rollouts—a guard is kept only if it explains repeated failures while hiding no logged successes (no hand-tuning). Each agent's LLM serves as a policy over these options, equipped with a private LoRA adapter trained via a per-agent variant of multi-agent GRPO (PA-MAGRPO). Behavioral audits then assess agent interaction patterns alongside reward.
AI.result: The approach lifts frozen LLM backbones from zero reward to competent play across three games and four small model backbones. Behavioral audits reveal that reward and cooperation decouple: rising reward may indicate one agent has learned to solo the task while its partner idles. Cooperation emerges only when the task structurally demands it. Reward alone is therefore an unreliable readout of cooperative behavior.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical action abstraction via auto-generated symbolic options, combined with lightweight per-agent LoRA fine-tuning (PA-MAGRPO), enables small frozen LLMs to succeed in spatial cooperative games where they previously failed. Critically, the work demonstrates that behavioral evaluation must accompany reward-based metrics in multi-agent LLM systems, as reward alone can obscure whether true cooperation is taking place.

title: Exposed by Design: A Dynamic Security Assessment of Internet-Facing MCP Servers at Scale
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has seen rapid adoption since its November 2024 launch, with over 21,000 server instances detectable on the public internet. We present the first dynamic behavioral security assessment of internet-facing MCP servers, combining passive discovery across eleven data sources (crt.sh, HuggingFace, GitHub, npm, Smithery, PyPI, Censys, FOFA, Shodan, glama.ai, and pulsemcp.com) with active dynamic testing using Corvus, a purpose-built framework implementing 34 test modules covering 10 MCP-specific vulnerability classes. Across four measurement runs spanning July 2026, we confirm 640 production MCP servers and dynamically audit 414, uncovering 68 reportable vulnerabilities including SQL injection, SSRF targeting cloud metadata services, prompt template injection, and path traversal via cursor manipulation. We find that 91.8% of dynamically audited servers lack OAuth authentication, 687 tool instances across confirmed servers expose shell execution capabilities without access controls, and 41.6% of confirmed servers disappear within three days between consecutive measurement runs---indicating rapid deployment cycles without security review. We report on our responsible disclosure pipeline and release Corvus as an open-source framework for MCP security evaluation.

AI.tldr: First dynamic behavioral security assessment of internet-facing MCP servers, uncovering 68 vulnerabilities across 414 audited servers, with 91.8% lacking OAuth and 687 tool instances exposing unprotected shell execution.
AI.motivation: The rapid proliferation of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers on the public internet (21,000+ detectable instances) creates an urgent need to understand their security posture. Prior to this work, no dynamic behavioral security assessment of internet-facing MCP servers existed, leaving the MCP ecosystem's vulnerability landscape unexplored.
AI.method: A dual-phase methodology: (1) passive discovery aggregating MCP server instances from 11 diverse data sources (crt.sh, HuggingFace, GitHub, npm, Smithery, PyPI, Censys, FOFA, Shodan, glama.ai, pulsemcp.com); (2) active dynamic testing using Corvus, a custom-built framework implementing 34 test modules across 10 MCP-specific vulnerability classes. Four measurement runs were conducted spanning July 2026.
AI.result: Confirmed 640 production MCP servers; dynamically audited 414, revealing 68 reportable vulnerabilities (SQL injection, SSRF targeting cloud metadata services, prompt template injection, path traversal via cursor manipulation). Key findings: 91.8% lack OAuth authentication; 687 tool instances expose shell execution without access controls; 41.6% of confirmed servers disappear within three days between consecutive measurement runs, indicating rapid, unreviewed deployment cycles.
AI.conclusion: The MCP ecosystem exhibits significant security immaturity, characterized by widespread absence of authentication, dangerous tool exposure, and ephemeral deployment patterns that hinder security review. The release of Corvus as an open-source framework, alongside a responsible disclosure pipeline, aims to catalyze security improvements across the MCP landscape.

title: MolecularCanvas: LLM-assisted Small-Molecule Drug Discovery via Structure-Guided Constraints
summary: Small-molecule drug discovery relies on iterative molecular optimization, where chemists repeatedly modify candidate compounds to balance multiple competing properties such as efficacy, toxicity, and solubility. Recent advances in generative AI (GenAI) have shown promise in accelerating this process by automatically proposing new molecular structures or targeted modifications. However, existing GenAI-based molecular design tools remain poorly aligned with experts' real-world workflows. Specifically, they offer limited support for specifying structure-level modification intents on molecules, provide insufficient transparency into model-generated modifications, and lack integrated support for downstream property evaluation with external computational tools. To address these challenges, we introduce MolecularCanvas, an interactive system that enables users to iteratively construct an optimization context by integrating high-level goals, structure-level annotations, property constraints, and reference-based preferences. This context guides the generation of candidate molecules across diverse molecular structures. MolecularCanvas further enhances transparency by providing evidence for AI-generated suggestions and streamlines molecular evaluation by integrating commonly used computational tools for property assessment into a unified interface. Finally, a user study with 12 participants demonstrates the usefulness and effectiveness of MolecularCanvas in helping users optimize candidate molecules.

AI.tldr: MolecularCanvas is an interactive AI-assisted molecular optimization system that integrates high-level goals, structure-level annotations, property constraints, and reference-based preferences into a unified workflow, addressing the transparency and evaluation gaps of existing GenAI molecular design tools.
AI.motivation: Existing generative AI tools for molecular design are misaligned with chemists' real workflows: they lack support for structure-level modification intents, provide poor transparency into model-generated modifications, and do not integrate downstream property evaluation with external computational tools.
AI.method: The authors developed MolecularCanvas, an interactive system where users iteratively build an optimization context combining high-level goals, structure-level annotations, property constraints, and reference-based preferences. The system provides transparency evidence for AI suggestions and integrates external computational tools for property assessment within a unified interface. A user study with 12 participants evaluated the system.
AI.result: The user study with 12 participants demonstrated that MolecularCanvas is useful and effective in helping users optimize candidate molecules.
AI.conclusion: MolecularCanvas successfully bridges the gap between GenAI molecular design tools and real-world chemist workflows by providing structure-level annotation support, transparency, and integrated property evaluation, as validated by positive user study results.

title: PADRAIG: Precise Android Automated Input Generation
summary:
