Android automated test input generation has been a highly researched topic for over a decade and has shown promising results with a variety of approaches. Random input generation is commonly used and the easiest to maintain, but ultimately inefficient. Systematic and search-based approaches produce effective tests but require a disproportionally large generation runtime. Model-based approaches have the additional overhead of modelling the application under test (AUT) but they result in a faster test generation.
  In this paper we present Precise AnDRoid Automated Input Generation (PADRAIG), a model-based test input generation framework that uses a detailed control flow model of the AUT to generate tests that can achieve higher line coverage, with a lower test generation runtime than the state of the art. We compare the line coverage achieved, and the generation runtime of PADRAIG against 3 state of the art tools, each of which uses a different test input generation technique. Our results, using 19 randomly selected Android apps from the F-Droid application store, show that PADRAIG achieves, on average, 16% more coverage of the AUT than the state of the art and it can generate tests with, on average, 84% less runtime.

AI.tldr: PADRAIG is a model-based Android test input generation framework that uses a detailed control flow model to achieve 16% higher line coverage on average while reducing generation runtime by 84% compared to three state-of-the-art tools, as evaluated on 19 F-Droid apps.
AI.motivation: Existing Android test input generation approaches suffer from a fundamental trade-off: random approaches are easy to maintain but inefficient; systematic and search-based approaches achieve good coverage but are too slow; model-based approaches have modeling overhead but generate tests faster. No existing approach simultaneously achieves high coverage and low generation runtime.
AI.method: PADRAIG employs a model-based test input generation framework that constructs a detailed control flow model of the application under test (AUT). This fine-grained model captures the app's control flow structure, enabling precise and efficient test generation. The framework is evaluated against three state-of-the-art tools, each representing a different generation technique (random, systematic/search-based, and model-based). Evaluation uses 19 randomly selected apps from the F-Droid store, measuring both line coverage achieved and test generation runtime.
AI.result: On 19 randomly selected F-Droid apps, PADRAIG achieves on average 16% higher line coverage than the state of the art, while reducing test generation runtime by an average of 84%.
AI.conclusion: A detailed control flow model-based approach can simultaneously outperform existing techniques in both coverage and runtime, breaking the trade-off observed in prior Android test generation research. PADRAIG demonstrates that model-based test generation, when using sufficiently precise models, is both more effective and dramatically more efficient than random, systematic, or search-based alternatives.

title: H+ Embedding: Harmonizing Global and Token-Level Retrieval with Context-Dependent Phrases
summary: Terminology-intensive retrieval, especially in medical settings, depends on preserving multi-word entities, abbreviations, numerical constraints, and compositional concepts. However, existing representations lie at two extremes: single-vector retrievers often over-compress local relevance signals, while token-level late interaction retains every tokenizer subword at substantial indexing, storage, and scoring cost. This mismatch raises a natural question: can context-dependent phrases provide a useful retrieval unit between global vectors and tokens? We introduce H+ Embedding, a unified multi-granularity retriever that predicts variable-length phrase partitions, preserves uncovered tokens as singletons, and applies importance-guided unit selection with weighted MaxSim interaction. Across 16 scientific, medical, and bilingual tasks, its phrase retrieval branch exceeds the global retrieval branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10. It also nearly matches Token while using 13.7% fewer document vectors and outperforms content-independent grouping rules under moderate vector budgets. Context-dependent phrase interaction therefore provides an intermediate quality-cost point between global compression and token-level interaction for practical retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: H+ Embedding introduces context-dependent phrase partitions as a retrieval unit between global single-vector and token-level representations, achieving near-token quality with 13.7% fewer document vectors and outperforming global retrieval by 6.91 macro nDCG@10 across medical, scientific, and bilingual tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing dense retrieval methods fall at two extremes: single-vector models over-compress local relevance signals critical for terminology-intensive domains (medical abbreviations, multi-word entities, numerical constraints), while token-level late interaction preserves every subword but incurs prohibitive indexing, storage, and scoring costs. The authors ask whether context-dependent phrases can serve as a more efficient intermediate retrieval unit.
AI.method: The proposed H+ Embedding is a unified multi-granularity retriever that: (1) predicts variable-length phrase partitions from contextualized token representations, (2) preserves uncovered tokens as singleton units, (3) applies importance-guided unit selection to control the vector budget, and (4) employs weighted MaxSim interaction for scoring. This enables a phrase-level retrieval branch alongside the standard global vector branch.
AI.result: On 16 benchmarks spanning scientific, medical, and bilingual retrieval tasks, the phrase retrieval branch surpasses the global retrieval branch by 6.91 macro nDCG@10. It nearly matches Token-level late interaction performance while using 13.7% fewer document vectors. Under moderate vector budgets, it also outperforms content-independent grouping rules (e.g., fixed n-gram or sliding window chunking).
AI.conclusion: Context-dependent phrase interaction provides a compelling intermediate quality-cost operating point between global single-vector compression and token-level late interaction, making it practically suitable for deployment in terminology-intensive retrieval systems.

title: UniHEAR: Unified Heterogeneous-Source Attentive Retrieval for Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering
summary: Knowledge-Based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) requires retrieving relevant entity knowledge from external sources to answer visually grounded questions. Existing retrieval-augmented systems suffer from two critical limitations. First, relying on a single retrieval modality creates a Single-Source Retrieval Bottleneck, missing ground-truth entities that are only accessible through complementary sources. Second, dual-tower pointwise rerankers suffer from Retrieval-Source-Blind Reranking, as they overlook retrieval origins and candidate-level retrieval priors, leading to redundant modality reliance. To address these challenges, we propose UniHEAR, a unified lightweight framework for heterogeneous-source entity retrieval and reranking. UniHEAR constructs a Coarse Retrieval Descriptor for each candidate entity, and introduces Retrieval-Guided Attentive Modality Gating to condition modality attention weights on this descriptor, further complemented by Entropy-Weighted Source Fusion of coarse retrieval priors. A hybrid training strategy combining contrastive learning with an auxiliary modality-preserving loss unifies entity-level and section-level retrieval within a single model. Extensive experiments on E-VQA and InfoSeek demonstrate that UniHEAR achieves state-of-the-art retrieval and VQA performance, improving Recall@1 by 6.7 and 1.2 points over the strongest baselines while maintaining a lightweight reranking architecture. Code and model are available at https://github.com/iven-luo/UniHEAR.

AI.tldr: UniHEAR is a lightweight framework that unifies heterogeneous-source entity retrieval and reranking for KB-VQA. It addresses the Single-Source Retrieval Bottleneck via coarse retrieval descriptors and Retrieval-Guided Attentive Modality Gating, and solves Retrieval-Source-Blind Reranking through Entropy-Weighted Source Fusion. It achieves SOTA on E-VQA and InfoSeek, with Recall@1 improvements of 6.7 and 1.2 points.
AI.motivation: Existing KB-VQA retrieval-augmented systems suffer from two key limitations: (1) a Single-Source Retrieval Bottleneck, where relying on a single retrieval modality misses ground-truth entities accessible only through complementary sources; and (2) Retrieval-Source-Blind Reranking, where dual-tower pointwise rerankers ignore retrieval origins and candidate-level retrieval priors, causing redundant modality reliance.
AI.method: UniHEAR constructs a Coarse Retrieval Descriptor for each candidate entity, then applies Retrieval-Guided Attentive Modality Gating to condition modality attention weights on this descriptor. It uses Entropy-Weighted Source Fusion to integrate coarse retrieval priors. A hybrid training strategy combines contrastive learning with an auxiliary modality-preserving loss, unifying entity-level and section-level retrieval within a single model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on E-VQA and InfoSeek benchmarks show UniHEAR achieves state-of-the-art retrieval and VQA performance, improving Recall@1 by 6.7 and 1.2 points respectively over the strongest baselines, while maintaining a lightweight reranking architecture.
AI.conclusion: UniHEAR effectively addresses both the single-source bottleneck and source-blind reranking problems in KB-VQA through a unified, lightweight framework. Its heterogeneous-source fusion and modality-aware gating mechanisms set a new state of the art, demonstrating that incorporating retrieval provenance into reranking yields substantial performance gains.

title: Can LLM Agents Price Competitively? A Dynamic Multi-Attribute Auction Benchmark for Agentic Commerce
summary: Agentic commerce is moving from concept to deployed infrastructure: payment networks, retailers, and AI platforms are setting the stage for agents to transact on behalf of merchants and consumers. Yet whether the LLMs behind these agents can price competently in real markets, where customer preferences are hidden, competitors adapt in real time, and demand can shift without warning, has not been systematically tested. We introduce Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auction under these conditions. Despite its dynamics, the benchmark is grounded in closed-form customer utilities, enabling exact evaluation. Across 11 frontier LLMs from four providers, the leading agents on customer acquisition (e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro) are often not the leading agents on profit (e.g. Opus 4.6). The ranking shifts again under demand shocks: agents that learned fastest pre-shock are typically the slowest to revise their beliefs afterwards, while Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest despite not leading on profit. However, even the strongest agent captures less than a third of hindsight-optimal profit, suggesting current LLMs are progressing in agentic commerce but leave substantial headroom.

AI.tldr: Bazaar is a dynamic multi-attribute auction benchmark for testing LLM pricing competence in agentic commerce. Across 11 frontier LLMs, leaders in customer acquisition differ from leaders in profit, rankings shift under demand shocks, and even the best agent captures less than one-third of hindsight-optimal profit.
AI.motivation: Agentic commerce is being deployed in real-world payment networks and retail platforms, yet the pricing competence of LLM-based agents under realistic market conditions — hidden customer preferences, adaptive competitors, and demand shocks — has not been systematically evaluated.
AI.method: The authors introduce Bazaar, a dynamic sealed-bid benchmark for multi-attribute auctions. The benchmark uses closed-form customer utility functions, allowing exact evaluation of agent performance despite dynamic market conditions. Eleven frontier LLMs from four providers are tested.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Top-performing agents on customer acquisition (e.g., Gemini 3.1 Pro) are often not top performers on profit (e.g., Opus 4.6). (2) Under demand shocks, agents that learned fastest pre-shock are typically slowest to revise beliefs post-shock. (3) Gemini 3.1 Pro recovers fastest from shocks despite not leading on profit. (4) The best agent captures less than one-third of hindsight-optimal profit.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier LLMs show meaningful progress in agentic commerce pricing but leave substantial headroom. No single model dominates across all metrics, and adaptability to demand shocks remains a key weakness, highlighting a gap between current capabilities and fully competent autonomous pricing agents.

title: From Monoliths to Swarms: A Study of Attack Surface Evolution in the Transition to Multi-Agent Web Systems
summary:
Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents are increasingly evolving from single-agent systems (SAS) to multi-agent systems (MAS). While MAS can lead to improved task performance by decomposing complex tasks across specialized sub-agents, such role decomposition introduces new structural attack surfaces that are absent in SAS. This expanded attack surface remains poorly understood and inadequately categorized.
  To address this, we propose a taxonomy to categorize attack vectors specific to web-based MAS, accounting for vulnerabilities introduced or amplified by the involvement of multiple agents. We further present a test-bed WebMASLab to analyze web agent security against a fully external, web-only adversary. To isolate the effect of architecture, we keep the user task, tool surface, and browser substrate fixed, and compare single- and multi-agent setups. We evaluate three adversarial scenarios, across three conditions (baseline, prompt-hardened, and reasoning-enabled), including a novel MAS-specific Telephone Loop attack that exploits cross-agent delegation to create cyclical task loops. The attack is inert against SAS but compromises MAS when powered by three of the four frontier models evaluated (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4), averaging 80% across them at baseline. Only the fourth model, Claude Sonnet 4.6, resists the attack with a 92% detection rate. For the rest, the detection is 0% at baseline, reaching 33% with prompt-hardening for one model. We also show that obvious defenses do not generalize; prompt-hardening collapses one model's ASR from 100% to 8% while providing only modest reduction to the others. Our findings demonstrate that the transition from single- to multi-agent web systems changes the security landscape. Role specialization may not only lead to performance optimization but also introduce new architectural risks that require further study and defenses.

AI.tldr: This paper examines security vulnerabilities introduced when web agents transition from single-agent to multi-agent architectures. It proposes a taxonomy of MAS-specific attack vectors, presents a test-bed called WebMASLab, and demonstrates a novel "Telephone Loop" attack that exploits cross-agent delegation, which is inert against single-agent systems but highly effective against multi-agent setups using frontier LLMs.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based web agents evolve from single-agent (SAS) to multi-agent systems (MAS) with specialized sub-agents, new structural attack surfaces emerge. These MAS-specific vulnerabilities remain poorly understood and inadequately categorized, motivating a systematic security analysis of the architectural transition.
AI.method: The authors propose a taxonomy categorizing attack vectors specific to web-based MAS. They build WebMASLab, a test-bed that isolates architectural effects by holding constant the user task, tool surface, and browser substrate. They evaluate three adversarial scenarios under three conditions (baseline, prompt-hardened, reasoning-enabled), and introduce a novel MAS-specific Telephone Loop attack that exploits cross-agent delegation to create cyclical task loops. Four frontier models are tested: Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.
AI.result: The Telephone Loop attack achieves an average 80% attack success rate (ASR) against three of four frontier models (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, GPT-5.4) at baseline, with 0% detection. Claude Sonnet 4.6 resists with 92% detection. Prompt-hardening collapses one model's ASR from 100% to 8% but provides only modest reduction for others. Detection improves to only 33% with prompt-hardening for one model. Obvious defenses do not generalize across models.
AI.conclusion: The transition from single-agent to multi-agent web systems fundamentally changes the security landscape. While role specialization enables performance optimization, it also introduces new architectural risks. These findings underscore the need for further study and robust defenses tailored to MAS architectures.

title: Visualizing Placement Proposals for Window Arrangement in Mixed Reality: A Comparative User Study
summary: Adaptive mixed reality (MR) interfaces typically optimize window layouts on behalf of the user, with limited consideration for individual preferences. A promising alternative keeps users in the loop by presenting layout proposals for them to select from, but how these proposals should be visualized remains underexplored. We compare three proposal-visualization techniques for window placement, Situated Icon Preview, Situated Window Preview, and 3D Preview, against a Manual Positioning baseline. The techniques differ in level of detail and degree of interaction-space context. In a within-subjects user study, 24 participants completed a multi-stage trip-planning task in VR, individually placing seven sequentially introduced windows using each technique. We thereby focus on single-window placement under predefined proposal positions. We measured layouting time, number of layout changes, task load, user experience, and preference, complemented by semi-structured interviews. Although Situated Icon Preview and Situated Window Preview reduced layouting time compared to Manual Positioning - with Situated Window Preview also faster than 3D Preview - participants preferred direct manual control. We discuss the factors shaping this preference (perceived control, cognitive cost, familiarity, and informativeness of the proposal) and outline implications for hybrid approaches, as a promising combination of proposal-based suggestions with manual refinement.

AI.tldr: This paper compares three techniques for visualizing MR window-layout proposals (Situated Icon Preview, Situated Window Preview, 3D Preview) against Manual Positioning. While the preview techniques reduced layouting time, users preferred direct manual control, highlighting a speed-vs-preference tension and motivating hybrid approaches.
AI.motivation: Adaptive MR interfaces auto-optimize layouts with little regard for individual user preferences. Proposal-based selection keeps users in the loop, but how to visualize these proposals is underexplored. The work aims to fill this gap by systematically comparing visualization techniques for window-placement proposals.
AI.method: A within-subjects user study with 24 participants completing a multi-stage VR trip-planning task. Each participant placed seven sequentially introduced windows using four techniques: Manual Positioning (baseline), Situated Icon Preview, Situated Window Preview, and 3D Preview. These differ in level of detail and interaction-space context. Metrics included layouting time, number of layout changes, task load (NASA-TLX), user experience (UEQ), and subjective preference, plus semi-structured interviews.
AI.result: Situated Icon Preview and Situated Window Preview significantly reduced layouting time vs. Manual Positioning; Situated Window Preview was also faster than 3D Preview. Despite these efficiency gains, participants preferred direct manual control overall. Preference was shaped by perceived control, cognitive cost, familiarity, and informativeness of proposals.
AI.conclusion: Proposal-based previews can improve layout efficiency but do not replace the user's desire for direct control. The authors advocate for hybrid approaches that combine proposal-based suggestions with manual refinement, balancing speed with user agency.

title: Improving Mobile User Interface Testing with Model Driven Monkey Search
summary:
Testing mobile applications often relies on tools, such as Exerciser Monkey for Android systems, that simulate user input. Exerciser Monkey, for example, generates random events (e.g., touches, gestures, navigational keys) that give developers a sense of what their application will do when deployed on real mobile phones with real users interacting with it. These tools, however, have no knowledge of the underlying applications' structures and only interact with them randomly or in a predefined manner (e.g., if developers designed scenarios, a labour-intensive task) -- making them slow and poor at finding bugs.
  In this paper, we propose a novel control flow structure able to represent the code of Android applications, including all the interactive elements. We show that our structure can increase the effectiveness (higher coverage) and efficiency (removing duplicate/redundant tests) of the Exerciser Monkey by giving it knowledge of the test environment. We compare the interface coverage achieved by the Exerciser Monkey with our new Monkey++ using a depth first search of our control flow structure and show that while the random nature of Exerciser Monkey creates slow test suites of poor coverage, the test suite created by a depth first search is one order of magnitude faster and achieves full coverage of the user interaction elements. We believe this research will lead to a more effective and efficient Exerciser Monkey, as well as better targeted search based techniques for automated Android testing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel control flow structure for Android apps to guide test input generation, turning random Monkey testing into systematic Monkey++ testing that achieves full interface coverage an order of magnitude faster.
AI.motivation: Existing Android testing tools like Exerciser Monkey generate random or manually scripted user inputs without understanding the app's structure, making them slow and ineffective at finding bugs.
AI.method: The authors construct a control flow representation that captures all interactive elements within an Android application's code. They then replace Exerciser Monkey's random event generation with a depth-first search traversal of this structure, yielding a tool called Monkey++.
AI.result: Monkey++ achieves full coverage of user interaction elements and produces test suites that are one order of magnitude faster than the random baseline, while eliminating duplicate and redundant tests.
AI.conclusion: Injecting structural knowledge into test generation transforms random testing into efficient, high-coverage automated testing, and the approach paves the way for improved search-based techniques in Android test automation.

title: Agentic Coding in the Wild: Characterizing GitHub Copilot Traces at Production Scale
summary:
AI coding agents like GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, and Codex interleave multi-step LLM inference with tool execution, creating a workload different from chatbots. We present the first production-scale characterization of this workload using sampled GitHub Copilot traces from June 2026, comprising 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens.
  Our analysis reveals distinctive workload properties with important systems implications. For example, agentic coding sessions consist of sparse user-initiated turns, each unfolding into an autonomous agent loop of LLM calls almost always coupled with tool execution. This structure yields KV cache hit rates averaging 90% within a turn, but falling to 55\% across turn boundaries and drastically invalidated after events like model switches or context compaction. Diverse workflows and user behaviors are observed with variable and long-tailed token consumption, time span, and tool calls. We highlight the difference between quick agentic turnaround times and the minutes-long user idle periods at turn boundaries, and design a lightweight idle-time predictor that captures 86-90\% of total idle time, enabling proactive decisions for efficient resource orchestration. These findings challenge assumptions underlying current LLM-serving systems and provide an empirical foundation for agent-native infrastructure.

AI.tldr: First production-scale characterization of AI coding agent workloads (GitHub Copilot, 3.2M users, 761M LLM calls), revealing distinctive patterns—sparse user turns with dense autonomous agent loops, high intra-turn KV cache hit rates (90%) but sharp drops across turn boundaries (55%), and long user idle periods—that challenge current LLM-serving assumptions and motivate agent-native infrastructure design.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-serving systems are designed for chatbot workloads (single-turn, stateless). AI coding agents introduce a fundamentally different workload pattern—multi-step LLM inference interleaved with tool execution—yet no production-scale characterization exists to inform systems design for this emerging agentic paradigm.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of sampled production traces from GitHub Copilot (June 2026), covering 3.2M users, 13M sessions, 761M LLM calls, and 95T tokens. The authors characterize session structure, KV cache behavior, token consumption distributions, inter-turn timing, and user behavior patterns, then design a lightweight idle-time predictor.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Sessions consist of sparse user turns each unfolding into autonomous agent loops with tight LLM-tool coupling. (2) KV cache hit rates are ~90% within turns but drop to ~55% across turn boundaries, with further degradation from model switches and context compaction. (3) Token consumption, session duration, and tool calls exhibit long-tailed distributions. (4) A lightweight idle-time predictor captures 86–90% of total idle time, surfacing opportunities for proactive resource orchestration.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-serving systems, optimized for chatbot workloads, are ill-suited for agentic coding workloads. The findings provide an empirical foundation for designing agent-native infrastructure that accounts for autonomous agent loops, cache invalidation patterns, and predictable user idle periods.

title: Auditing Semantic Gains in Sequential Recommendation: A Lightweight Recovery Test
summary: Recent semantic and generative-retrieval recommenders report substantial improvements over ID-only sequential baselines, but it remains unclear whether these gains arise from language-model reasoning, semantic-ID generation, end-to-end semantic architectures, stronger offline item representations, or complementary semantic and collaborative signals. We investigate this attribution ambiguity through LIME-Rec, a lightweight and auditable recovery test. LIME-Rec combines three independent experts: a SASRec sequential expert, an ItemCF co-occurrence expert, and a semantic expert based on frozen BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5 item embeddings. Their full-catalog scores are normalized per user and combined through auditable score-level fusion followed by bounded history calibration. The fusion gate and calibration head are fitted on validation data only, require no serving-time language-model inference, and keep each expert contribution separately inspectable. On Amazon Beauty, Toys, and Sports, LIME-Rec achieves R@10 scores of 0.0996, 0.1105, and 0.0593, outperforming the strongest comparison baseline by 7.0%-12.0%. Three-expert fusion without history calibration consistently outperforms calibrated SASRec, showing that calibration alone does not explain the recovery. Randomly permuting item-text embeddings across item IDs reduces R@10 by 13.6%-17.5%, indicating that the gains depend on genuine item-text correspondence rather than additional representation capacity. These results suggest that lightweight recovery from offline item representations and transparent fusion should be ruled out before improvements are attributed to serving-time language modeling, semantic-ID generation, or heavier semantic machinery.

AI.tldr: LIME-Rec introduces a lightweight, auditable recovery test that fuses SASRec, ItemCF, and frozen semantic embeddings via score-level fusion, outperforming complex semantic recommenders and showing that gains stem from offline item representations rather than serving-time language modeling.
AI.motivation: There is attribution ambiguity in recent semantic and generative-retrieval recommenders — it is unclear whether reported improvements come from language-model reasoning, semantic-ID generation, end-to-end architectures, offline representations, or complementary signals. The authors aim to disentangle these factors.
AI.method: LIME-Rec combines three independent experts: (1) a SASRec sequential expert, (2) an ItemCF co-occurrence expert, and (3) a semantic expert using frozen BGE-base embeddings. Full-catalog scores are normalized per user and fused via an auditable score-level fusion gate with bounded history calibration. The gate and calibration head are fitted only on validation data, requiring no LM inference at serving time, and each expert's contribution remains separately inspectable.
AI.result: On Amazon Beauty, Toys, and Sports, LIME-Rec achieves Recall@10 of 0.0996, 0.1105, and 0.0593, outperforming the strongest baseline by 7.0%–12.0%. Three-expert fusion without calibration beats calibrated SASRec, ruling out calibration as the sole explanation. Randomly permuting item-text embeddings drops R@10 by 13.6%–17.5%, confirming dependence on genuine item-text correspondence rather than mere capacity.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight recovery from offline item representations with transparent fusion should be ruled out as a baseline before attributing gains to serving-time language modeling, semantic-ID generation, or heavier semantic architectures.

title: Cross-Task Dissociation in Frontier Vision-Language Model Theory of Mind
summary: Do frontier vision-language models present a coherent Theory-of-Mind (ToM) profile across tasks, matching the same human reference group, or does that profile fragment from one paradigm to the next? We evaluate a shared panel of nine frontier VLMs on two psychology-derived benchmarks: the Keysar Director Task (visual perspective-taking under egocentric interference) and the Frith-Happé animated triangles scored with the Castelli rubric (intention attribution from pure motion). On the Director Task, without chain-of-thought, the panel makes the egocentric error on 78\% of trials like children rather than adults; variation is substantial across models, and reasoning rescues several models. On the triangles, the panel under-attributes intention: its ToM profile sits more than three times closer to the high-functioning-autistic-adult (HF-ASD) mean than to the typical-development-adult (TD) mean, while Goal-Directed and Random stay near TD. No model is nearest TD on both tasks; the model that looks adult-like on the Director Task falls on the HF-ASD side on the triangles, and the most TD-like model on the triangles is child-like on the Director Task. We report group-level descriptions, not diagnostic labels for any model.

AI.tldr: Nine frontier VLMs show a fragmented Theory-of-Mind profile: they make child-like egocentric errors on the Keysar Director Task but resemble high-functioning autistic adults on the Frith-Happé triangles, with no model appearing neurotypical on both benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To determine whether frontier vision-language models exhibit a coherent Theory-of-Mind profile across different psychological paradigms — specifically, whether the same models resemble the same human reference group (e.g., neurotypical adults, children, autistic adults) consistently, or whether their profile fragments across tasks.
AI.method: Nine frontier VLMs were evaluated on two psychology-derived benchmarks: (1) the Keysar Director Task, measuring visual perspective-taking under egocentric interference; (2) the Frith-Happé animated triangles scored with the Castelli rubric, measuring intention attribution from pure motion. Performance was compared against human reference groups: typical-development adults (TD), children, and high-functioning autistic adults (HF-ASD).
AI.result: On the Director Task (without chain-of-thought), models made the egocentric error on 78% of trials, resembling children; reasoning rescued several models. On the Frith-Happé triangles, the panel's ToM profile was over three times closer to the HF-ASD mean than to the TD mean, though Goal-Directed and Random attributions stayed near TD. Crucially, no model was nearest TD on both tasks — models appearing adult-like on one task showed child-like or HF-ASD-like profiles on the other.
AI.conclusion: Frontier VLMs lack a coherent, unified Theory-of-Mind profile across paradigms. Their ToM-like behavior is task-fragmented, raising concerns about overinterpreting competence from any single benchmark. The authors emphasize these are group-level descriptions, not diagnostic labels.

title: Reflection, Education, Consistency: Towards Best Ethics Practices At Security And Privacy Conferences
summary:
Research ethics is a controversial and emotionally charged topic in the security and privacy community, sparking discussions at conferences and on social media. In recent years, some of the leading conferences have introduced interventions such as mandatory ethics sections, with mixed reactions within the community. Program committee chairs and steering committees increasingly emphasize ethics, yet there is limited empirical validation on ethics procedures and interventions, as well as no explicitly communicated goals.
  To support a shared understanding in our community and guide informed decisions at the conference level, we examined past ethics policies at the top-four conferences and conducted in-depth semi-structured interviews with senior and junior (n=20) community members, including some (former) chairs of program and research ethics committees. In these, we explored reasons for and goals of ethics procedures and discussed existing ethics interventions as well as possible new approaches proposed by our team.
  While the community appears to be evolving toward the identified goals, i.e., raising ethical awareness and preventing the publication of unethical work, we identified the lack of ethical education within the community itself as a major obstacle to further progress on this matter. Ethical education is often passed to the universities. Interviewees also mentioned challenges with the complexity of ethics policies and the lack of consistency across different conferences, as well as policies changing year-to-year. Several participants warned that over-regulation may lead to backlash, encouraging mere compliance, such as people turning to LLMs for ethics sections rather than undertaking in-depth consideration. In response, we suggest a coordinated, community-wide ethics steering effort and take a first step by introducing an open ethics wiki.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the state of research ethics in the security and privacy community through analysis of conference ethics policies and interviews with 20 community members. It identifies goals (raising awareness, preventing unethical publications), obstacles (lack of ethical education, policy complexity and inconsistency), and risks (over-regulation leading to superficial compliance). The authors propose a coordinated community-wide ethics steering effort and introduce an open ethics wiki.
AI.motivation: Despite growing emphasis on ethics by program committee chairs and steering committees at top security/privacy conferences, there is limited empirical validation of ethics procedures and interventions, no explicitly communicated goals, and mixed community reactions to interventions like mandatory ethics sections.
AI.method: The study employs a two-pronged approach: (1) examination of past ethics policies at the top-four security/privacy conferences, and (2) in-depth semi-structured interviews with 20 senior and junior community members, including former chairs of program and research ethics committees.
AI.result: The community is evolving toward identified goals (raising ethical awareness, preventing unethical publications), but faces obstacles including lack of ethical education (often externalized to universities), complexity/inconsistency of ethics policies across conferences, and year-to-year policy changes. Interviewees warned that over-regulation risks backlash and superficial compliance (e.g., using LLMs to generate ethics sections).
AI.conclusion: The authors recommend a coordinated, community-wide ethics steering effort and contribute a first step by introducing an open ethics wiki to foster shared understanding and consistency.

title: Seeing Through the Forecast Clutter: Communicating Climate Forecast Distributions with Weighted Multiple Forecast Visualizations
comment: Accepted to IEEE VIS 2026 Full Paper
summary: Forecasts often diverge because different models make varying assumptions to account for underlying uncertainty. Readers who consume forecasts may wish to survey the shape and spread of these multiple forecasts to get a full account of the different predictions. One approach to visualizing multiple forecasts is through Confidence Interval (CI) plots. However, while the summative CI plots can communicate uncertainty of an ensemble, they obscure attributes of individual forecasts that can lead to inaccurate perceptions of the distribution of these forecasts (e.g., implying a normal distribution when non-existent). To address this challenge, we investigate the use of multiple forecast visualization (MFV) in communicating nuanced forecast distributions through two preregistered experiments using climate forecast data. In Experiment 1 (480 participants), we compared how well MFV and CI plots can represent the distribution of multiple forecasts. We found that, compared to CI plots, MFV improved participants' ability to identify the underlying distribution of forecasts and reduced the likelihood of assuming normality. Building on Experiment 1, we examined in Experiment 2 (900 participants) whether a downsampled MFV showing 9 forecasts might be able to communicate additional forecast properties using linewidth and opacity without negatively impacting distribution perception. We found that visually weighting forecasts by linewidth or opacity preserves readers' perception of the underlying distribution. We discuss how these findings suggest the use of downsampled and weighted MFV to cut through forecast clutter by aligning perceived distribution with the underlying forecast distribution, while opening up design opportunities to use weighting to communicate additional forecast attributes.

AI.tldr: Confidence Interval plots can misrepresent the distribution of ensemble forecasts (e.g., falsely implying normality). Multiple Forecast Visualization (MFV) improves viewers' ability to perceive the true underlying forecast distribution, and downsampled/weighted MFV preserves this benefit while offering design flexibility for communicating additional forecast attributes.
AI.motivation: Traditional summative uncertainty visualizations like Confidence Interval (CI) plots obscure the distributional properties of individual forecasts within an ensemble, potentially leading viewers to incorrectly assume normality or miss multimodal/clustered patterns. The authors aim to address this perceptual limitation by investigating MFV as an alternative.
AI.method: Two preregistered experiments using climate forecast data. Experiment 1 (N=480) compared MFV vs. CI plots on participants' ability to identify the underlying distribution of multiple forecasts. Experiment 2 (N=900) tested whether a downsampled MFV (9 forecasts) using linewidth and opacity as visual weighting channels could communicate additional forecast properties without degrading distribution perception.
AI.result: Experiment 1: MFV significantly improved identification of the underlying forecast distribution and reduced false assumptions of normality compared to CI plots. Experiment 2: Visually weighting forecasts by linewidth or opacity in downsampled MFV preserved accurate distribution perception.
AI.conclusion: Downsampled and weighted MFV effectively aligns perceived distribution with the true underlying forecast distribution while reducing visual clutter. Weighting via linewidth or opacity opens design opportunities to encode additional forecast attributes without sacrificing distributional understanding.

title: SMS Opt-In/Opt-Out Consent Record Architecture in Enterprise CRM Systems: Compliance Patterns for Multi-Tenant Managed Packages
comment: 8 pages - Companion to arXiv:2607.12943 and arXiv:2607.15529
summary: Regulatory frameworks such as the Telephone Consumer Protection Act (TCPA) impose strict consent requirements on enterprise messaging systems: organizations must obtain and record explicit opt-in consent before sending SMS communications, and must immediately honor opt-out requests. While CRM platforms provide rich contact and lead data models, they do not natively model consent state as a first-class record type. This gap becomes architecturally significant in multi-tenant managed packages distributed via enterprise application marketplaces, where the package cannot assume or modify the installing organization's schema. This paper presents a production consent record architecture, generalized from patterns implemented within a CRM-native messaging managed package serving independent enterprise organizations spanning healthcare, financial services, and sales operations. We describe the data model design, keyword-based consent capture, a hash-based uniqueness strategy for deduplication, suppression enforcement at message send time, and the multi-tenant constraints that shaped these design decisions.

AI.tldr: Presents a production architecture for managing SMS consent records within a multi-tenant CRM managed package, addressing TCPA compliance through a first-class consent data model, keyword-based capture, hash-based deduplication, and send-time suppression enforcement.
AI.motivation: CRM platforms lack native first-class consent record types, creating an architectural gap when implementing TCPA-compliant SMS messaging in multi-tenant managed packages that cannot modify the host organization's schema.
AI.method: Design and implementation of a consent record architecture featuring: (1) a dedicated consent data model decoupled from the CRM schema, (2) keyword-based opt-in/opt-out capture, (3) hash-based uniqueness strategy for deduplication, and (4) suppression enforcement at message send time, all operating within multi-tenant managed package constraints.
AI.result: The architecture was generalized from production patterns deployed across independent enterprises in healthcare, financial services, and sales operations, demonstrating viability under TCPA regulatory requirements.
AI.conclusion: First-class consent modeling is architecturally necessary for compliant enterprise messaging in multi-tenant CRM environments. The hash-based deduplication and send-time suppression patterns provide a robust, schema-independent solution for managed packages.

title: Collaborative Memory Augmentation for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative Recommendation (GR) has exhibited great potential by modeling item transitions as a sequence-to-sequence task. Despite the success of GR, existing frameworks primarily focus on modeling individual user sequences within a constrained internal parametric space, failing to explicitly leverage cross-user collaborative signals. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{OMEGA}, a cOllaborative MEmory augmentation framework for Generative recommendAtion. OMEGA bridges the gap between implicit parametric knowledge and explicit collaborative signals. We first introduce a latent context compression method that utilizes learnable query tokens to distill sequential user behavior into compact representations, significantly reducing storage overhead. These compressed representations are aggregated into a collaborative memory bank, serving as an explicit repository of global behavioral patterns. To ensure precise knowledge acquisition, we design a lightweight and target-aware retrieval mechanism that identifies pertinent memories by considering both sequence-level and target-level similarities. Furthermore, a context-aware integration module, equipped with a gated cross-attention mechanism, is employed to adaptively fuse the retrieved collaborative memories with the local user context while mitigating the interference of noisy patterns. Empirical evaluations on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that OMEGA significantly outperforms existing advanced GR models, validating the potential of external memory as a complement to the generative paradigm.

AI.tldr: OMEGA introduces a collaborative memory augmentation framework for generative recommendation that stores compressed user behavior representations in an external memory bank and retrieves them via a target-aware mechanism, outperforming existing GR models.
AI.motivation: Existing Generative Recommendation (GR) models operate within constrained internal parametric spaces and only model individual user sequences, failing to explicitly leverage cross-user collaborative signals that are essential for capturing global behavioral patterns.
AI.method: OMEGA comprises three components: (1) latent context compression using learnable query tokens to distill sequential user behavior into compact representations; (2) a collaborative memory bank aggregating these compressed representations as explicit global behavioral patterns; (3) a lightweight target-aware retrieval mechanism considering both sequence-level and target-level similarities; and (4) a context-aware integration module with gated cross-attention that adaptively fuses retrieved memories with local user context while suppressing noise.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that OMEGA significantly outperforms existing advanced GR models, validating the effectiveness of external memory as a complement to the generative paradigm.
AI.conclusion: External collaborative memory augmentation effectively complements parametric generative recommendation models by explicitly encoding cross-user signals, bridging the gap between implicit knowledge and explicit collaborative patterns.

title: Neural operator learning for collision-aware trajectory planning of spacecraft swarms
comment: 27 pages, 6 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Nature Machine Intelligence. Video abstract included as ancillary file
summary: Autonomous spacecraft swarms must plan fuel-efficient, collision-free maneuvers in increasingly congested orbits, yet classical trajectory optimization scales poorly as pairwise safety constraints multiply with swarm size, and learning-based planners rarely transfer across swarm sizes or debris densities. Here we introduce a permutation-equivariant neural operator that maps distributions of spacecraft, targets and debris to collision-aware trajectories for an entire swarm in a single forward pass, paired with a batched Gauss-Newton finish that enforces exact orbital dynamics. The operator is trained without optimal-trajectory labels, combining self-supervised physics objectives with adversarial threats generated against its own rollouts. Trained on ten spacecraft, it generalizes zero-shot to swarms of 1,000 amid more than 11,000 catalogued objects, matching a per-agent optimal-control solver's accuracy, evading worst-case threats that a debris-blind baseline cannot, and reducing proximity within the swarm several-fold. Physics-grounded operator learning thus offers a fast, scalable alternative to optimal control for crowded orbits.

AI.tldr: A permutation-equivariant neural operator, trained without optimal-trajectory labels using self-supervised physics objectives and adversarial threats, maps spacecraft/debris distributions to collision-aware trajectories in one forward pass. Trained on 10 spacecraft, it zero-shot generalizes to 1,000+ spacecraft amid 11,000+ debris objects, matching per-agent optimal control accuracy while reducing proximity and evading threats.
AI.motivation: Classical trajectory optimization for autonomous spacecraft swarms scales poorly with swarm size due to pairwise safety constraints. Learning-based planners fail to transfer across varying swarm sizes or debris densities. A scalable, transferable approach is needed for fuel-efficient, collision-free maneuvering in congested orbital environments.
AI.method: A permutation-equivariant neural operator maps distributions of spacecraft, targets, and debris to collision-aware trajectories in a single forward pass. Training uses self-supervised physics objectives combined with adversarial threats generated against the operator's own rollouts, eliminating the need for optimal-trajectory labels. A batched Gauss-Newton refinement step enforces exact orbital dynamics post-inference.
AI.result: Trained on only 10 spacecraft, the operator zero-shot generalizes to swarms of 1,000 spacecraft with over 11,000 catalogued debris objects. It matches per-agent optimal-control solver accuracy, evades worst-case debris threats that a debris-blind baseline cannot handle, and reduces intra-swarm proximity several-fold.
AI.conclusion: Physics-grounded operator learning provides a fast, scalable alternative to optimal control for trajectory planning in crowded orbits, overcoming both the scalability limits of classical optimization and the transfer limitations of conventional learning-based planners.

title: Trimming: Decoupling Multiplicative Depth from Modulus Chains in RNS-CKKS via Rational Levels
summary:
Recent work on Grafting decouples scale factors from ciphertext moduli, enabling more flexible precision management in RNS-CKKS. However, the multiplicative depth remains fundamentally constrained by the modulus chain structure.
  In this paper, we propose \emph{Trimming}, a novel fine-grained level management mechanism that decouples multiplicative depth from modulus chains in RNS-CKKS via rational levels. The key idea is to introduce an auxiliary trimming modulus chain composed of smaller NTT-friendly modulus factors, which enables partial modulus transitions instead of directly discarding an entire modulus factor. By replacing conventional discrete level reductions with fine-grained modulus factor refinement, Trimming provides a rational-level abstraction beyond the traditional integer-based modulus chain representation.
  Our approach preserves the compatibility with existing RNS-CKKS arithmetic while enabling more flexible depth management and adaptive modulus transitions. Similar to Grafting, which addresses the precision bottleneck, Trimming targets the depth bottleneck in RNS-CKKS and contributes toward a fully decoupled RNS-CKKS architecture.
  The proposed framework will be further validated through concrete implementation and experimental evaluation to investigate its practical performance and computational overhead in real-world homomorphic encryption applications.

AI.tldr: Trimming introduces rational levels to decouple multiplicative depth from modulus chains in RNS-CKKS, using an auxiliary trimming modulus chain of smaller NTT-friendly factors for fine-grained, partial modulus transitions instead of coarse discrete level drops.
AI.motivation: RNS-CKKS multiplicative depth is fundamentally constrained by the modulus chain structure. While Grafting decouples scale factors from ciphertext moduli for precision flexibility, no analogous mechanism exists for depth — depth reductions still require discarding entire modulus factors, creating a bottleneck.
AI.method: The authors propose Trimming, which introduces an auxiliary trimming modulus chain composed of smaller NTT-friendly modulus factors. This enables partial modulus transitions (fine-grained modulus factor refinement) rather than discarding an entire modulus factor at each level. The result is a rational-level abstraction that replaces traditional integer-based discrete level reductions, while maintaining full compatibility with existing RNS-CKKS arithmetic.
AI.result: This is a proposal paper; concrete implementation and experimental validation are stated as future work. The framework's practical performance and computational overhead remain to be evaluated in real-world HE applications.
AI.conclusion: Trimming targets the depth bottleneck in RNS-CKKS, complementing Grafting (which addresses the precision bottleneck), and contributes toward a fully decoupled RNS-CKKS architecture where both precision and depth are managed independently of the modulus chain.

title: Revibing Code from Papers: Reimplementing HCI Artifacts
summary: Software artifacts for most technical HCI research projects are unavailable. The lack of access to these imposes limits on academic knowledge production. It is difficult to: extend or reuse research artifacts; use strong baselines in evaluating follow-up work; and perform replication or reproducibility research. In this work, we demonstrate the potential of new agentic AI technologies to revibe interactive software: reimplement systems directly from research papers. To measure the success of the approach, we describe a revibeability metric. By revibing recent research papers from UIST, and interviewing their original authors, we demonstrate the plausibility (and limitations) of revibed system. The results are encouraging. In many cases producing code suitable for strong baseline use. We argue that this may represent a fundamental shift in how we produce, use, and evaluate research artifacts in the technical HCI community.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using agentic AI to "revibe" (reimplement) interactive software systems directly from research papers, addressing the widespread unavailability of HCI research artifacts. The authors introduce a "revibeability" metric to evaluate success and demonstrate the approach by revibing recent UIST papers, validating results through author interviews. The findings suggest this could fundamentally change how the HCI community produces, uses, and evaluates research artifacts.
AI.motivation: Most technical HCI research projects lack available software artifacts, which constrains academic progress by hindering: (1) extension and reuse of prior work, (2) use of strong baselines in follow-up evaluations, and (3) replication and reproducibility studies. This inaccessibility represents a structural limitation on knowledge production in the field.
AI.method: The authors employ agentic AI technologies to automatically reimplement ("revibe") interactive software systems from their textual descriptions in research papers. They define a "revibeability" metric to quantify success. The approach is validated by applying it to recent UIST papers and conducting interviews with the original authors of those papers to assess the plausibility and limitations of the revibed systems.
AI.result: The results are encouraging: in many cases, the revibed code is of sufficient quality to serve as a strong baseline for follow-up research. Author interviews confirm the plausibility of the approach while also revealing its limitations.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that agentic-AI-driven reimplementation may represent a fundamental shift in how the technical HCI community produces, uses, and evaluates research artifacts, potentially transforming knowledge production practices in the field.

title: LoopsBench: From Harness Engineering to Loop Engineering in Benchmarking Coding Agent
summary: Coding agent infrastructure is shifting from harness engineering toward loop engineering as coding agents are deployed for sustained long-horizon software development. Existing benchmarks often center on localized tasks or end-state outcomes, offering limited insight into sustained execution. We introduce LOOPSBENCH, a long-horizon benchmark for loop engineering in coding agent evaluation. Each task is a dependency DAG over separately testable development units with source-evidenced prerequisite edges. LOOPSBENCH comprises 112 tasks from authentic sources spanning 8 programming languages and 9 domains. Its flow-aware runtime releases tests along the ready frontier and retains completed nodes as regression obligations. We evaluate frontier coding agents paired with widely used loop implementations. The strongest configuration, Opus-4.7 with Claude Code and outer continuation, resolves 25.00% of tasks. Recorded plans recover only part of the source-recovered prerequisite DAG, and regression events remain visible across the evaluated loop profiles. We open source the benchmark data and code, including all tasks, more than 5,300 development units, and executable tests, at microsoft/Loopsbench.

AI.tldr: LOOPSBENCH is a new benchmark for evaluating coding agents on long-horizon software development tasks structured as dependency DAGs. It features 112 tasks across 8 languages and 9 domains, with flow-aware testing that releases tests along the ready frontier and retains completed nodes for regression. The best agent (Opus-4.7 with Claude Code) solves only 25% of tasks, revealing significant gaps in planning and regression handling.
AI.motivation: Current coding agent benchmarks focus on localized, short-horizon tasks or final-state outcomes, failing to capture the challenges of sustained, long-horizon software development where agents must manage complex task dependencies, incremental progress, and regression avoidance across multiple development units.
AI.method: LOOPSBENCH structures each task as a dependency DAG of separately testable development units with source-evidenced prerequisite edges. It employs flow-aware runtime that releases tests along the ready frontier (units whose dependencies are satisfied) and retains completed nodes as regression obligations. The benchmark comprises 112 authentic tasks across 8 programming languages and 9 domains, with over 5,300 development units and executable tests.
AI.result: The strongest configuration — Opus-4.7 with Claude Code and outer continuation — resolves only 25.00% of tasks. Agent-recorded plans recover only partial portions of the source-recovered prerequisite DAG, and regression events (breaking previously passing units) persist across all evaluated loop profiles.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier coding agents remain far from mastering long-horizon loop engineering. Significant gaps exist in both planning (recovering true dependency structures) and execution (avoiding regressions). LOOPSBENCH provides a rigorous framework for measuring and improving these capabilities, and is released as open source to the community.

title: Shared Organizational Memory for Enterprise Coding Agents: System Design and Deployment Snapshot
summary: Enterprise coding agents rely on tools and retrieval, yet enterprise knowledge often remains outside public training data and formal documentation: internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, and tacit workflows. Existing knowledge interfaces expose stored resources but still depend on agents recognizing and explicitly recording lessons worth reusing, disconnecting capture from the coding workflow and leaving development experience repeatedly rediscovered. We report an ongoing production deployment of a shared organizational memory system that makes capture a platform-level part of coding work: it collects task-adjacent experience with contributor approval, curates it into reusable question-answer memories, gates obvious security and privacy risks, and retrieves memories for future agents. This short paper describes the deployed lifecycle and an operational snapshot. Effects on retrieval and coding tasks remain under evaluation.

AI.tldr: A production system that captures coding task-adjacent experience into a shared organizational memory, curates it into reusable Q&A memories with security/privacy gating, and retrieves them for future enterprise coding agents—addressing the gap where enterprise knowledge (internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions) is not captured by agents during routine work.
AI.motivation: Enterprise coding agents depend on tools and retrieval, but critical organizational knowledge—internal DSLs, proprietary platforms, local conventions, recent fixes, tacit workflows—remains outside public training data and formal documentation. Existing knowledge interfaces require agents to explicitly recognize and record reusable lessons, disconnecting capture from actual coding workflows. This causes development experience to be repeatedly rediscovered rather than systematically retained.
AI.method: The authors describe a deployed shared organizational memory system with a four-stage lifecycle: (1) Capture—collects task-adjacent experience during coding work with contributor approval; (2) Curation—transforms captured experience into reusable question-answer memory pairs; (3) Gating—applies automated checks for obvious security and privacy risks before storage; (4) Retrieval—serves relevant memories to future coding agents. The system makes capture a platform-level function integrated into the coding workflow.
AI.result: The paper reports on an ongoing production deployment and provides an operational snapshot of the system in use. However, quantitative effects on retrieval quality and downstream coding task performance remain under evaluation and are not yet reported.
AI.conclusion: Integrating memory capture as a platform-level primitive within the coding workflow—rather than requiring agents to self-identify reusable knowledge—offers a promising architectural approach for retaining enterprise-specific development experience. Formal evaluation of the system's impact on agent coding performance is still forthcoming.

title: Real-Time Hybrid Retrieval in Hyperbolic Space for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Edge Devices
summary: This paper presents a hybrid document retrieval system designed for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that operates entirely within the Lorentz model of hyperbolic geometry. Unlike conventional dense retrievers confined to Euclidean space, this system projects pretrained word embeddings into hyperbolic space through a learned HyTE-H transformation, whose exponential volume growth suits the hierarchical organization of natural language. Documents are segmented into overlapping chunks, indexed by their Lorentz embeddings, and retrieved through a two-stage pipeline that first applies BM25 lexical scoring, then re-ranks candidates using Lorentzian inner-product similarity. A tunable parameter $α$ blends the BM25 score with the hyperbolic similarity score. The system was evaluated on five datasets from the BEIR benchmark suite, SciFact, NFCorpus, ArguAna, SciDocs, and FiQA, achieving NDCG@10 scores of 0.654, 0.304, 0.342, 0.150, and 0.217 respectively with word embeddings alone, without fine-tuned neural encoders or cross-attention rerankers. The system supports real-time indexing of user-supplied documents and resource-efficient querying over tens of thousands of moderately sized documents, so hyperbolic retrieval can run on edge devices at interactive latencies.

AI.tldr: A hybrid document retrieval system for RAG that operates entirely in hyperbolic (Lorentz) space, combining BM25 lexical scoring with Lorentzian similarity re-ranking, achieving competitive NDCG@10 scores on BEIR benchmarks using only word embeddings without fine-tuned neural encoders.
AI.motivation: Conventional dense retrievers operate in Euclidean space, which poorly captures the hierarchical, tree-like structure inherent in natural language. Hyperbolic geometry, with its exponential volume growth, is a more natural fit for modeling linguistic hierarchies, enabling better semantic organization of document embeddings.
AI.method: The system projects pretrained word embeddings into the Lorentz model of hyperbolic geometry via a learned HyTE-H transformation. Documents are segmented into overlapping chunks and indexed by their Lorentz embeddings. Retrieval follows a two-stage pipeline: (1) BM25 lexical scoring for candidate generation, (2) re-ranking using Lorentzian inner-product similarity. A tunable parameter α blends the BM25 and hyperbolic similarity scores.
AI.result: Evaluated on five BEIR benchmark datasets — SciFact (0.654), NFCorpus (0.304), ArguAna (0.342), SciDocs (0.150), and FiQA (0.217) — using word embeddings alone, without fine-tuned neural encoders or cross-attention rerankers. The system supports real-time indexing and resource-efficient querying over tens of thousands of documents at interactive latencies on edge devices.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic retrieval is a viable, resource-efficient alternative to Euclidean dense retrievers for RAG, offering competitive retrieval quality without requiring fine-tuned encoders, and is lightweight enough for edge deployment.

title: HetGPS: Scalable Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Physics-Anchored Adaptive Safety for EV Charging
summary: Safety interventions for large populations of network-coupled agents must protect shared constraints without unnecessarily overriding task-oriented policy decisions. We present HetGPS, a hybrid graph-control framework synergizing learned graph risk with physics-anchored correction by separating intervention magnitude from corrective direction. An action-conditioned graph residual model schedules state-dependent intervention authority, while a physics model determines its direction. For electric vehicle (EV) charging, we couple this filter with a parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic policy, enabling topology-aware coordination with a learned model size independent of fleet size. Across five nested distribution networks with 200--3,218 EVs and 100 evaluation days, Adaptive Authority reduces bus--step voltage violations from 3.93--7.74\% without filtering to 0.52--3.44\%, while maintaining 99.06--100\% departure success. Relative to the same physics-directed projection with fixed authority, it improves mean reward on all five networks and lowers the mean safety score on four. The deployed policy-and-risk model contains 383,702 learned parameters at every scale; at 3,218 EVs, a matched centralized SAC actor is about $170\times$ larger. A policy trained on the eight-transformer system transfers zero-shot to the 16- and 32-transformer systems, attaining 0.57--0.75\% violation rates and at least 99.99\% departure success. These results show that learned graph risk can allocate intervention authority at scale while feeder physics anchors corrective action.

AI.tldr: HetGPS is a hybrid graph-control framework for multi-agent safety that combines a learned graph neural network risk model (deciding intervention magnitude) with a physics-based model (deciding corrective direction). Applied to large-scale EV charging coordination across distribution networks, it achieves low voltage violations while maintaining high departure success, with a compact model that transfers zero-shot to larger grids.
AI.motivation: Safety interventions in large-scale networked multi-agent systems (e.g., EV charging fleets) must protect shared physical constraints (e.g., voltage limits on distribution feeders) without overruling task-oriented RL policies unnecessarily. Existing approaches either lack scalability across fleet sizes or fail to separate the magnitude of intervention from its direction, leading to inefficient trade-offs between safety and task performance.
AI.method: HetGPS introduces an action-conditioned graph residual model that predicts state-dependent intervention authority (magnitude), while a physics model determines the corrective direction. This filter is coupled with a parameter-shared heterogeneous graph soft actor-critic (SAC) policy, enabling topology-aware coordination with a learned model size independent of fleet size. The framework performs Adaptive Authority control — dynamically adjusting how much to override the RL policy based on learned graph risk.
AI.result: Across five nested distribution networks (200–3,218 EVs, 100 evaluation days), Adaptive Authority reduces bus-step voltage violations from 3.93–7.74% (unfiltered) to 0.52–3.44%, while maintaining 99.06–100% departure success. It improves mean reward on all five networks and lowers mean safety score on four, compared to fixed-authority physics-directed projection. The policy-and-risk model uses only 383,702 learned parameters at any scale; at 3,218 EVs, a matched centralized SAC actor is ~170× larger. Zero-shot transfer from an 8-transformer training system to 16- and 32-transformer systems yields 0.57–0.75% violation rates and ≥99.99% departure success.
AI.conclusion: Learned graph risk can effectively allocate intervention authority at scale, while feeder physics anchors corrective action. This separation of magnitude and direction enables compact, transferable safety filters for large-scale networked agent coordination.

title: TI-StegoAlign: Channel-Guided Post-Training for Generative Text Steganography under Tokenization Inconsistency
summary: Generative text steganography enables LLM agents to exchange secret information through task-relevant messages. Yet most methods evaluate recovery on sender-side tokens, whereas the receiver observes only surface text. Detokenization and receiver-side retokenization can alter token boundaries, desynchronize coding states, and cause such evaluation to overestimate receiver-side recovery. Existing remedies rely on inference-time filtering or verification, correcting individual outputs without adapting the generation policy to the receiver-side channel. To address these limitations, we propose TI-StegoAlign, a channel-guided post-training framework. The Bit-Consistent Supervised Objective (BCSO) enlarges local coding margins at realized sender-side embedding positions. Channel-Conditioned Preference Optimization (CCPO) then aligns complete stegotexts using receiver-realistic recovery, text quality, and anti-steganalysis feedback. TI-StegoAlign updates only LoRA parameters and requires no tokenization-specific correction during communication. Experimental results show 100% receiver bit accuracy. Compared with the strongest baselines, TI-StegoAlign achieves a 21.6% reduction in normalized perplexity deviation and a 6.3% relative improvement in anti-steganalysis performance.

AI.tldr: TI-StegoAlign is a channel-guided post-training framework for generative text steganography that addresses the tokenization mismatch between sender and receiver by aligning the generation policy to the receiver-side channel, achieving 100% receiver bit accuracy with improved text quality and anti-steganalysis performance.
AI.motivation: Existing generative text steganography methods evaluate recovery based on sender-side tokens, but in practice the receiver only sees surface text. Detokenization and receiver-side retokenization can alter token boundaries and desynchronize coding states, causing sender-side evaluation to overestimate actual recovery. Current remedies use inference-time filtering or verification to correct individual outputs but fail to adapt the underlying generation policy to the receiver-side channel.
AI.method: TI-StegoAlign employs two components: (1) Bit-Consistent Supervised Objective (BCSO), which enlarges local coding margins at realized sender-side embedding positions; and (2) Channel-Conditioned Preference Optimization (CCPO), which aligns complete stegotexts using receiver-realistic recovery feedback, text quality signals, and anti-steganalysis feedback. The framework updates only LoRA parameters and requires no tokenization-specific corrections during inference.
AI.result: TI-StegoAlign achieves 100% receiver bit accuracy. Compared to the strongest baselines, it yields a 21.6% reduction in normalized perplexity deviation and a 6.3% relative improvement in anti-steganalysis performance.
AI.conclusion: By directly adapting the generation policy to the receiver-side channel rather than relying on post-hoc corrections, TI-StegoAlign eliminates the sender-receiver tokenization mismatch problem in generative text steganography, enabling reliable secret communication through LLM agents with high fidelity and stealth.

title: SkinSpline: A Body-Attached Skeleton-Supported Haptic Interface for Continuous Skin Deformation through Physical Interpolation
comment: 4 pages. To appear in the Proceedings of the 2026 ACM International Symposium on Wearable Computers (ISWC '26), October 11--15, 2026, Shanghai, China
summary: We present SkinSpline, a body-attached skeleton-supported haptic interface that renders continuous skin deformation through physical interpolation of sparse mechanical actuation. SkinSpline combines a low-resolution array of rack-and-pinion linear actuators with an elastic interlocking skeleton that transforms discrete actuator motions into smooth surface deformation, enabling continuous cutaneous feedback without dense actuator arrays. The system includes a modular hardware architecture, a configurable control pipeline, and a visual interface supporting real-time configuration and actuation. We demonstrate SkinSpline through multiple scenarios, including wave rendering, video-synchronized rhythmic touch, visually driven water-wave feedback in VR, and sensor-based remote touch reproduction. SkinSpline explores an alternative approach to continuous on-body haptic rendering by leveraging structural coupling between sparse actuation and deformable surfaces.

AI.tldr: SkinSpline is a body-attached haptic interface that uses sparse linear actuators with an elastic interlocking skeleton to render continuous skin deformation, enabling smooth cutaneous feedback without dense actuator arrays.
AI.motivation: Traditional haptic interfaces require dense actuator arrays to produce continuous skin sensations, which increases complexity, cost, and form-factor. The work is motivated by the need for a more efficient approach that achieves continuous cutaneous feedback using sparse mechanical actuation through structural coupling and physical interpolation.
AI.method: SkinSpline employs a low-resolution array of rack-and-pinion linear actuators combined with an elastic interlocking skeleton. The skeleton physically interpolates between discrete actuator motions, transforming them into smooth, continuous surface deformation across the skin. The system includes modular hardware, a configurable control pipeline, and a real-time visual interface for configuration and actuation.
AI.result: The system was demonstrated across multiple scenarios: wave rendering, video-synchronized rhythmic touch, visually driven water-wave feedback in VR, and sensor-based remote touch reproduction, validating the approach of sparse-actuator continuous haptic rendering.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging structural coupling between sparse actuation and deformable surfaces offers a viable alternative approach for continuous on-body haptic rendering, reducing actuator density while maintaining rich cutaneous feedback.

title: OrEdge: Efficient Multi-Modal Anomaly Detection in Distributed Software Systems via Orthogonal-Domain Learning
summary: We introduce Orthogonal-Edge (OrEdge), a lightweight framework for real-time anomaly detection in multi-modal distributed software systems. Unlike existing approaches that rely on computationally expensive attention- and graph-based architectures, OrEdge leverages orthogonal-domain temporal representations to achieve accurate anomaly detection with substantially lower computational complexity and model size. It jointly analyzes heterogeneous monitoring data, including logs, metrics, and traces, to identify abnormal software behavior, capture temporal dependencies, and reduce redundancy across observability signals. At its core, OrEdge incorporates OrEdgeCore, a lightweight orthogonal-domain reconstruction module that captures recurring temporal patterns while suppressing transient variations. Evaluated on three real-world microservice datasets (MSDS, SN, and TT), OrEdge achieves competitive detection performance while reducing the reconstruction model size to at most 9.6K parameters, compared with 20K--143K parameters in existing methods. This compact design enables efficient deployment on resource-constrained edge devices: on Raspberry Pi platforms, OrEdge achieves sub-second inference and reduces inference latency by over an order of magnitude compared with existing approaches. Extensive ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, orthogonal basis evaluations, and qualitative case studies further validate the effectiveness of each design component. Overall, OrEdge demonstrates that orthogonal-domain temporal modeling provides an effective alternative to computationally intensive attention- and graph-based architectures, achieving a favorable balance between detection accuracy and computational efficiency for real-time multi-modal anomaly detection in edge environments. The code is available at https://github.com/theamrzaki/MicroService_Twin_Original.

AI.tldr: OrEdge is a lightweight orthogonal-domain framework for real-time multi-modal anomaly detection in distributed systems, achieving competitive accuracy with only 9.6K parameters and sub-second inference on Raspberry Pi—over 10x faster than existing attention/graph-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing anomaly detection methods for multi-modal distributed systems rely on computationally expensive attention- and graph-based architectures, making them impractical for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. There is a need for an accurate yet lightweight alternative that can process heterogeneous observability data (logs, metrics, traces) in real time at the edge.
AI.method: OrEdge employs orthogonal-domain temporal representations via a core module called OrEdgeCore. This lightweight reconstruction module captures recurring temporal patterns while suppressing transient variations by leveraging orthogonal bases. The framework jointly analyzes heterogeneous monitoring data (logs, metrics, traces) to identify abnormal software behavior, capture temporal dependencies, and reduce redundancy across observability signals—all without relying on attention or graph neural networks.
AI.result: On three real-world microservice datasets (MSDS, SN, TT), OrEdge achieves competitive detection performance with at most 9.6K parameters (vs. 20K–143K for existing methods). On Raspberry Pi, it achieves sub-second inference with over an order of magnitude latency reduction. Ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, orthogonal basis evaluations, and qualitative case studies validate each design component.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal-domain temporal modeling is an effective alternative to attention- and graph-based architectures, offering a favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-off for real-time multi-modal anomaly detection in edge environments.

title: AgentStream: How Well Do Self-Evolving LLM Agents Perform Under Streaming Tasks?
