Aggregate action rates conceal significant differences in action sequences, opponent responses, and sensitivity to race position. Patterns across 3–5 player races are model-specific rather than reflecting a uniform effect of adding competitors. These findings demonstrate that LLM behavior in multi-agent race simulations is fragile and representation-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent AI-race simulations require validity checks and trajectory-level analysis before interpreting LLM outputs as strategic, human-like, or safety-aware. Without such auditing, apparent strategic behavior may reflect superficial pattern matching rather than genuine understanding. The findings are exploratory and limited to the specific models, prompts, and decoding settings tested.

title: A False Average: Chain-of-Thought Monitors Collapse Where They Are the Only Defense
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring is meant to catch the reward hacks that look clean in the actions and betray themselves only in the reasoning. We show that this is exactly where an adversary who controls the reasoning can defeat it. Rewriting only an agent's reasoning to read as good-faith engineering, while copying every command and output verbatim so the exploit is unchanged, drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on that subset from about 95% to under 11% in one gradient-free shot. A monitor's aggregate accuracy is a false average: dominated by hacks the actions give away, it hides the near-total collapse this rewrite produces on the subset where CoT monitoring is the only signal. The attack transfers across monitor families and agent models, reproduces with live agents, though against a calibrated monitor evasion concentrates in the strongest agent. Trace-only defenses recover it only partially, even one primed on the attack, because the rewrite stays truthful about what happened and lies only about intent; only information from outside the trace helps substantially. A probe on an open-weight surrogate monitor's activations separates the hacks its verdict misses, but a causal control shows this is a detector, not evidence the monitor secretly knows.

AI.tldr: Adversaries can defeat chain-of-thought monitoring by rewriting only the reasoning portion to appear benign while preserving the exploit's actions verbatim, dropping catch rates from ~95% to under 11% in a single gradient-free shot. This reveals that monitor aggregate accuracy is misleadingly inflated by action-obvious hacks, and trace-only defenses recover only partially because the rewritten reasoning remains factually truthful about what happened, lying only about intent.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought monitoring is proposed as a safety mechanism to detect reward hacking that is invisible in agent actions but apparent in reasoning. The authors challenge this assumption by investigating whether an adversary who controls the reasoning can systematically defeat CoT monitors, exposing a fundamental vulnerability in relying on reasoning traces as an oversight signal.
AI.method: The attack rewrites an agent's reasoning to appear as good-faith engineering while copying all commands and outputs verbatim (preserving the exploit unchanged). This is done in a single gradient-free shot. The authors evaluate against held-out monitors across multiple monitor families and agent models, test transferability, reproduce with live agents, examine trace-only defenses (including those primed on the attack), and probe open-weight surrogate monitor activations to separate missed hacks. A causal control distinguishes detection from the monitor "secretly knowing."
AI.result: The rewrite drops a held-out monitor's catch rate on the targeted subset from ~95% to under 11%. Aggregate accuracy is dominated by hacks revealed through actions, masking near-total collapse on the subset where CoT monitoring is the sole signal. The attack transfers across monitor families and agent models. Evasion concentrates in the strongest agent against a calibrated monitor. Trace-only defenses recover performance only partially, even when primed on the attack, because the rewrite stays truthful about events and lies only about intent. Outside-trace information helps substantially. Activation probes can separate missed hacks, but causal control shows this reflects detection capability, not evidence the monitor covertly retains knowledge of the hack.
AI.conclusion: CoT monitoring is brittle against adversarial reasoning rewrites. The false sense of security from aggregate accuracy metrics conceals catastrophic failure on the very cases where reasoning oversight is most needed. Defenses relying solely on the trace are insufficient because distinguishing deceptive from genuine intent requires information beyond the reasoning text itself.

title: Who's That Player?: Externalizing Query Interpretation in Spoken XR Sports Interaction
summary: XR sports viewing enables spectators to follow play from immersive, spatially anchored perspectives while accessing contextual analytics directly within the scene. In such settings, speech offers a practical interaction modality because text entry and menu navigation can interrupt attention during fast-paced gameplay. However, spoken queries are often underspecified: viewers may omit which player, time period, field location, or metric they intend. When systems resolve these ambiguities implicitly, their assumptions remain hidden, making misinterpretations difficult to notice and correct (repair). We investigate how externalizing a system's interpretation of spoken queries can support inspection and correction of such misunderstandings in XR sports viewing. Through a formative study, we identified four recurring ambiguity types (referential, spatial, temporal, and metric) that characterize ambiguous spoken queries in this context. We develop a design space that organizes externalization along three dimensions (ambiguity type, interpretation state, externalization strategy) and instantiate it in an interactive XR soccer viewing system that combines situated visual cues with supporting analytic views. A within-subjects user study (N=16) comparing externalized interpretation against a voice-only baseline reveals that externalization is associated with higher inspectability on most measured dimensions and increased explicit repair language overall. However, repair occurred in only 38% of misaligned externalization trials, and this visibility-action gap varied by ambiguity type, indicating that transparency and correction affordance are orthogonal design axes.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how to externalize a system's interpretation of ambiguous spoken queries in XR sports viewing, organizing design dimensions (ambiguity type, interpretation state, externalization strategy) and evaluating a prototype system. Results show externalization improves inspectability and repair language, but a visibility-action gap persists — users repaired only 38% of misaligned interpretations, revealing transparency and correction affordance as orthogonal design axes.
AI.motivation: In XR sports viewing, speech is a practical interaction modality because manual input disrupts attention during fast-paced gameplay. However, spoken queries are frequently underspecified (omitting which player, time period, location, or metric), forcing systems to resolve ambiguities implicitly. When these assumptions remain hidden, misinterpretations are difficult to notice and correct. The core motivation is to explore whether making the system's interpretation visible (externalization) can support users in inspecting and repairing misunderstandings.
AI.method: The work proceeds in three phases: (1) a formative study identifying four recurring ambiguity types in spoken XR sports queries — referential, spatial, temporal, and metric; (2) development of a design space along three dimensions (ambiguity type, interpretation state, externalization strategy) and its instantiation in an interactive XR soccer viewing prototype combining situated visual cues with supporting analytic views; (3) a within-subjects user study (N=16) comparing the externalized interpretation system against a voice-only baseline, measuring inspectability, explicit repair language, and repair rates across ambiguity types.
AI.result: Externalized interpretation was associated with higher inspectability on most measured dimensions and increased explicit repair language overall compared to the voice-only baseline. However, repair occurred in only 38% of trials where externalization revealed misaligned interpretations. This visibility-action gap varied by ambiguity type, demonstrating that making interpretations visible does not guarantee users will correct them.
AI.conclusion: Transparency (externalizing system interpretations) and correction affordance (enabling users to repair errors) are orthogonal design axes in XR speech interfaces. Designers should not assume that increased visibility alone leads to corrective action. Future systems must actively scaffold the repair process, potentially tailoring mechanisms to specific ambiguity types, to bridge the observed visibility-action gap.

title: AiFlow: Token-Native Reactive Orchestration with Bounded Backpressure for Streaming LLM Applications
comment: 24 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables, 1 algorithm, and 1 code listing. Public implementation: https://github.com/ModelEngine-Group/fit-framework
summary: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly operate as streaming workflows combining retrieval, tool calls, safety filters, and multi-agent coordination. Although contemporary frameworks expose provider deltas, workflow nodes often treat generation as coarse request-response steps, leaving queue management, worker allocation, ordering, and backpressure to ad hoc callback code. This paper presents AiFlow, a token-native reactive orchestration model that normalizes provider deltas into typed Context<T> events propagated through a directed streaming graph. Each node is managed by a Node Guardian that declares and enforces local queue bounds, worker concurrency, ordering, overflow policy, cancellation propagation, and retry discipline. We formalize the bounded-memory property, present the compilation from a compact DSL and JSON graph form, and provide static validation for type safety, state concurrency, and injection compatibility. Controlled microbenchmarks, captured DeepSeek trace replay (30 runs), descriptive online runs, LangGraph baselines, a streaming RAG workload, and an Ollama local-backend check show that AiFlow does not alter provider-side Model TTFT but reduces Application TTFPT by 70.9-94.7\% versus aggregation and keeps runtime-owned queue depth within declared bounds (93.7-96.5\% MaxQ reduction versus unbounded policies). The supplementary artifact contains scripts, raw traces, machine-readable tables, checksums, and an API-free smoke test; the public implementation is available through the FIT Framework repository.

AI.tldr: AiFlow introduces a token-native reactive orchestration model for LLM streaming workflows, using typed Context<T> events and Node Guardians to manage concurrency, backpressure, and ordering, achieving 70.9–94.7% reduction in application-side Time-To-First-Produced-Token versus aggregation baselines.
AI.motivation: LLM applications increasingly operate as complex streaming workflows (retrieval, tool calls, safety filters, multi-agent coordination), but current frameworks treat generation as coarse request-response steps, forcing developers to handle queue management, worker allocation, ordering, and backpressure through ad hoc callbacks. This creates reliability and efficiency gaps.
AI.method: AiFlow normalizes provider deltas into typed Context<T> events propagated through a directed streaming graph. Each node is governed by a Node Guardian that declares and enforces local queue bounds, worker concurrency, ordering, overflow policy, cancellation propagation, and retry discipline. The system includes a compact DSL and JSON graph form with static validation for type safety, state concurrency, and injection compatibility, and provides a formal proof of the bounded-memory property.
AI.result: AiFlow preserves provider-side Model Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) unchanged, while reducing Application Time-To-First-Produced-Token (TTFPT) by 70.9–94.7% compared to aggregation approaches. Runtime-owned queue depth remains within declared bounds, achieving 93.7–96.5% MaxQ reduction versus unbounded policies. Validation spans controlled microbenchmarks, DeepSeek trace replay (30 runs), LangGraph baselines, streaming RAG workloads, and Ollama local-backend checks.
AI.conclusion: AiFlow demonstrates that a token-native reactive orchestration approach with declarative Node Guardians can dramatically reduce application-level latency and enforce bounded resource usage in LLM streaming workflows, without impacting provider-side generation latency. The implementation is publicly available through the FIT Framework repository.

title: MemoryForge: Synthesize Lifelong Memory for Human-Like LLM Agents
summary: Equipping Large Language Models (LLMs) with human-like personas is crucial for agentic applications, such as role-play and user simulation. Traditional prompt-based methods rely on descriptive conditioning by injecting static textual profiles, which often makes agents show generic behaviors due to a lack of realistic life memory. To fill this gap, we introduce memory-based conditioning, a paradigm inspired by the cognitive psychology, which replaces abstract profiles with an autobiographical memory base, enabling frozen LLMs to dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memory to guide their behaviors. We formalize its enabling task as customized lifelong memory synthesis and propose MemoryForge, a novel framework to synthesize such lifelong memory from brief target personas. MemoryForge has three key components: a context generator for socio-historical grounding, a life organizer for developmental coherence toward the target identity, and a multi-resolution simulator that balances broad temporal summaries with high-fidelity episodic experiences. Experiments on PersonaGym for role-play and SimulatorArena for user-simulation, show that the synthesized memory base by MemoryForge enables frozen LLMs to exhibit more human-like behaviors than strong descriptive conditioning baselines across multiple metrics and LLM backbones.

AI.tldr: MemoryForge synthesizes realistic autobiographical memories from brief persona descriptions, enabling frozen LLMs to dynamically retrieve situation-relevant memories for more human-like role-play and user simulation, outperforming static descriptive conditioning methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional prompt-based persona methods use static textual profiles, which produce generic agent behaviors due to a lack of realistic, situated life memory. The authors aim to replace abstract profiles with dynamic, memory-based conditioning grounded in autobiographical memory.
AI.method: MemoryForge framework with three components: (1) a context generator for socio-historical grounding of the persona, (2) a life organizer ensuring developmental coherence toward the target identity, and (3) a multi-resolution simulator balancing broad temporal summaries with high-fidelity episodic experiences. The synthesized memory base enables retrieval-augmented conditioning of frozen LLMs.
AI.result: Evaluated on PersonaGym (role-play) and SimulatorArena (user simulation), MemoryForge-synthesized memories enabled frozen LLMs to exhibit more human-like behaviors than strong descriptive conditioning baselines, across multiple metrics and LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: Memory-based conditioning via synthesized autobiographical memory is a viable and effective paradigm shift from static descriptive profiles for building more human-like LLM agents in role-play and user simulation tasks.

title: Geometric Self-Supervised Pre-training for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
summary:
Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) techniques have emerged as a highly efficient alternative to traditional exact algorithms for solving routing problems such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). However, the generalization capabilities of these Reinforcement Learning-based models are severely hindered when scaling to high-dimensional instances. This issue has been mitigated in other domains, like computer vision and natural language processing, by adopting a self-supervised pre-training strategy. Nevertheless, its application to routing graphs, which lack complex topological attributes beyond 2D spatial coordinates, remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework specifically designed to capture spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions. By applying isometric transformations, such as rotations and axial reflections, the model learns robust structural representations prior to the policy optimization phase. Empirical results demonstrate that this strategy consistently outperforms models trained from scratch (baselines), achieving a 7.23\% improvement in tour length for massive zero-shot extrapolation scenarios (TSP1,000). Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits remarkable computational efficiency, delivering speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over the exact solver Concorde at massive scales.
  The source code and pre-trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/davidaguadocosano/TSP-GeoPretrain.git.

AI.tldr: Proposes a geometric self-supervised pre-training framework for neural combinatorial optimization on TSP that uses isometric transformations (rotations, reflections) to learn robust spatial representations, achieving 7.23% improvement in zero-shot TSP1000 extrapolation and up to 100x speedup over Concorde.
AI.motivation: NCO models for routing problems suffer from poor generalization when scaling to high-dimensional instances. While self-supervised pre-training has succeeded in CV and NLP, applying it to routing graphs is challenging because these graphs lack complex topological attributes beyond 2D spatial coordinates. The authors aim to bridge this gap by designing a pre-training strategy tailored to the geometric nature of routing problems.
AI.method: A geometric self-supervised pre-training framework that applies isometric transformations (rotations and axial reflections) to 2D coordinate inputs. The model learns spatial invariance and global relative distance distributions in a self-supervised manner before the reinforcement learning-based policy optimization phase.
AI.result: The proposed method consistently outperforms models trained from scratch, achieving a 7.23% improvement in tour length on massive zero-shot extrapolation (TSP1,000). It also delivers speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over the exact solver Concorde at large scales.
AI.conclusion: Geometric self-supervised pre-training effectively mitigates the generalization limitations of NCO models on large-scale TSP instances, offering both superior solution quality and dramatic computational efficiency gains over exact solvers.

title: HyperAgent4POI: Dynamic Semantic Message Passing on Multi-Agent Hypergraphs for Missing-Modality Recommendation
summary: Next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation benefits from textual and visual content that describes venue semantics, yet such content is often incomplete in real-world services. Missing modalities weaken POI representations and reduce the semantic evidence available for ranking. The resulting representations also provide unreliable evidence for modeling higher-order user--POI interactions. We propose HyperAgent4POI, which uses Dynamic Semantic Message Passing (DSMP) to perform modality completion and soft incidence refinement within each hypergraph layer. Persistent node agents share a frozen Llama backbone and use role-specific adapters to produce node-to-hyperedge messages. Semantic hyperedge motifs formed from these messages guide soft incidence scoring and modality completion. Final node representations are cached for online ranking without LLM calls. Experiments on three real-world LBSN datasets show consistent ranking gains over 15 baselines across modality-missing rates, while cached inference provides practical online efficiency. Under a 60% modality-missing rate, HyperAgent4POI improves NDCG@20 over the strongest baseline by 8.2% on average across the three datasets.

AI.tldr: HyperAgent4POI addresses incomplete multimodal POI data in next-POI recommendation by using a frozen LLM backbone with role-specific adapters to perform modality completion and soft incidence refinement via dynamic semantic message passing on hypergraphs, achieving significant ranking gains with cached, efficient online inference.
AI.motivation: Real-world location-based services often have incomplete textual and visual content describing POI semantics. Missing modalities weaken POI representations, reduce semantic evidence for ranking, and undermine higher-order user-POI interaction modeling. Existing methods lack effective mechanisms for modality completion and robust hypergraph incidence learning under such missing data conditions.
AI.method: The authors propose HyperAgent4POI, which features: (1) Dynamic Semantic Message Passing (DSMP) operating within hypergraph layers for simultaneous modality completion and soft incidence refinement; (2) persistent node agents that share a frozen Llama backbone with role-specific adapters to generate node-to-hyperedge messages; (3) semantic hyperedge motifs derived from these messages that guide soft incidence scoring and modality completion; and (4) caching of final node representations for online ranking, eliminating LLM inference latency at serving time.
AI.result: Experiments on three real-world LBSN datasets show consistent ranking improvements over 15 baselines across varying modality-missing rates. Under a 60% modality-missing rate, HyperAgent4POI improves NDCG@20 over the strongest baseline by 8.2% on average across the three datasets, while cached inference ensures practical online efficiency.
AI.conclusion: HyperAgent4POI effectively addresses the practical challenge of incomplete multimodal content in POI recommendation by leveraging LLM-based agents within a hypergraph framework. The approach combines semantic richness from frozen LLMs with efficient cached inference, achieving state-of-the-art ranking performance without compromising online serving latency.

title: CRAFTS: Collaborative Role-Adaptive Fine-Tuning of LLM Agents for Chemical Process Simulation
summary: Constructing an executable chemical-process model remains manually intensive. Chemical engineers translate underspecified requests into coupled decisions about unit operations, thermodynamics, streams, specifications, degrees of freedom (DoF), initialization, solver repair, and optimization; one error can invalidate the model. CRAFTS mirrors the staged workflow of chemical engineers by decomposing simulation building into bounded subtasks assigned to seven bounded roles, with deterministic IDAES/Pyomo gates between stages. Given a natural-language request, process flowsheet diagram (PFD) evidence, and curated chemical-engineering knowledge, Input Understanding and Intent recover requirements, constraints, and process semantics; visual, topology, and specification specialists translate them into typed simulator contracts; and Debug and Optimization support bounded repair and eligible optimization. Fine-tuning is applied to the three schema-critical visual, topology, and specification roles, while the remaining roles use untuned Qwen. The resulting VisualGraphIR, TopologyIR, SpecIR, BuildPlan, and SolveReport expose unit, port, thermodynamic, numerical, and execution decisions. Compatible constructors, property packages, and runners are attached only after semantic artifacts pass engineering gates. We introduce OpenIDAES-450, a 450-case IDAES process- simulation dataset, and evaluate the complete seven-role LangChain/LangGraph workflow through solve and eligible optimization on its frozen 82-case held-out split. CRAFTS completes the prescribed validation and execution contract for for 91.5% of cases and achieves unit, stream, and directed-connection F1 scores of 0.815, 0.791, and 0.782. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of role specialization, typed intermediate representations, and deterministic engineering gates for reliable automated process-model construction.

AI.tldr: CRAFTS is a seven-role LLM-based workflow that automates chemical process model construction from natural language and PFD inputs, using typed intermediate representations and deterministic engineering gates. It achieves 91.5% completion rate on a held-out 82-case test set with strong F1 scores for unit, stream, and connection identification.
AI.motivation: Manually constructing executable chemical-process models is labor-intensive and error-prone. Chemical engineers must translate underspecified natural-language requests into numerous interdependent decisions spanning unit operations, thermodynamics, streams, specifications, degrees of freedom, initialization, solver repair, and optimization. A single mistake can invalidate the entire model. The motivation is to automate this complex, multi-stage workflow reliably.
AI.method: CRAFTS decomposes simulation building into bounded subtasks assigned to seven specialized roles — Input Understanding, Intent, Visual, Topology, Specification, Debug, and Optimization — orchestrated via a LangChain/LangGraph workflow. Three schema-critical roles (Visual, Topology, Specification) are fine-tuned, while the remaining four use untuned Qwen. The pipeline produces typed intermediate representations (VisualGraphIR, TopologyIR, SpecIR, BuildPlan, SolveReport) that expose all key decisions. Deterministic IDAES/Pyomo gates validate semantic artifacts before constructors, property packages, and runners are attached. A new dataset, OpenIDAES-450 (450 IDAES simulation cases), is introduced for training and evaluation.
AI.result: On the frozen 82-case held-out split of OpenIDAES-450, CRAFTS completed the prescribed validation and execution contract for 91.5% of cases. It achieved unit F1 of 0.815, stream F1 of 0.791, and directed-connection F1 of 0.782.
AI.conclusion: Role specialization, typed intermediate representations, and deterministic engineering gates are effective strategies for reliable automated process-model construction, as demonstrated by CRAFTS' strong completion rate and F1 performance.

title: Domain Decoupling Attack: Exploiting the Validation Gap Between Protective DNS and Shared Edge Routing
summary: Network attackers often conceal malicious communication within legitimate Internet traffic. Existing CDN-based evasion techniques rely on SNI--Host inconsistency, insufficient domain ownership verification, or provider-specific routing rewrites, which limit their applicability in modern CDN environments. We identify a validation gap in DNS-based authorization, where permission derived from an allowed domain applies to a shared IP and can be reused to reach another tenant in both CDN and non-CDN shared-hosting environments. This paper presents the Domain Decoupling Attack (DDA), which resolves an allowed domain to obtain permission for a shared edge IP and subsequently connects to the same address while presenting the hidden domain consistently in both TLS SNI and HTTP Host. Measurements of 1,069,048 domains across six continents produce 18,025,068 successful probes and identify exposure rates of 95.8% overall, 99.26% for CDN domains, 92.75% for non-CDN domains, and 97.7% for non-CDN cross-tenant IPs, while laboratory experiments reveal a structural limitation of DNS-bound access control on shared addresses. These results clarify the security risks of DNS-derived IP authorization and support the evaluation and improvement of access-control mechanisms in CDN and non-CDN shared-hosting environments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Domain Decoupling Attack (DDA), which exploits a DNS-based authorization gap allowing an attacker to reuse permission from an allowed domain to access a hidden domain sharing the same IP, consistently presenting the hidden domain in TLS SNI and HTTP Host headers. Measurements across 1M+ domains reveal ~95.8% exposure rates, highlighting structural weaknesses in DNS-derived IP access control in shared-hosting environments.
AI.motivation: Existing CDN-based evasion techniques rely on SNI–Host inconsistency, insufficient domain ownership verification, or provider-specific routing rewrites, limiting their applicability in modern CDN environments. The authors identified a fundamental validation gap in DNS-based authorization mechanisms where permission bound to an IP address can be reused to reach co-tenants on shared infrastructure, a problem not adequately addressed by current defenses.
AI.method: The authors designed the Domain Decoupling Attack (DDA): (1) resolve an allowed domain to obtain a shared edge IP, (2) connect to that same IP while presenting a different, hidden domain consistently in both TLS SNI and HTTP Host headers. They then conducted large-scale empirical measurements of 1,069,048 domains across six continents, generating 18,025,068 successful probes to quantify exposure rates across CDN, non-CDN, and cross-tenant scenarios, supplemented by controlled laboratory experiments.
AI.result: The measurements yielded 18,025,068 successful probes with exposure rates of 95.8% overall, 99.26% for CDN domains, 92.75% for non-CDN domains, and 97.7% for non-CDN cross-tenant IPs. Laboratory experiments confirmed a structural limitation of DNS-bound access control on shared addresses, demonstrating that the vulnerability is intrinsic rather than configurational.
AI.conclusion: DNS-derived IP authorization on shared infrastructure introduces systemic security risks. The high exposure rates across both CDN and non-CDN environments demonstrate that current access-control mechanisms are structurally inadequate. These findings support the need for reevaluation and improvement of authorization mechanisms that rely solely on DNS-based permission models in shared-hosting environments.

title: The Assistant Erased You: Measuring Loss of Authorship Signals in AI-Mediated Communication
summary: Research on AI-mediated communication has examined how AI assistance shapes interpersonal perceptions and reduces stylistic diversity across users. We ask a complementary question at the individual level: after a message is rewritten by an AI writing assistant, can its author still be distinguished from others? We introduce the Idiolect Erasure Rate (IER), defined as the reduction in authorship-attribution accuracy following AI-assisted rewriting. We evaluate IER on three pre-generative-AI corpora using a stylometric model and the authorship-specific LUAR model. Heavy rewriting substantially weakens authorship signals in personal blogs and workplace email, reducing LUAR attribution by as much as 66.5 percentage points, but has a much smaller effect on topic-structured news, where topic remains predictive of authorship. Additional analyses suggest that rewriting produces stylistic convergence despite substantial semantic overlap, and that content-sensitive attributers understate the loss captured by authorship-specific models. Heavily rewritten messages may also evade AI-text detectors, making them difficult both to attribute to their human authors and to identify as AI-assisted, a phenomenon we call double erasure. IER measures computational attributability rather than human recognition, and we release it as an open and reproducible protocol for evaluating authorship-signal loss in AI-mediated communication.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Idiolect Erasure Rate (IER), a metric quantifying how much AI-assisted rewriting reduces the ability to attribute text to its original author. Heavy rewriting erases up to 66.5 percentage points of authorship signal in personal writing while having less effect on topic-structured news. The authors identify "double erasure," where rewritten texts evade both authorship attribution and AI detection.
AI.motivation: Prior work on AI-mediated communication has focused on interpersonal perception and aggregate stylistic homogenization. This paper addresses a complementary, individual-level question: can an author still be identified after their message is rewritten by an AI assistant? Understanding this is critical for privacy, accountability, and the preservation of individual voice in an era of ubiquitous AI writing tools.
AI.method: The authors define the Idiolect Erasure Rate (IER) as the reduction in authorship-attribution accuracy post-rewriting. They evaluate IER across three pre-generative-AI corpora (personal blogs, workplace email, topic-structured news) using two attribution models: a traditional stylometric model and the authorship-specific LUAR (Learning Universal Authorship Representations) model. Multiple rewriting strengths are tested, and additional analyses examine stylistic convergence, semantic overlap, and AI-detector evasion.
AI.result: Heavy AI rewriting reduces LUAR attribution accuracy by up to 66.5 percentage points for blogs and workplace email, but has a substantially smaller effect on topic-structured news (where topic signals persist). Rewriting induces stylistic convergence despite high semantic overlap with originals. Content-sensitive attributers underestimate the authorship-signal loss captured by authorship-specific models like LUAR. Heavily rewritten messages also evade AI-text detectors, producing "double erasure."
AI.conclusion: IER provides a reproducible, computational protocol for measuring authorship-signal loss under AI-mediated communication. The phenomenon of double erasure — where rewritten texts can neither be attributed to their human author nor identified as AI-assisted — raises significant concerns for accountability, privacy, and authenticity. The authors release IER as an open tool for ongoing evaluation.

title: Can Perplexity Serve as a Cognitive Signal for Code Understandability?
summary: Recent work suggests that token-level perplexity from large language models can align with localized human confusion during code comprehension. This raises a natural question: can perplexity also serve as a snippet-level signal for code understandability? We conduct an empirical study of this question across multiple human-grounded datasets, including method-level understandability judgments, output-prediction tasks, and accepted understandability-improvement patches. Despite prior token-level evidence, we find that simple snippet-level aggregations of token perplexity, such as average, median, or peak perplexity, do not reliably correlate with human understandability. We then investigate why this happens. First, token perplexity is highly skewed and heavy-tailed across code structures; extreme spikes arise not only from semantically meaningful constructs, but also from identifiers, literals, types, separators, and tokenization artifacts. Second, human understandability labels often lack consensus, making whole-snippet difficulty a noisy target. Third, perplexity distributions and their alignment with human difficulty vary substantially across models and tokenizers. These findings explain why prior token-level perplexity--confusion alignment does not directly transfer to snippet-level understandability. Overall, our study positions perplexity as a promising but delicate cognitive signal: useful for localized code confusion, but requiring code-aware aggregation, consensus-aware evaluation, and model-sensitivity analysis before it can support reliable code-understandability measurement.

AI.tldr: Token-level perplexity aligns with localized human confusion during code comprehension, but simple snippet-level aggregations (mean, median, peak) fail to correlate with human understandability judgments. The authors attribute this to skewed perplexity distributions, noisy human labels, and model/tokenizer variability, concluding that perplexity is a promising but delicate cognitive signal requiring code-aware methods for snippet-level use.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that token-level perplexity from LLMs aligns with localized human confusion during code reading. This paper investigates whether perplexity can be elevated to a snippet-level signal for measuring overall code understandability, a natural next step with practical implications for automated code quality assessment.
AI.method: The authors conduct an empirical study across multiple human-grounded datasets: (1) method-level understandability judgments, (2) output-prediction tasks, and (3) accepted understandability-improvement patches. They test simple snippet-level aggregations of token perplexity (average, median, peak) against human judgments. They then perform diagnostic analysis investigating three failure sources: statistical properties of perplexity distributions, inter-annotator agreement in human labels, and cross-model/tokenizer sensitivity.
AI.result: Snippet-level aggregations of token perplexity do not reliably correlate with human understandability across all three datasets. Three root causes are identified: (1) token perplexity is highly skewed and heavy-tailed, with spikes from both semantic constructs and superficial artifacts (identifiers, literals, tokenization); (2) human understandability labels show low consensus, making whole-snippet difficulty a noisy target; (3) perplexity distributions and their human-alignment vary substantially across different models and tokenizers.
AI.conclusion: Token perplexity is a useful but delicate cognitive signal. It works for localized code confusion but does not trivially transfer to snippet-level understandability. Reliable snippet-level measurement would require code-aware aggregation strategies, consensus-aware evaluation protocols, and model-sensitivity analysis. The paper positions perplexity as promising but cautions against naive application at coarser granularities.

title: AgentMemBench: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Long-Term Memory Management Strategies in Conversational AI Agents
comment: 22 pages, 3 figures submitted on Neural Computing and Applications
summary: Long-term memory remains a critical bottleneck for conversational AI agents, whose finite context windows cannot support coherent recall across thousands of turns. We present AgentMemBench, a unified, reproducible benchmark evaluating five memory management strategies under identical conditions: in-context windowing (ICW), external key-value store (EKV), graph-based episodic memory (GEM), compression-based summarisation (CBS), and web-augmented memory (WAM). All are assessed across three public datasets covering long-term multi-session dialogue (LoCoMo), task-oriented document grounding (MultiDoc2Dial), and persona-grounded multi-session chat (MSC), using Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k, Answer F1, an LLM-judge Faithfulness score, Memory Footprint, and Latency over 491 annotated question turns. Generation and judging both use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (4-bit), with greedy decoding for determinism. Our results show that (1) EKV dominates on every quality axis (macro Recall@5 0.792, MRR 0.677, F1 0.156, Faithfulness 0.354); (2) long-range recall is decisive: on LoCoMo, where the gold turn lies many sessions back, ICW, WAM, GEM, and CBS retrieve almost nothing (Recall@5 <= 0.005) while EKV alone reaches 0.573, showing that recency windows, summaries, and entity graphs collapse at long horizons and only dense retrieval scales; (3) CBS is the runner-up on retrieval (0.556); (4) WAM equals ICW on in-corpus recall by construction, since external results carry no in-corpus provenance; and (5) EKV's recall advantage carries a footprint cost (~5,100 vs ~300 tokens for ICW/WAM), an explicit accuracy-efficiency trade-off. We additionally evaluate two published memory systems (MemGPT/Letta, HippoRAG) against the same harness, and release all code, environment, and result artefacts for full reproducibility.

AI.tldr: AgentMemBench is a benchmark evaluating five long-term memory strategies for conversational AI, finding that external key-value (dense retrieval) dominates all quality metrics but at higher memory cost, while windowing, summaries, and entity graphs fail catastrophically at long retrieval horizons.
AI.motivation: Conversational AI agents suffer from limited context windows, preventing coherent recall over thousands of turns. Existing memory strategies lack systematic, reproducible comparison under identical conditions, leaving practitioners without clear guidance on accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.
AI.method: AgentMemBench evaluates five memory strategies (ICW, EKV, GEM, CBS, WAM) across three public datasets (LoCoMo, MultiDoc2Dial, MSC) using 491 annotated question turns. Metrics include Recall@k, MRR, nDCG@k, Answer F1, LLM-judge Faithfulness, Memory Footprint, and Latency. Generation and judging use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (4-bit) with greedy decoding. Two published systems (MemGPT/Letta, HippoRAG) are also evaluated.
AI.result: EKV dominates all quality axes (Recall@5 0.792, MRR 0.677, F1 0.156, Faithfulness 0.354). On LoCoMo with long-range recall, ICW/WAM/GEM/CBS retrieve near nothing (Recall@5 ≤0.005) while EKV reaches 0.573. CBS is runner-up on retrieval (0.556). WAM equals ICW on in-corpus recall. EKV's memory footprint is ~5,100 vs ~300 tokens for ICW/WAM, representing a clear accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Dense retrieval (EKV) is the only strategy that scales to long retrieval horizons, but carries a significant memory cost. Recency windows, entity graphs, and summarization collapse at long horizons. The authors release all code, environment, and results for reproducibility.

title: RF-HOI: Recognize Human-Object Interaction with Radio Frequency Signals
summary: Recognizing Human-Object Interactions (HOI) is essential for intelligent systems, underpinning applications in virtual and augmented reality, embodied AI, and assistive robotics. However, vision-based HOI methods face challenges in privacy concerns and poor light conditions. In this work, we introduce RF-HOI, the first framework that only uses radio frequency (RF) signals for HOI recognition. A key challenge of RF-HOI is that single-modality RF sensing is insufficient to recognize both actions and the objects being interacted with. RF-HOI addresses this through a novel modality fusion that combines mmWave radar and RFID, enabling simultaneous action recognition and target identification. Another challenge is limited training data across diverse setups, which impairs the generalizability of the recognition model. To overcome this, we develop a simulator that synthesizes multimodal RF data for diverse HOIs at scale, allowing us to fine-tune with only a small amount of real-world data. Experiment results show that RF-HOI outperforms all baselines, approaching vision model performance, and that our diverse synthetic training data can significantly boost our system's performance on real-world scenarios. These results highlight the potential of multimodal RF sensing for robust and privacy-preserving HOI recognition as well as the effectiveness of our RF data synthesis.

AI.tldr: RF-HOI is the first framework to use only radio frequency signals (mmWave radar + RFID) for human-object interaction recognition, overcoming privacy and lighting limitations of vision-based methods. It introduces multimodal RF fusion and a synthetic data simulator to address data scarcity, achieving near-vision performance.
AI.motivation: Vision-based HOI recognition suffers from privacy concerns and poor performance in low-light conditions. RF sensing offers a privacy-preserving alternative, but single-modality RF is insufficient to simultaneously recognize actions and identify the objects being interacted with. Additionally, limited real-world RF training data across diverse setups impairs model generalizability.
AI.method: The authors propose RF-HOI, which (1) fuses mmWave radar (for action recognition) with RFID (for object/target identification) into a unified multimodal RF sensing framework, and (2) develops a simulator that synthesizes large-scale multimodal RF data across diverse HOI scenarios, enabling effective fine-tuning with only a small amount of real-world data.
AI.result: RF-HOI outperforms all RF-based baselines and approaches the performance of vision-based models. The diverse synthetic training data significantly boosts real-world performance, demonstrating the effectiveness of the RF data synthesis pipeline.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal RF sensing is a viable and effective paradigm for robust, privacy-preserving HOI recognition. The combination of sensor fusion (radar + RFID) and scalable synthetic data generation successfully addresses the core challenges of modality insufficiency and data scarcity.

title: A Self-Triggered Agentic Push Recommendation System
summary: Push notification is a critical recommendation scenario on large-scale platforms, allowing the system to proactively reach users outside the application to improve long-term re-engagement. However, designing an optimal push system requires handling a complex action space for the "whether and when" delivery problem under strict system resource constraints. Existing solutions typically fall into two passive paradigms: pre-planned frequency methods that allocate delivery times via offline modeling, limiting real-time adaptability; and fixed-interval triggering methods that periodically poll the system, creating a strict dilemma between excessive computational overhead and diminished optimal timing capture. Furthermore, such multi-stage frameworks severely suffer from local optima. To overcome these limitations, in this paper, we propose STEPS, a proactive, Self-Triggered End-to-end Agentic Push Recommendation System, which is already fully deployed at Douyin with over 1 billion users. STEPS reformulates push recommendation as a self-triggered agentic process in which the system decides not only whether to send a push, but also when to invoke itself again, thereby forming a closed loop that balances real-time effectiveness and efficiency. Specifically, STEPS consists of two decision transformer-based agents: a planning agent that schedules the next system invocation using a gated ordinal regression method, and an execution agent that decides whether to send a push based on trajectory rewards. Furthermore, we introduce a lightweight filtering agent to both control computational overhead and act as a crucial safeguard against unreasonable planning behaviors. Online A/B testing demonstrates that STEPS significantly increases user active days by 0.2843% and reduces the push permission disablement rate by 1.9089%, while the filtering agent reduces computational overhead by 79.42%.

AI.tldr: STEPS is a self-triggered end-to-end agentic push recommendation system deployed at Douyin (1B+ users) that uses decision transformer-based agents to jointly optimize "whether and when" to send push notifications, improving user active days by 0.2843% while reducing computational overhead by 79.42%.
AI.motivation: Existing push notification systems suffer from two passive paradigms: (1) pre-planned frequency methods that lack real-time adaptability, and (2) fixed-interval triggering methods that face a dilemma between computational cost and timing precision. Both approaches also lead to local optima due to their multi-stage frameworks.
AI.method: STEPS reformulates push recommendation as a self-triggered agentic process with two decision transformer-based agents: a planning agent (using gated ordinal regression to schedule next system invocation) and an execution agent (deciding push sending based on trajectory rewards). A lightweight filtering agent is introduced to control computational overhead and prevent unreasonable planning behaviors.
AI.result: Online A/B testing shows a 0.2843% increase in user active days, a 1.9089% reduction in push permission disablement rate, and a 79.42% reduction in computational overhead via the filtering agent.
AI.conclusion: STEPS provides a proactive, closed-loop solution that effectively balances real-time effectiveness and computational efficiency for large-scale push recommendation, overcoming the limitations of passive, locally optimal multi-stage frameworks.

title: Where Reasoning Diverges: Localized Multi-Agent Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate commonly exchanges complete reasoning traces even when disagreements concern only a few intermediate claims. We introduce Localized Multi-Agent Debate (LMAD), an inference-time protocol that represents agent traces as typed nodes, locates their earliest conflict, and restricts debate to the corresponding local segments. Guarded resolution extends a shared committed state so that later conflicts can be addressed without reopening accepted steps. We evaluate a single fixed LMAD configuration on four multi-hop question-answering benchmarks using ten backbones from four model families. Our method achieves the highest macro-averaged judge accuracy across all ten backbones, outperforming the strongest conventional baseline by up to 7.20 percentage points.

AI.tldr: LMAD is a multi-agent debate protocol that identifies the earliest point of disagreement in reasoning traces and restricts debate to that local segment, avoiding redundant exchange of already-agreed-upon reasoning. It outperforms conventional debate baselines across 10 model backbones on multi-hop QA tasks.
AI.motivation: Conventional multi-agent debate wastes computation by exchanging complete reasoning traces even when agents only disagree on a few intermediate claims. This inefficiency motivates a more targeted approach that focuses debate precisely where conflicts arise.
AI.method: LMAD represents agent reasoning traces as typed nodes, algorithmically locates the earliest conflict between agents, and restricts debate to the corresponding local segments. A "guarded resolution" mechanism extends a shared committed state so that later conflicts can be resolved without revisiting previously accepted steps.
AI.result: A single fixed LMAD configuration evaluated on four multi-hop QA benchmarks across ten backbones from four model families achieved the highest macro-averaged judge accuracy across all backbones, surpassing the strongest conventional baseline by up to 7.20 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Localizing debate to the earliest conflict point with guarded resolution is an effective and robust inference-time strategy that consistently improves multi-agent debate performance across diverse model families and benchmarks.

title: Improving the Security of Containerized Workloads using Transparency and Traceability Services
summary: Containerized workloads are commonly built via CI/CD pipelines, stored in registries, and executed across heterogeneous infrastructures, including cloud and edge environments. A single compromised build step or credential can turn routine automation into large-scale distribution of malicious artifacts, motivating integrity, transparency, and enforceable deployment-time checks. In this paper, we present an architecture for verifiable container image distribution that addresses key-management challenges and enables policy-enforced admission-time verification. A transparency service generates one-time signing keys bound to authenticated identities, records signing events in an append-only transparency registry, and returns cryptographically verifiable proofs of inclusion. These proofs and identity attributes are attached to image metadata and evaluated by policy-as-code at admission time, so only compliant artifacts are deployed. We implement a proof-of-concept integrated with GitHub Actions and GitLab Runners and evaluate how the resulting pipeline mitigates common supply-chain attacks under a realistic threat model.

AI.tldr: A transparency service generates one-time signing keys bound to authenticated identities, records signing events in an append-only registry, and produces verifiable inclusion proofs attached to container image metadata. Policy-as-code evaluates these proofs at admission time to ensure only compliant artifacts are deployed, mitigating supply-chain attacks in CI/CD pipelines.
AI.motivation: Containerized workloads built via CI/CD are vulnerable to supply-chain attacks where a single compromised build step or credential can enable large-scale distribution of malicious artifacts. Existing approaches lack integrated integrity guarantees, transparency, and enforceable deployment-time checks across heterogeneous cloud/edge infrastructures.
AI.method: The architecture comprises: (1) a transparency service that generates one-time signing keys cryptographically bound to authenticated identities; (2) an append-only transparency registry recording all signing events; (3) verifiable inclusion proofs returned for each signing event; (4) proofs and identity attributes attached to image metadata; (5) policy-as-code evaluation at admission time to enforce compliance. A proof-of-concept is implemented with GitHub Actions and GitLab Runners integration.
AI.result: The proof-of-concept demonstrates that the pipeline effectively mitigates common supply-chain attacks under a realistic threat model. The system provides end-to-end verifiability from build to deployment, combining cryptographic signing, transparency logging, and policy enforcement at admission time.
AI.conclusion: Verifiable container image distribution, combining one-time signing keys, append-only transparency registries, inclusion proofs, and policy-as-code admission control, offers a practical defense against CI/CD supply-chain attacks while addressing key-management challenges in heterogeneous deployment environments.

title: Rethinking PPG-based Sleep Staging: Datasets, Metrics, and Benchmarks
summary: Automated sleep staging assigns discrete stage labels to successive time epochs throughout an overnight recording; conventionally each window spans at least 30 seconds, reflecting the minimum temporal resolution of the clinical scoring standard. Wearable photoplethysmography (PPG) has attracted sustained interest as an ambulatory alternative to laboratory-based polysomnography, which relies on electroencephalography (EEG) and other recording modalities that are impractical outside clinical environments. Yet PPG-based staging trails EEG-based methods by a substantial margin, and we argue this gap largely reflects a mismatch between signal and task. Within a stable stage, PPG's inter-stage feature differences are more subtle than those in EEG; yet at stage boundaries, PPG's principal cardiovascular features, heart rate variability and pulse morphology, shift sharply within seconds. The conventional practice of assigning one label to each 30-second epoch therefore suppresses feature that is concentrated near boundaries. We address this gap in two steps. First, we develop a label expansion pipeline based on Hidden Semi-Markov Models that converts coarse epoch labels into sec-level annotations. To assess whether these expanded labels are reliable enough for downstream supervision, we validate them on a separate expert-reviewed dataset and through an auxiliary sleep-wake task whose labels are independent of the expansion pipeline. Second, we use the resulting sec-level supervision on MESA to improve conventional four-class epoch-level staging across four architecturally diverse baselines by 3.7--5.7\,pp in accuracy against the original epoch labels, with supplementary zero-shot evaluation on CFS showing that the transfer benefit persists under cohort and annotation-protocol shift.

AI.tldr: PPG-based sleep staging lags behind EEG methods because 30-second epoch labels suppress boundary-rich cardiovascular features. The authors propose a Hidden Semi-Markov Model pipeline to expand coarse epoch labels into second-level annotations, validate these expanded labels, and use them for supervision, achieving 3.7–5.7 pp accuracy gains across four baselines with transfer benefits confirmed on an external cohort.
AI.motivation: PPG-based automated sleep staging underperforms EEG-based methods, and the authors argue this gap stems from a temporal mismatch: PPG's discriminative cardiovascular features (heart rate variability, pulse morphology) shift sharply at stage boundaries within seconds, yet conventional 30-second epoch labeling pools entire windows, diluting these boundary-concentrated signals.
AI.method: A two-step approach: (1) A label expansion pipeline using Hidden Semi-Markov Models (HSMMs) converts coarse 30-second epoch labels into second-level annotations. Validation is performed via a separate expert-reviewed dataset and an auxiliary sleep-wake classification task with labels independent of the expansion pipeline. (2) The resulting second-level supervision is applied to train four architecturally diverse baseline models on the MESA dataset for four-class epoch-level staging, with zero-shot evaluation on the CFS cohort to test cross-cohort and cross-protocol generalization.
AI.result: Second-level supervision improved four-class epoch-level staging accuracy by 3.7–5.7 percentage points across all four baseline architectures on MESA. Zero-shot evaluation on CFS confirmed that the transfer benefit persists under cohort shift and annotation-protocol shift.
AI.conclusion: The temporal mismatch between PPG signal dynamics and conventional 30-second epoch labeling is a key bottleneck in PPG-based sleep staging. HSMM-based label expansion to second-level resolution effectively recovers boundary-rich information, yielding consistent and transferable accuracy improvements across diverse model architectures and datasets.

title: Understanding Online Failure Prediction in Linux Through Complementary Multi-View Explainability
comment: Accepted for publication in the 37th IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE) 2026
summary: Accurate Online Failure Prediction (OFP) has been shown to be feasible in Operating Systems (OSs) settings, but prediction alone is not sufficient for practical adoption. Without diagnostic insight, operators have limited basis to trust alerts or decide how to respond. Moreover, even when predictive accuracy is high, it is often unclear whether models are capturing meaningful failure processes or merely exploiting workload-specific noise and incidental correlations in telemetry. This paper reports a practical experience building and evaluating an explainable OFP pipeline for Linux OSs. We combine consensus-based feature selection for detection with temporal onset analysis, subsystemlevel causal analysis, and complementary diagnostic mechanisms to support failure interpretation. Evaluated under strict crossworkload conditions with frozen training artifacts, it achieved 91-94% detection on unseen workloads without retraining, while maintaining false alarm rates below 1%. However, failure mode diagnosis proved substantially more sensitive to workload shift, and several diagnostics mechanisms showed limited effectiveness for specific failure types. Our experience highlights three main lessons: i) detection generalizes more robustly than diagnosis across workload changes; ii) early-warning capability depends strongly on the failure mode, ranging from 38 to 215 seconds in our study; and iii) unseen failure modes are not reliably diagnosable from related training modes alone, providing 0% accuracy under Leave-One-Mode-Out (LOMO) evaluation. Taken together, these results show the value of complementary explainability mechanisms for interpreting accurate failure predictions, revealing when predictive signals reflect transferable failure structure and when diagnostic generalization breaks down under workload variation.

AI.tldr: An explainable online failure prediction pipeline for Linux OSs achieves 91–94% detection accuracy with <1% false alarms under cross-workload conditions, but diagnosis proves far more brittle—failing entirely (0% accuracy) on unseen failure modes. The study reveals that detection generalizes far better than diagnosis across workload shifts.
AI.motivation: Prior OFP work demonstrates feasibility but lacks practical adoption because operators cannot trust or act on predictions without diagnostic insight. It is also unclear whether models capture genuine failure processes or merely exploit workload-specific noise and incidental correlations.
AI.method: The authors build an explainable OFP pipeline combining: (1) consensus-based feature selection for detection, (2) temporal onset analysis, (3) subsystem-level causal analysis, and (4) complementary diagnostic mechanisms. Evaluation uses strict cross-workload conditions with frozen training artifacts, plus Leave-One-Mode-Out (LOMO) evaluation for unseen failure modes.
AI.result: Detection achieved 91–94% recall on unseen workloads with <1% false alarm rate. Diagnosis was far more workload-sensitive, with 0% accuracy under LOMO evaluation. Early-warning lead time ranged from 38 to 215 seconds depending on failure mode. Several diagnostic mechanisms showed limited effectiveness for specific failure types.
AI.conclusion: Three key lessons: (i) detection generalizes more robustly than diagnosis across workload changes; (ii) early-warning capability is strongly failure-mode-dependent; (iii) unseen failure modes are not reliably diagnosable from related training modes. Complementary explainability mechanisms help reveal when predictive signals reflect transferable structure versus when diagnostic generalization collapses.

title: DLLM-TTS: Block Discrete Diffusion Language Model for Text-to-Speech Synthesis
summary: Current text-to-speech systems face a trade-off: autoregres- sive codec language models produce highly intelligible speech but require large-scale models and training data and decode tokens sequentially, while non-autoregressive approaches im- prove speed at the cost of linguistic accuracy. We present DLLM-TTS, a framework that formulates TTS as conditional block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 neural audio codec to- kens. The model decomposes sequences into blocks and applies masked diffusion within each block while processing blocks se- quentially, learning both local acoustic coherence and global text-speech alignment. During inference, parallel token pre- diction within blocks enables efficient generation with a real- time factor (RTF) of 0.15. A 0.6B-parameter model trained on 20K hours achieves competitive performance on the Seed- TTS-eval benchmark, demonstrating that block discrete diffu- sion language models enable practical and data-efficient speech synthesis with parallel generation.

AI.tldr: DLLM-TTS proposes a block discrete diffusion language model for TTS that operates on X-Codec2 neural audio codec tokens, decomposing sequences into blocks with parallel token prediction within each block, achieving a real-time factor of 0.15 with a 0.6B model trained on only 20K hours.
AI.motivation: Existing TTS systems suffer from a fundamental trade-off: autoregressive codec language models deliver high intelligibility but are slow due to sequential decoding and demand massive models/data; non-autoregressive methods are faster but degrade linguistic accuracy. The authors seek to resolve this trade-off with a method that combines the strengths of both paradigms.
AI.method: DLLM-TTS frames TTS as conditional block discrete diffusion over X-Codec2 neural audio codec tokens. The model decomposes token sequences into blocks, applies masked diffusion within each block for parallel generation, and processes blocks sequentially. This jointly learns local acoustic coherence (intra-block) and global text-speech alignment (inter-block). At inference, parallel token prediction within blocks enables efficient generation.
AI.result: A 0.6B-parameter DLLM-TTS model trained on 20K hours of data achieves competitive performance on the Seed-TTS-eval benchmark, with a real-time factor (RTF) of 0.15 during inference.
AI.conclusion: Block discrete diffusion language models represent a practical and data-efficient approach to speech synthesis, enabling parallel generation within blocks while maintaining sequential coherence across blocks, effectively bridging the gap between autoregressive and non-autoregressive paradigms.

title: WM-Cov: Test Adequacy for Interactive World-Model-Style Autonomous Driving Simulation
summary: World models and generative simulators are emerging as interactive testing infrastructure for autonomous driving because they can react to the ego planner and produce counterfactual, rare, and safety-critical rollouts. This changes a test scenario from a fixed replayed trajectory into an interactive scenario family whose realized evolution depends on the planner under test. The unresolved question is therefore not only whether dangerous rollouts can be generated, but what valid closed-loop evidence is enough to support a specified testing intent and stopping decision. This paper formulates interactive world-model-style testing adequacy and introduces WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that converts raw provider outputs into requested, realized, and valid evidence. WM-Cov reports adequacy through coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision. Studies on executed TeraSim/SUMO events, WM-like mixed trace pools, and a real DriveArena TrafficManager--WorldDreamer matrix show that dangerous-looking events can include valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. The DriveArena matrix evaluates two planners, two horizons, six prompt conditions, and 360 ego-route requests; 304 attempts become fully realized evidence and 56 remain partial. A disjoint 80-request route-slice check yields 74 fully realized and 6 partial attempts. The results support evaluating world-model-style testing by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget, rather than by raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes interactive world-model testing adequacy for autonomous driving, introducing WM-Cov, an evaluation layer that measures coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism, artifact suppression, and evidence precision — shifting evaluation from raw generated failures to convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget.
AI.motivation: World models and generative simulators enable interactive, counterfactual testing for autonomous driving, but the field lacks a rigorous framework for determining what constitutes sufficient closed-loop evidence to support a testing intent or stopping decision. Raw generation of dangerous rollouts is insufficient without assessing validity, duplicates, artifacts, and partial realizations.
AI.method: The authors propose WM-Cov, a provider-agnostic evaluation layer that sits atop world-model outputs and converts them into three evidence categories: requested, realized, and valid. It quantifies adequacy via multiple metrics including coverage growth, valid-failure discovery, failure-mode diversity, realism scores, artifact suppression, duplicate accounting, and valid-evidence precision. Validation is conducted across TeraSim/SUMO events, WM-like mixed trace pools, and a DriveArena TrafficManager–WorldDreamer matrix (two planners, two horizons, six prompt conditions, 360 ego-route requests; plus an 80-request disjoint route-slice check).
AI.result: Dangerous-looking events frequently contain valid ADS failures, duplicates, partial realizations, and artifacts. From 360 DriveArena requests, 304 became fully realized evidence and 56 remained partial. The disjoint 80-request check yielded 74 fully realized and 6 partial. Results demonstrate that evaluating world-model testing by convergence of valid interactive evidence under budget is more meaningful than relying on raw generated failures or prompt coverage alone.
AI.conclusion: World-model-style testing adequacy should be assessed through the lens of converged valid interactive evidence rather than raw generated failures. WM-Cov provides a systematic framework for this, enabling reliable stopping decisions grounded in evidence quality and coverage growth across diverse failure modes.

title: SmartGR: Hierarchy and Beam-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation (GR) has emerged as a promising paradigm for recommender systems. Scaling up GR models can improve recommendation performance, but it also substantially increases inference cost. Knowledge distillation provides a practical solution by transferring knowledge from a large GR model to a lightweight one. However, existing distillation methods do not account for two GR-specific challenges: imbalanced distillation difficulty across the semantic ID (SID) hierarchy and incorrect prefix pruning during beam search. To address these challenges, we propose SmartGR, a novel distillation framework that utilizes Hierarchy-Aware SID Distillation to transfer the teacher's modeling capability across the hierarchy and leverages Beam-Aware Ranking Distillation to distill the teacher's ranking preferences during beam search. Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of SmartGR, improving the performance by 8.6% while achieving a 2.39$\times$ inference speedup on average.

AI.tldr: SmartGR is a knowledge distillation framework for generative recommendation that addresses two GR-specific challenges: imbalanced distillation difficulty across the semantic ID hierarchy and incorrect prefix pruning during beam search. It proposes Hierarchy-Aware SID Distillation and Beam-Aware Ranking Distillation, achieving 8.6% performance improvement with 2.39× inference speedup.
AI.motivation: Scaling up generative recommendation (GR) models improves performance but incurs prohibitive inference cost. While knowledge distillation can transfer knowledge from large to lightweight models, existing methods fail to address two GR-specific issues: (1) the semantic ID (SID) hierarchy creates imbalanced distillation difficulty across different hierarchical levels, and (2) beam search decoding suffers from incorrect prefix pruning, degrading the distilled model's ranking quality.
AI.method: SmartGR introduces two key components: (1) Hierarchy-Aware SID Distillation, which transfers the teacher model's modeling capability across different levels of the SID hierarchy by accounting for varying distillation difficulty at each level; and (2) Beam-Aware Ranking Distillation, which distills the teacher's ranking preferences specifically during the beam search decoding process to mitigate incorrect prefix pruning.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four benchmark datasets demonstrate SmartGR's effectiveness and efficiency: it improves recommendation performance by 8.6% on average while achieving a 2.39× inference speedup compared to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: SmartGR effectively addresses the unique challenges of distilling generative recommendation models by incorporating hierarchy-aware and beam-aware distillation strategies. The framework enables practical deployment of high-quality GR models with significantly reduced inference cost, making large-scale generative recommendation more feasible in real-world applications.

title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
comment: 41 pages, 21 figures, 6 tables. Under review at a journal
summary: Code agents spend much of their effort simply locating the right code inside a repository. Two approaches dominate current practice. In Semantic Search, the agent retrieves code blocks from a vector index built from the repository in advance. In Deep Agentic Search (also known as grep-search by subagent), a planning agent delegates the exploration to a separate subagent that works in an isolated context window and returns only a condensed result. The second design, which is considered good context engineering practice, exists to protect the main agent from context pollution (also known as context rot), the loss of accuracy that occurs as unrelated material accumulates in the context window. Recent code agents (such as Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, etc) have adopted it quickly, but there is little evidence on whether it produces better answers. We compare the two approaches on SWE-QA, a benchmark for repository-level code question answering. Semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly against 46.2% for deep agentic search, and it produced each correct answer at less than half the cost. To explain the gap, we then coded every failed run into a taxonomy of failure modes. The taxonomy shows that deep agentic search did not remove failures but introduced a new class of them: the single largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at the hand-off between the planner and its sub-agent, and these were usually silent, ending in a fluent and confident answer that was wrong. Deep agentic search addresses a real problem and is now the preferred design in many code agents. However, our results show that the protection it offers may not be free, and that for read-only questions over a repository that can be indexed, retrieval was the stronger and cheaper option.

AI.tldr: Comparing two code search strategies for repository-level QA, semantic search significantly outperformed deep agentic search (65.2% vs 46.2% accuracy) at less than half the cost. Deep agentic search introduced a new failure mode: 41.8% of its failures stemmed from silent, fluent-but-wrong hand-off errors between planner and sub-agent.
AI.motivation: Deep agentic search (grep-search by subagent) has been rapidly adopted by recent code agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) based on the intuition that isolating exploration in a sub-agent protects the main agent from context pollution. However, there is little empirical evidence on whether this design actually produces better answers compared to simpler semantic search over pre-built vector indices.
AI.method: The authors benchmarked both approaches on SWE-QA, a repository-level code question-answering dataset. They then performed a qualitative failure analysis, coding every incorrect run into a taxonomy of failure modes to understand the mechanistic reasons behind the performance gap.
AI.result: Semantic search achieved 65.2% accuracy vs. 46.2% for deep agentic search, with each correct answer costing less than half. The failure taxonomy revealed that 41.8% of deep agentic search failures occurred at the planner/sub-agent hand-off, typically producing fluent, confident, but incorrect answers. Context pollution protection came at a substantial accuracy and cost penalty.
AI.conclusion: For read-only repository-level QA where indexing is feasible, retrieval-based semantic search is both stronger and cheaper than deep agentic search. The context protection offered by sub-agent delegation is not free and introduces its own failure modes, challenging the prevailing design preference in current code agents.

title: From Chasing Ghosts to Missed Attacks: Perspectives and Perceptions of SOC Practitioners on LLM Integration, Risks, and Readiness
summary: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) process large volumes of security events, requiring analysts to accurately detect and assess ongoing cyberattacks under time pressure. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) suggest potential benefits for security operations, yet their practical suitability for real-world SOC workflows remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted 25 semi-structured interviews with SOC practitioners who had prior experience with LLMs, complemented by interactive scenarios to anticipate challenges and identify opportunities for the responsible integration of LLM-based tools into SOC workflows. We identified 15 LLM use cases grouped into six functional categories. While LLMs are valued for automating repetitive, low-level tasks such as report automation, practitioners rate high-impact tasks such as incident analysis as not yet feasible, reporting limitations in technical depth, context awareness, and organization-specific knowledge. They locate these limitations less in the models than in the readiness of their SOCs and human factors driving over-reliance. Despite concerns, practitioners express a strong willingness to adopt LLMs, describing competitive pressure that leaves few alternatives. This work contributes an empirical, practitioner-driven analysis of LLM use across SOC roles and organizations and derives concrete design and integration requirements for human-centered, operationally safe LLM-assisted security operations.

AI.tldr: 25 semi-structured interviews with SOC practitioners reveal 15 LLM use cases across 6 functional categories. LLMs are valued for low-level automation (e.g., report generation) but are not yet trusted for high-impact tasks like incident analysis due to limitations in technical depth, context awareness, and organizational knowledge. Practitioners attribute these gaps more to SOC readiness and human factors than to model capability, and express strong willingness to adopt LLMs driven by competitive pressure.
AI.motivation: Despite growing interest in applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to security operations, their practical suitability, limitations, and integration challenges within real-world SOC workflows remain poorly understood from the perspective of practitioners.
AI.method: The authors conducted 25 semi-structured interviews with SOC practitioners who had prior LLM experience, supplemented by interactive scenarios to surface anticipated challenges and opportunities. Thematic analysis was used to identify use cases, functional categories, and socio-technical barriers.
AI.result: Six functional categories encompassing 15 discrete LLM use cases emerged, spanning report automation (high feasibility) to incident analysis (low feasibility). Key barriers include insufficient technical depth, lack of context awareness, missing organization-specific knowledge, SOC infrastructure readiness gaps, and human-factor risks such as over-reliance. Adoption willingness remains high due to competitive pressure.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show promise for automating repetitive, low-stakes SOC tasks but are not yet suitable for high-impact analytical work. Successful integration requires addressing both technical limitations and socio-technical factors, yielding concrete design requirements for human-centered, operationally safe LLM-assisted security operations.

title: Collascope: Supporting Serendipitous Asset Exploration for Collage-Based Storytelling
comment: To be published at ACM UIST 2026
summary: Collage-based storytelling requires visual elements that support emerging narratives and inspire creative reinterpretation. Existing tools, however, rely largely on keyword- and image-based retrieval, offering limited support for serendipitous exploration beyond existing assets. We introduce Collascope, an interactive system that helps creators (1) concretize story intent with interactive element groups, (2) expand the exploration space based on concepts or cutouts towards conceptual and visual dimensions, and (3) develop grounded, traceable ideas in parallel with collage composition.
