Collascope's attribute-aware visual retrieval method, instantiated with collage-relevant visual dimensions, enables creators to retrieve cutouts through dimension-specific visual projections rather than holistic similarity. In a within-subject study (N=12) against a conventional search baseline, our participants used unexpected results and even gaps in the asset collection to redirect narratives, shift tone, and enrich compositions. Scene Parts helped organize exploration into manageable subtasks, while participants used association in distinct ways depending on whether exploration was guided by a clear goal, an evolving story, or visual intuition.

AI.tldr: Collascope is an interactive system for collage-based storytelling that supports serendipitous visual exploration through concept- and cutout-based expansion along conceptual and visual dimensions, using attribute-aware retrieval with dimension-specific projections rather than holistic similarity.
AI.motivation: Existing collage tools rely on keyword- and image-based retrieval, which limits serendipitous exploration and creative reinterpretation beyond existing assets. Creators need better support for emerging narratives and grounded, traceable ideation during composition.
AI.method: Collascope introduces: (1) interactive element groups (Scene Parts) to concretize story intent, (2) dual-axis exploration space expansion via concepts and cutouts across conceptual and visual dimensions, and (3) an attribute-aware visual retrieval method using collage-relevant visual dimensions that retrieves cutouts through dimension-specific projections. A within-subject study (N=12) compared Collascope against a conventional search baseline.
AI.result: Participants used unexpected retrieval results and gaps in the asset collection to redirect narratives, shift tone, and enrich compositions. Scene Parts helped organize exploration into manageable subtasks. Participants engaged in distinct association strategies depending on whether exploration was guided by a clear goal, an evolving story, or visual intuition.
AI.conclusion: Dimension-specific visual projection retrieval, combined with structured exploration scaffolds like Scene Parts, effectively supports serendipitous discovery and parallel development of narrative and visual ideas in collage-based storytelling.

title: Unreliable in Practice? A Comprehensive Study of Errors in LLM-Generated Code
comment: Accepted for publication in the 37th IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE) 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being widely used for coding, with reports indicating that AI now generates an increasing share of production code. Studies show that LLMs can significantly improve developer productivity, yet they still struggle with more complex coding tasks. Just as understanding error modes in human-written code has been central to improving software quality, identifying and characterizing the errors in LLM-generated code is critical for setting realistic expectations and designing mitigation strategies. Prior research has been limited in scope, often focusing on a single language, a small number of problems, or a limited selection of models. As a result, there is still no comprehensive understanding of which errors are common and which are specific to certain models or languages. To address these gaps and develop a deeper understanding of the quality of LLM-generated code, we analyzed a corpus of 86,726 code samples that contained compilation or runtime errors. These samples were generated by seven LLMs across four compiled languages. We classified errors by their underlying causes using an LLM, manually validated these classifications, and performed a comparative analysis. This labeled data is then used to measure error prevalence by model, language, and problem difficulty, to identify common error patterns. Results show that, although error types vary strongly across languages and models, even the largest models frequently make simple mistakes. We also observe that generated code often omits basic input validation or memory-safety checks, which can lead to overflows, resource exhaustion, or other reliability/security issues.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 86,726 error-containing code samples from seven LLMs across four compiled languages reveals that even the largest models frequently make simple mistakes, error types vary strongly by language and model, and generated code often lacks basic input validation and memory-safety checks, leading to reliability and security vulnerabilities.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LLM code generation errors has been narrow — limited to single languages, few problems, or few models. There is no comprehensive, cross-model, cross-language understanding of which errors are common versus model- or language-specific, hindering realistic expectation-setting and effective mitigation design.
AI.method: The authors collected a corpus of 86,726 code samples (with compilation or runtime errors) generated by seven LLMs across four compiled languages. They used an LLM to classify errors by their underlying causes, manually validated the classifications, and performed comparative analysis. Labeled data was used to measure error prevalence by model, language, and problem difficulty, and to identify common error patterns.
AI.result: Error types vary strongly across languages and models. Even the largest, most capable LLMs frequently make simple mistakes. Generated code commonly omits basic input validation and memory-safety checks, leading to overflows, resource exhaustion, and other reliability/security issues.
AI.conclusion: Understanding the nature and distribution of LLM coding errors is essential for improving code generation quality. The findings highlight that model scaling alone does not eliminate basic errors and that language- and model-specific error profiles can inform targeted mitigation strategies, such as enforcing input validation and memory safety in generated code.

title: Obshazard-bench: Benchmarking Multimodal Foundation Models for Real-Time Disaster Intelligence from Raw Earth Observation Streams
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to interpret Earth observation data, yet their capability to support real-world disaster emergency response remains insufficiently evaluated. Existing remote sensing benchmarks largely rely on static, post-hoc, and expert-processed products, such as gridded reanalysis data, which are difficult to align with operational disaster scenarios where hazards evolve rapidly and decisions must be made under strict time constraints. To bridge this gap, we introduce Obshazard-bench, a real-time, observation-driven benchmark for evaluating disaster intelligence in MLLMs. Unlike image-centric or post-event benchmarks, Obshazard-bench directly integrates raw, high-frequency satellite sounding streams from diverse satellite sensors with concurrent ground-station observations, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators, bypassing delayed expert-processing and physical-inversion pipelines. The benchmark covers 8 major disaster categories and 28 sub-categories across more than 60 countries, incorporating over 120 historically documented extreme-event cases and thousands of lifecycle-oriented VQA samples. Moreover, Obshazard-bench further defines a three-stage evaluation taxonomy aligned with the operational disaster workflow: Predictive Crisis Anticipation for pre-disaster risk detection and early forecasting, Active Evolution Reasoning for in-situ disaster tracking and termination prediction, and Multi-faceted Impact Quantification for post-disaster magnitude deduction, humanitarian burden estimation, and socio-economic impact assessment. Experiments on representative general-purpose and Earth-focused foundation models reveal substantial limitations in transforming raw multi-channel physical observations into temporally grounded and decision-relevant disaster reasoning.

AI.tldr: Obshazard-bench is a real-time, observation-driven benchmark for evaluating disaster intelligence in MLLMs, using raw satellite sounding streams, ground-station data, and socio-economic indicators. It spans 8 disaster categories across 60+ countries and defines a three-stage evaluation taxonomy (pre-disaster anticipation, in-situ evolution reasoning, post-disaster impact quantification). Experiments reveal significant limitations in current models' disaster reasoning capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing benchmarks for MLLMs rely on static, post-hoc, expert-processed products (e.g., gridded reanalysis data) that fail to align with operational disaster scenarios requiring real-time, temporally-grounded reasoning under strict time constraints. There is a gap in evaluating MLLMs' ability to process raw, high-frequency observational data for disaster response.
AI.method: The authors introduce Obshazard-bench, which directly integrates raw, high-frequency satellite sounding streams from diverse sensors with concurrent ground-station observations, historical disaster records, and socio-economic indicators, bypassing delayed expert-processing pipelines. The benchmark covers 8 major disaster categories and 28 sub-categories across 60+ countries, with 120+ extreme-event cases and thousands of lifecycle-oriented VQA samples. A three-stage evaluation taxonomy is defined: Predictive Crisis Anticipation, Active Evolution Reasoning, and Multi-faceted Impact Quantification.
AI.result: Experiments on representative general-purpose and Earth-focused foundation models reveal substantial limitations in transforming raw multi-channel physical observations into temporally grounded and decision-relevant disaster reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs, including Earth-specialized models, are insufficient for operational disaster intelligence when evaluated on raw, real-time observational data. Obshazard-bench exposes critical gaps in temporal reasoning and decision-relevant understanding, highlighting the need for models that can process streaming physical observations for time-sensitive disaster response.

title: CrystalMem: Elastic Memory for Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Knowledge Crystallization
summary: Memory for self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents is often provisioned as if its byte budget only grows. Cloud platforms, however, adjust quotas with load and cost, and we show that capability does not follow the budget back up: after a squeeze-and-recover cycle, the agent settles below its pre-squeeze level, a gap we call memory hysteresis. The cause is structural. Deletion and one-way compression discard the material needed for later rebuilding, and we prove that any policy that only keeps or drops entries carries a residual-deficit floor. We propose CrystalMem (Crystallized Memory), an elastic memory sidecar that demotes entries across four fidelity states under a crystallization-energy schedule, orders demotions by advantage-weighted influence with dependency coupling, and recovers capability through verified recrystallization under explicit compute and byte caps. Across seven environments, seventeen methods, and six backbones, with multi-tenant serving and a physical edge-cloud deployment, CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting and closes the loop left open by every baseline. From a 50% byte budget, CrystalMem matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision on every environment; at equal budgets, it leads by +4.6 pp on average.

AI.tldr: CrystalMem introduces an elastic memory sidecar for LLM agents that maintains capability across memory budget squeeze-and-recover cycles. It addresses "memory hysteresis" — the irreversible capability loss after memory deletion and re-expansion — using a four-fidelity-state crystallization mechanism with dependency-aware ordering. At equal budgets, it outperforms baselines by +4.6 pp on average; at 50% budget, it matches full-provision baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for self-evolving LLM agents assume ever-growing byte budgets, but real cloud platforms dynamically adjust quotas. The authors identify a phenomenon called "memory hysteresis": after a squeeze-and-recover cycle (budget reduction followed by restoration), agent capability settles below the pre-squeeze level and never fully recovers. This stems from structural causes — deletion and one-way compression irreversibly discard material needed for later rebuilding. The paper proves a theoretical residual-deficit floor for any keep-or-drop policy, motivating a fundamentally different approach.
AI.method: CrystalMem is an elastic memory sidecar with three core mechanisms: (1) **Four-fidelity state model** — memory entries are demoted across states (full, compressed, seed, evicted) rather than binary kept/dropped, following a crystallization-energy schedule that preserves reconstruction potential. (2) **Advantage-weighted influence ordering** — demotion priority is determined by each entry's marginal contribution to task success, with dependency coupling to account for inter-entry relationships. (3) **Verified recrystallization** — when budget recovers, entries are selectively reconstructed (recrystallized) under explicit compute and byte caps, with verification ensuring restored entries actually improve capability. The system operates as a sidecar decoupled from the agent backbone.
AI.result: Evaluation spans 7 environments, 17 methods, and 6 backbones, including multi-tenant serving and a physical edge-cloud deployment. CrystalMem achieves the highest restored capability in every setting, closing the hysteresis loop left open by all baselines. At a 50% byte budget, it matches the strongest budgeted baseline at full provision. At equal budgets, it leads by +4.6 percentage points on average across environments.
AI.conclusion: Memory hysteresis is a structural, provable limitation of binary keep/drop memory policies. CrystalMem's crystallized memory approach — multi-fidelity state transitions, influence-aware ordering, and verified recrystallization — fully closes the hysteresis gap, enabling elastic LLM agent memory that gracefully handles dynamic cloud quotas without permanent capability degradation.

title: Douyin Multimodal Embedding Model Technical Report
summary: Multimodal representation learning is a cornerstone of modern AI. By encoding multimodal queries and targets into vectors, it powers industrial search and recommendation and underpins modern agents. Real-world platforms with complex modalities and massive-scale content, such as Douyin, Xiaohongshu, and YouTube, demand both efficiency under billion-scale indexing and fine-grained discrimination for hard matching. Existing MLLM embedding models rarely satisfy both. Contrastive models are efficient but rely on pair-level supervision too coarse for fine-grained distinctions, while CoT-based models improve discrimination through explicit generation impractical to serve online. We present Douyin Multimodal Embedding (DME), a model trained in two stages to combine both strengths. Stage 1 performs large-scale contrastive pre-training that establishes a unified multimodal embedding space with broad modality and task coverage. Stage 2 supplements semantic sufficiency, the property that an embedding is grounded in retrieval-relevant evidence and preserves fine-grained counterpart-side semantics, via two mechanisms. Evidence-Grounded Typed Latent Reasoning organizes retrieval evidence through hidden-space latent reasoning, and Cross-Conditional Reconstruction enforces counterpart-side semantics through cross-directional autoregressive reconstruction. Both act only during training and add only marginal query-side overhead, so DME serves as efficiently as a standard contrastive encoder. On MMEB-v2, DME reaches state-of-the-art results at comparable scales for its 2B and 9B variants (74.8 and 78.4), with especially strong video and visual-document tasks. In production, DME delivers a 2.92% relative gain on Douyin's in-house offline evaluation set, is deployed across Douyin scenarios such as generative, image, and AI search, and yields a 0.1% Lifetime (LT) gain in online A/B testing on Douyin search.

AI.tldr: DME combines contrastive pre-training with two training-only mechanisms — Evidence-Grounded Typed Latent Reasoning and Cross-Conditional Reconstruction — to achieve both billion-scale efficiency and fine-grained multimodal discrimination. It achieves SOTA on MMEB-v2 and delivers measurable gains in Douyin's production search systems.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal platforms (Douyin, Xiaohongshu, YouTube) need embedding models that are both efficient at billion-scale indexing and capable of fine-grained discrimination for hard matches. Existing contrastive models are fast but rely on coarse pair-level supervision, while CoT-based models improve discrimination via explicit generation, making them impractical for online serving. No existing MLLM embedding model satisfies both requirements simultaneously.
AI.method: DME uses a two-stage training paradigm. Stage 1: large-scale contrastive pre-training to build a unified multimodal embedding space with broad modality/task coverage. Stage 2: two auxiliary training mechanisms — (1) Evidence-Grounded Typed Latent Reasoning, which organizes retrieval evidence through hidden-space latent reasoning without explicit text generation; (2) Cross-Conditional Reconstruction, which enforces counterpart-side semantics via cross-directional autoregressive reconstruction. Both mechanisms operate only during training, adding only marginal query-side overhead at inference, preserving the efficiency of a standard contrastive encoder.
AI.result: DME achieves state-of-the-art results on MMEB-v2 at comparable scales: 74.8 (2B) and 78.4 (9B), with particular strength in video and visual-document tasks. In production on Douyin, it yields a 2.92% relative gain on in-house offline evaluation and a 0.1% Lifetime (LT) gain in online A/B testing across generative, image, and AI search scenarios.
AI.conclusion: DME successfully bridges the gap between contrastive efficiency and CoT-level discrimination by incorporating latent reasoning and cross-modal reconstruction as training-only objectives. This design enables state-of-the-art multimodal embedding performance while remaining practical for billion-scale industrial deployment, validated by both offline benchmarks and online A/B gains.

title: Securing Agentic AI: From Per-Action Checks to Trajectory Assurance
comment: 6 pages. Accepted to the ACM AI Leadership Summit 2026 (Visionary Track)
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly used to execute consequential tasks in environments governed by operational constraints, organizational policies, regulatory requirements, and technical standards. Their safety is therefore determined not by the correctness of individual actions, but by whether their overall behavior remains consistent with the rules and invariants of the systems in which they operate. As large language model (LLM)-based agents become more autonomous and increasingly delegate tasks across organizational boundaries, securing them evolves from a single challenge into a broad and interconnected landscape spanning the entire agentic stack. At the single-agent level, untrusted inputs through prompts, memory, retrieved knowledge, and tool interfaces create attack surfaces. In multi-agent settings, delegation and communication introduce challenges related to identity, trust, capability control, and decision transparency, while the underlying model routing and execution control plane remains vulnerable to manipulation and to unverified model provenance. Perhaps the most fundamental challenge is behavioral containment: sequences of individually permissible actions may collectively violate system-level constraints and safety invariants. At the broader level, supply-chain integrity, provenance, accountability, and end-to-end observability remain largely open problems. A common principle unifies these directions: security must become a verifiable property of the architectures, protocols, and runtimes that govern agent behavior, rather than an optional layer of guidance. Charting these challenges provides a roadmap toward trustworthy autonomous agent deployment.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys the security challenges of autonomous LLM-based agents across the entire agentic stack, arguing that safety depends on behavioral consistency with system-level constraints rather than individual action correctness. It identifies attack surfaces at single-agent, multi-agent, and supply-chain levels, with behavioral containment as the central challenge. The authors propose that security must become a verifiable architectural property rather than an optional guidance layer.
AI.motivation: As LLM-based agents become more autonomous and delegate tasks across organizational boundaries, traditional security approaches focused on individual action correctness are insufficient. Agent safety instead depends on whether overall behavior remains consistent with operational constraints, policies, regulations, and system invariants. The security landscape has expanded from a single problem into a broad, interconnected challenge spanning the entire agentic stack, necessitating a systematic analysis of emerging attack surfaces and a roadmap toward verifiable agent security.
AI.method: This is a survey/position paper that systematically taxonomizes and analyzes security challenges across the agentic stack. The authors structure the problem space across multiple levels: (1) single-agent attack surfaces (prompts, memory, retrieved knowledge, tool interfaces), (2) multi-agent challenges (identity, trust, capability control, decision transparency), (3) model routing and execution control plane vulnerabilities, and (4) supply-chain and provenance issues. The core analytical lens is behavioral containment — the problem that sequences of individually permissible actions can collectively violate system-level constraints and safety invariants.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that untrusted inputs permeate every interface of an LLM agent (prompts, memory, retrieval, tools), while multi-agent delegation introduces unresolved issues around identity, trust, and capability control. The model routing and execution layer is vulnerable to manipulation and unverified provenance. Behavioral containment emerges as the most fundamental challenge: individually valid actions can compose into system-level violations. Supply-chain integrity, provenance, accountability, and end-to-end observability remain largely open problems. A unifying principle is identified: security must be a verifiable property of architectures, protocols, and runtimes, not an optional layer.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that trustworthy autonomous agent deployment requires rethinking security as a verifiable architectural property embedded in the protocols and runtimes governing agent behavior. This represents a shift from treating security as an external guidance layer to making it intrinsic to agent system design. The taxonomy of challenges across the agentic stack provides a roadmap for future research toward verifiably secure autonomous agents.

title: Supporting Cybersecurity Risk Management for Medical Devices via the SECUMAN Ontology and Shapes
summary: We propose the SECUMAN ontology and shapes for representing and analysing cybersecurity risk-management documentation for medical devices. Cybersecurity risks are increasingly relevant for connected medical devices and may have direct consequences for patient safety. Current risk-management files are often maintained as semi-structured natural language text, which makes consistency checking, certification review, and reuse difficult. SECUMAN provides a formal OWL-based vocabulary for modelling security-risk context, assessment, control measures, and residual-risk evaluation, and uses SHACL constraints to check structural completeness and conformity with the intended documentation model. The ontology is aligned with VDE Spec 90025 and the related RISKMAN ontology and shapes, while extending their safety-oriented approach to concepts relevant to cybersecurity risk documentation such as threat scenarios, protection goals, attacker profiles, exposure levels, assets, and secure design arguments. SECUMAN is intended to support automated first-pass validation, traceability, and integration of cybersecurity and safety risk-management documentation.

AI.tldr: SECUMAN delivers an OWL ontology and SHACL shapes to formalize cybersecurity risk documentation for medical devices, enabling automated validation, traceability, and integration with safety risk-management files aligned with VDE Spec 90025 and RISKMAN.
AI.motivation: Medical device cybersecurity risk documentation is typically maintained as semi-structured natural language, hindering consistency checking, certification review, and reuse. Existing standards and ontologies (e.g., RISKMAN) focus on safety, lacking adequate coverage of cybersecurity-specific concepts.
AI.method: The authors developed SECUMAN as a formal OWL ontology that models security-risk context, assessment, control measures, and residual-risk evaluation. They complemented it with SHACL shapes to enforce structural completeness and conformity. The ontology extends RISKMAN's safety-oriented vocabulary with cybersecurity-specific concepts (threat scenarios, protection goals, attacker profiles, exposure levels, assets, secure design arguments) and aligns with VDE Spec 90025.
AI.result: The resulting artifact is a formal, machine-checkable vocabulary and constraint set for cybersecurity risk documentation of medical devices, intended to support automated first-pass validation and traceability.
AI.conclusion: SECUMAN demonstrates the feasibility of formalizing cybersecurity risk-management documentation for medical devices using semantic web technologies, bridging the gap between safety and security risk analysis and paving the way for automated, integrated certification review.

title: PartInteractor: Intent-Driven Part-Aware 3D Authoring for Continuous Co-Creation in XR
summary: As Extended Reality (XR) evolves into an immersive computing medium, interactive 3D authoring becomes essential for creative and functional workflows. However, existing generative XR systems produce monolithic outputs lacking explicit semantic structure, limiting post-generation control. We introduce PartInteractor, a representation-to-interaction framework that investigates how semantic part hierarchies can be incorporated into generative XR authoring, and exposed as first-class, directly manipulable units, turning one-shot prompt-to-object generation into continuous component-level co-creation. PartInteractor supports speech, sketch, and image inputs, integrating an LLM interpreter with a retrieval-generation strategy to scaffold user intent prior to 3D generation. Instead of producing monolithic objects, our system generates semantically decomposed 3D assets with explicit part hierarchies, enabling rich component-level interaction over object structure and composition. Our evaluations suggest that part-aware representation increases post-generation control and reduces reliance on whole-object regeneration, while intent scaffolding mitigates ambiguity and improves intent-result alignment, together supporting more expressive and controllable human-AI co-creation workflows. These results highlight part-aware representation and intent scaffolding as promising design considerations for future generative XR authoring systems.

AI.tldr: PartInteractor introduces semantic part hierarchies into generative XR authoring, enabling component-level co-creation through speech, sketch, and image inputs, with an LLM interpreter and retrieval-generation strategy that scaffold user intent prior to 3D generation.
AI.motivation: Existing generative XR systems produce monolithic 3D outputs without explicit semantic structure, severely limiting post-generation editing and control. Users cannot modify individual components without regenerating the entire object.
AI.method: A representation-to-interaction framework combining: (1) an LLM interpreter that processes speech, sketch, and image inputs; (2) a retrieval-generation strategy that scaffolds user intent before 3D generation; (3) semantically decomposed 3D asset generation with explicit part hierarchies; and (4) component-level interaction mechanisms treating parts as first-class manipulable units.
AI.result: Part-aware representation increased post-generation control and reduced reliance on whole-object regeneration. Intent scaffolding mitigated ambiguity and improved intent-result alignment. Together, these supported more expressive and controllable human-AI co-creation workflows.
AI.conclusion: Part-aware representation and intent scaffolding are promising design considerations for future generative XR authoring systems, shifting the paradigm from one-shot prompt-to-object generation toward continuous component-level co-creation.

title: Vul4Py: Benchmarking Automated Vulnerability Repair in Python with Paired Exploit and Functional Oracles
summary: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has advanced rapidly across program analysis, machine learning, and Large Language Models (LLMs), but a verifiable, head-to-head comparison of AVR approaches on Python is still missing. Python underpins critical web, data, and machine-learning infrastructure, yet existing Python benchmarks accept a patch on the strength of a proof-of-concept exploit alone, or apply a functional test only on the subset of entries whose upstream project happens to ship one. Both therefore miss functional regressions, in which a patch defeats the exploit but breaks unrelated behavior. We present Vul4Py, a Python AVR benchmark in which every entry carries a paired oracle: an exploit oracle that must fail on the vulnerable revision and pass on the fixed one, together with a project-native pytest functional oracle that must pass on both. Vul4Py comprises 100 real vulnerabilities from 60 open-source projects, spanning 60 distinct CWEs and the years 2017 to 2025, each packaged with a pinned, reproducible per-instance environment. Using Vul4Py, we compare six approaches in three categories: a specialized vulnerability repair tool, directly prompted LLMs, and software engineering agents. The agents dominate: OpenHands repairs 41 of 100 vulnerabilities, against 4 for the strongest directly prompted LLM and 2 for the specialized tool, despite all three sharing the same backbone model. The paired oracle is what makes these counts trustworthy: it rejects 15 of the 119 patches that an exploit-only oracle would accept, and 98 of the 104 patches it admits are manually confirmed to be semantically equivalent to the developer's patches

AI.tldr: Vul4Py is a Python AVR benchmark with paired exploit and pytest functional oracles. Using it, software engineering agents (OpenHands) repair 41/100 vulnerabilities, far outperforming directly prompted LLMs (4) and specialized tools (2). The paired oracle rejects 15 patches an exploit-only oracle would accept, with 98/104 admitted patches confirmed semantically equivalent to developer patches.
AI.motivation: Existing Python AVR benchmarks lack rigorous functional correctness validation — they either accept patches based solely on proof-of-concept exploits or apply functional tests only to entries whose upstream projects happen to ship them. This misses functional regressions where a patch defeats the exploit but breaks unrelated behavior, undermining trust in repair evaluation.
AI.method: The authors construct Vul4Py, a benchmark of 100 real vulnerabilities from 60 open-source Python projects (2017–2025, 60 distinct CWEs), each with a pinned reproducible environment and a paired oracle: (1) an exploit oracle that must fail on the vulnerable revision and pass on the fixed one, and (2) a project-native pytest functional oracle that must pass on both. They then benchmark six AVR approaches across three categories — a specialized vulnerability repair tool, directly prompted LLMs, and software engineering agents (e.g., OpenHands) — all sharing the same backbone model.
AI.result: OpenHands (agent) repairs 41/100 vulnerabilities, compared to 4 for the best directly prompted LLM and 2 for the specialized tool. The paired oracle proves critical: it rejects 15 of 119 patches that an exploit-only oracle would accept. Furthermore, 98 of the 104 patches admitted by the paired oracle are manually confirmed to be semantically equivalent to developer-authored fixes.
AI.conclusion: Paired exploit-plus-functional oracles are essential for trustworthy AVR evaluation. Software engineering agents substantially outperform directly prompted LLMs and specialized repair tools on Python vulnerability repair, and the Vul4Py benchmark provides a reproducible, rigorous foundation for future AVR research.

title: What Transfers from Text to Vision? Capability Scaling Laws and Transfer Dynamics for VLMs
summary: Choosing the right large language model (LLM) backbone is the most consequential decision when building a vision-language model (VLM), yet it remains fundamentally unprincipled: compute-based scaling laws fail to generalize across model families, and no framework exists for directly predicting VLM performance before training begins. We propose the Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law, the first cross-family framework that predicts VLM benchmark accuracy from directly observable textual capability. Given a low-dimensional capability score $S$ extracted from LLM textual benchmarks via PCA, we model VLM performance as a function of $S$, with a per-backbone transfer rate and an absorption rate that quantifies data-scaling efficiency. To fit and validate the framework, we train over 150 VLMs on 34 LLMs spanning 7 model families under a strictly controlled recipe. Evaluations on more than 200 textual and 50 multimodal benchmarks show that the law accurately extrapolates transfer rate from models up to 8B parameters to 72B-scale backbones, predicts full VLM training trajectories with high fidelity, and generalizes to entirely held-out model families. Beyond the scaling law, our analysis surfaces actionable insights: certain textual benchmarks negatively correlate with multimodal performance, exposing latent benchmark-gaming behavior; base LLMs outperform instruction-tuned counterparts as VLM backbones due to higher absorption rates and lower data-scaling decay; and different model families occupy distinct positions in the transfer--absorption space. The framework turns backbone selection from costly empirical sweeps into a principled, quantitative decision. Code and data are available at https://github.com/wangq-dev/CDMScaling.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Capability-Driven Multimodal Scaling Law, the first cross-family framework that predicts vision-language model (VLM) performance from LLM textual benchmark scores alone, trained on 150+ VLMs across 34 LLMs and 7 families, enabling principled backbone selection without costly empirical sweeps.
AI.motivation: Current LLM backbone selection for VLMs is unprincipled: compute-based scaling laws fail to generalize across model families, and no framework exists to predict VLM performance before training. This makes backbone choice a costly empirical process.
AI.method: The authors extract a low-dimensional capability score S from LLM textual benchmarks via PCA, then model VLM performance as a function of S with two key parameters: a per-backbone transfer rate and an absorption rate capturing data-scaling efficiency. They train over 150 VLMs on 34 LLMs spanning 7 model families under a strictly controlled recipe to fit and validate the framework across 200+ textual and 50+ multimodal benchmarks.
AI.result: The law accurately extrapolates transfer rate from 8B-parameter models to 72B-scale backbones, predicts full VLM training trajectories with high fidelity, and generalizes to held-out model families. Additional findings: certain textual benchmarks negatively correlate with multimodal performance (exposing benchmark-gaming); base LLMs outperform instruction-tuned counterparts due to higher absorption rates; and model families occupy distinct positions in transfer-absorption space.
AI.conclusion: The framework transforms VLM backbone selection from costly empirical sweeps into a principled, quantitative decision based on directly observable textual capability scores.

title: Trust and Its Betrayal under Three Representational Strategies
summary: Trust is a propositional attitude of a distinctive kind: to trust is to rely on another under conditions where reliance could be disappointed, and the disappointment of trust---betrayal---differs qualitatively from the disappointment of a prediction. We treat trust as a \emph{subjunctive} epistemic state: $A$ trusts $B$'s competence when $A$ believes that \emph{were $P$ true, $B$ would know it}, and $B$'s integrity when $A$ believes that \emph{were $B$ to know $P$, he would disclose it to $A$}. We develop three representations of this state---as lexicographic \emph{assumption} as \emph{ordinal closeness} in a Lewis--Stalnaker sphere system , and as \emph{strong belief} in a conditional probability system and for each we ask whether the Brandenburger--Keisler impossibility on common belief survives when the assumption of rationality is replaced by an assumption of trustworthiness. The three representations agree that every \emph{finite} depth of common trust is realizable while the \emph{completed} common-trust fixed point is the locus of difficulty, but they differ sharply in \emph{how} the difficulty manifests, and---our organizing finding---in how each survives a concrete betrayal. W show that the same betrayal refutes an agent's \emph{level ordering} under the lexicographic representation, contaminates her \emph{closeness ordering} in proportion to the betrayer's deliberateness under the ordinal representation, and merely \emph{shifts her operative conditioning hypothesis} while leaving her belief structure coherent under the strong-belief representation.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes trust as a subjunctive epistemic state with three representations—lexicographic assumption, ordinal closeness, and strong belief—and examines how each survives betrayal, showing they diverge sharply in how the Brandenburger-Keisler impossibility manifests when rationality is replaced by trustworthiness.
AI.motivation: Trust is underexplored in formal epistemology; the authors seek to model trust rigorously, distinguish it from mere prediction, and investigate whether classic impossibility results on common belief (Brandenburger-Keisler) persist when agents are trustworthy rather than rational.
AI.method: Trust is defined subjunctively: A trusts B's competence iff A believes "were P true, B would know it"; and B's integrity iff A believes "were B to know P, he would disclose it." Three formal representations are developed: (1) lexicographic assumption, (2) ordinal closeness in Lewis-Stalnaker sphere systems, and (3) strong belief in conditional probability systems. Each is tested against finite and completed common-trust fixed points and against a concrete betrayal scenario.
AI.result: All three representations agree that finite-depth common trust is realizable but the completed common-trust fixed point is problematic. They diverge under betrayal: the lexicographic representation suffers level-ordering refutation; the ordinal representation's closeness ordering is contaminated proportionally to the betrayer's deliberateness; the strong-belief representation merely shifts the operative conditioning hypothesis while preserving overall belief coherence.
AI.conclusion: The three representations of trust exhibit fundamentally different resilience to betrayal, with the strong-belief representation proving most robust. This has implications for how trust-based epistemic frameworks can circumvent impossibility results that plague rationality-based frameworks.

title: Disentangled Contrastive Learning for Zero-Shot Multilingual Dense Retrieval
summary: Multilingual dense retrieval aims to handle queries and documents across different languages based on a unified retriever model. The challenge lies in enabling robust retrieval transfer to low-resource languages where annotated retrieval data is often scarce. Although previous studies transfer high-resource supervision to low-resource languages in multilingual semantic representation learning, the shared representation often entangles semantic and linguistic features, which may interfere with optimizing semantic relevance for retrieval. Different from existing methods that focus on learning language-agnostic semantic features under such entanglement, we propose a disentangled contrastive learning~(DCL) method for multilingual dense retrieval by separating multilingual representations into semantic and linguistic subspaces. Specifically, we design disentangled optimization objectives based on hierarchical semantic alignment and language debiasing contrastive learning. By aligning retrieval-relevant semantics across languages at both sentence and token levels while capturing language-specific variations in the linguistic subspace, these objectives reduce language-induced interference in semantic matching. We jointly optimize them with the retrieval objective to facilitate stable zero-shot transfer from English supervision to multilingual dense retrieval. Extensive experiments on mMARCO and MIRACL show that our method consistently outperforms several strong baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness and generalization ability.

AI.tldr: DCL separates multilingual representations into semantic and linguistic subspaces via hierarchical alignment and language debiasing, enabling better zero-shot cross-lingual dense retrieval by reducing language interference in semantic matching.
AI.motivation: Existing multilingual dense retrieval methods entangle semantic and linguistic features in shared representations, causing language-specific variations to interfere with semantic relevance optimization, particularly harming zero-shot transfer to low-resource languages.
AI.method: Disentangled Contrastive Learning (DCL) separates representations into semantic and linguistic subspaces. It uses two complementary objectives: (1) hierarchical semantic alignment operating at both sentence and token levels to align retrieval-relevant semantics across languages, and (2) language debiasing contrastive learning to capture language-specific variations in the linguistic subspace. These are jointly optimized with the standard retrieval objective.
AI.result: DCL consistently outperforms several strong baselines on mMARCO and MIRACL benchmarks, demonstrating superior effectiveness and generalization in zero-shot cross-lingual dense retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling semantic and linguistic subspaces is an effective strategy for multilingual dense retrieval, enabling stable zero-shot transfer from high-resource (English) supervision to low-resource languages by mitigating language-induced interference in semantic matching.

title: A Data-Centric Perspective on Tree Visualizations
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures. To appear in IEEE VIS 2026 (short paper)
summary: Tree visualization (TreeVis) techniques span diverse designs. Existing taxonomies organize them by visual characteristics such as layout dimensionality, edge representation, and node alignment. However, this visual-centric perspective can obscure structural similarities and make it difficult to determine whether differences arise from data structures or visual encodings. We investigate TreeVis techniques from a data-centric perspective grounded in Prepared Tables, the final data state prior to visual encoding. Using TreeVis.net, we curate 133 two-dimensional techniques and characterize each by the object records and attribute roles required before encoding. Our analysis shows that the corpus is more concentrated at the prepared-data level than a visual reading would suggest. The techniques collapse to a small set of recurring object combinations and schemas. Many techniques across TreeVis representation categories share the same schema, suggesting that much of the apparent diversity of TreeVis designs lies in visual representation rather than fundamentally different pre-encoding data requirements. Prepared Table schemas therefore support reasoning about structural equivalence, sufficiency, and difference across TreeVis designs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a data-centric taxonomy for tree visualization by analyzing 133 techniques through their "Prepared Tables" — the final data state before visual encoding. Findings reveal that despite apparent visual diversity, most techniques collapse to a small set of recurring object-record schemas, indicating that structural differences are largely visual rather than data-driven.
AI.motivation: Existing tree visualization taxonomies are organized by visual characteristics (layout dimensionality, edge representation, node alignment), which obscures structural similarities and makes it unclear whether differences stem from data structures or visual encodings. A data-centric lens is needed to clarify these distinctions.
AI.method: The authors curate 133 two-dimensional TreeVis techniques from TreeVis.net and characterize each by its "Prepared Table" — the object records and attribute roles required immediately before visual encoding. They then analyze the corpus for recurring schemas and object combinations, mapping how techniques collapse at the data level.
AI.result: The corpus is far more concentrated at the prepared-data level than visual inspection would suggest. Techniques collapse into a small set of recurring object combinations and schemas, with many across different representation categories sharing identical schemas. This indicates that diversity in TreeVis is predominantly in visual representation, not pre-encoding data requirements.
AI.conclusion: Prepared Table schemas provide a principled basis for reasoning about structural equivalence, sufficiency, and difference across TreeVis designs, offering a complementary data-centric framework to traditional visual-centric taxonomies.

title: EduPluginBench: Executable Assurance for AI-Generated Educational Plugins
comment: 27 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology (TOSEM)
summary: Code-generation models can produce executable components, but compilation and functional tests do not establish compliance with least privilege, telemetry consent, provenance, privileged-write authority, lifecycle constraints, or bounded failure. We introduce EduPluginBench, an executable benchmark and staged admission method for generated plugins in governed software ecosystems. Across 1,440 activation-checked first-order mutants from 30 specifications, P0-P4 increased release-blocking-defect recall by 74.7 percentage points (specification-clustered 95% CI 73.4-75.8) over P0-P2, with no observed rejection among 120 clean references (95% Wilson upper bound 3.1%). A frozen transfer study of 600 unmodified generations from two current coding models found that 300/600 parsed, but none passed P0 or achieved P0-P4 conformance (95% upper bound 0.64%); downstream assurance estimands were undefined. An independently labelled Moodle study retained 16 vulnerable/fixed pairs; the frozen generic PHP detector found no vulnerable revisions. These negative transfer results prevent controlled contract consistency from being read as independent real-defect effectiveness. An earlier 540-generation diagnostic found that post-hoc bounded repair yielded 112 P0 passes, all nonconforming, with recall increasing from 13.4% to 100%. The artifact retains protocols, public-source provenance, raw generations, row-level decisions, audits, analysis code, and reproduction instructions.

AI.tldr: EduPluginBench is an executable benchmark and staged admission framework (P0–P4) for evaluating code-generation model outputs against governance requirements beyond compilation — including least privilege, telemetry consent, provenance, and lifecycle constraints. It achieves a 74.7 pp recall improvement over weaker checks with no false rejection of clean references, but zero current coding-model generations pass full conformance, and negative transfer results prevent reading controlled outcomes as real-world defect effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Existing code-generation evaluation stops at compilation and functional correctness, ignoring critical governance and security compliance dimensions — least privilege, telemetry consent, provenance tracking, privileged-write authority, lifecycle constraints, and bounded failure. Without systematic, executable checks for these properties, generated plugins pose unacceptable risk in governed software ecosystems.
AI.method: The authors introduce EduPluginBench, comprising 1,440 activation-checked first-order mutants derived from 30 specifications, 120 clean references, and a staged admission protocol spanning levels P0 through P4. They conduct a frozen transfer study using 600 unmodified generations from two current coding models and an independently labelled Moodle study with 16 vulnerable/fixed pairs. A diagnostic repair experiment on 540 generations tests post-hoc bounded repair. All artifacts — protocols, source provenance, raw generations, row-level decisions, audits, analysis code, and reproduction instructions — are retained.
AI.result: The full P0–P4 pipeline increased release-blocking-defect recall by 74.7 percentage points (95% CI 73.4–75.8) over P0–P2 alone, with zero false rejections among clean references (95% Wilson upper bound 3.1%). In the frozen transfer study, 300/600 generations parsed but none achieved P0 or P0–P4 conformance (95% upper bound 0.64%); downstream assurance estimands were undefined. The Moodle study found the frozen generic PHP detector identified no vulnerable revisions among 16 pairs. Post-hoc bounded repair of 540 generations yielded 112 P0 passes — all nonconforming — with recall increasing from 13.4% to 100%.
AI.conclusion: Staged, specification-grounded admission checks dramatically improve governance-relevant defect detection over compilation-and-test baselines alone, but current coding models produce zero fully conformant plugin generations. Negative transfer results indicate controlled contract consistency cannot be interpreted as independent real-defect effectiveness, cautioning against overclaiming from synthetic benchmarks without downstream validation.

title: Role Steering of Language Models for Social Simulations
summary: Social simulations built from language-model agents need role-conditioned behavior that can be checked before agents are placed into a simulated population. We introduce an activation-steering screening workflow for role-conditioned agents: define a role profile, extract a role-specific direction, sweep four steering coefficients, evaluate role-profile alignment, and pass or flag each candidate configuration. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, we apply the workflow to a mixed 275-role inventory with 228 role-agnostic questions, GPT-4.1-mini prompted role references, and GPT-4.1-mini judges. Role-specific directions receive higher judged role-profile alignment than an assistant-axis directional control from prior persona-vector work, with mean overall scores of 63.2 versus 41.1 across the tested grid. They also preserve high lexical diversity, while the control drops sharply at larger coefficients. The role-level screen is the main practical output: most roles improve as steering increases, but 38 roles decline across all six measured dimensions, showing why simulation builders should choose coefficients per role rather than deploy a uniform high-strength setting. We make our code and evaluation artifacts available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/anonymous-research-code-5F03/.

AI.tldr: A screening workflow using activation steering is introduced to verify role-conditioned behavior in language-model agents before deployment in social simulations. Role-specific steering directions outperform a generic assistant-axis baseline on role-profile alignment (63.2 vs 41.1) while preserving lexical diversity. Per-role coefficient tuning is necessary, as 38 of 275 roles degrade across all dimensions under uniform high-strength steering.
AI.motivation: Social simulations built from LM agents require role-conditioned behavior that can be reliably verified before agents are placed into a simulated population. Without screening, agents may fail to exhibit their assigned role profiles, undermining simulation validity.
AI.method: The authors propose an activation-steering screening workflow: (1) define a role profile, (2) extract a role-specific direction from the model's activations, (3) sweep across four steering coefficients, (4) evaluate role-profile alignment using a judge, and (5) pass or flag each candidate configuration. Experiments use OLMo-3-7B-Instruct with a 275-role inventory, 228 role-agnostic questions, GPT-4.1-mini for role references, and GPT-4.1-mini as judges. An assistant-axis directional control from prior persona-vector work serves as baseline.
AI.result: Role-specific directions achieve a mean judged role-profile alignment score of 63.2 versus 41.1 for the assistant-axis control across the tested steering coefficient grid. Lexical diversity remains high with role-specific steering but drops sharply at larger coefficients for the control. At the role level, most roles improve with increased steering, but 38 roles decline across all six measured dimensions, demonstrating the need for per-role coefficient selection rather than a uniform high-strength setting.
AI.conclusion: Activation-steering screening is an effective, practical tool for filtering role-conditioned LM agents before simulation deployment. The per-role variability in steering response underscores that simulation builders should tune coefficients individually rather than apply a one-size-fits-all approach. Code and artifacts are publicly released.

title: Learning to Coordinate Symbolic Tools: LLM Agents for Verified Sum-of-Squares Certificates
summary: Tool calling allows large language models (LLMs) to invoke external computation during problem solving, a useful capability in various fields including AI for mathematics. We study this setting through weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) decomposition, a machine-checkable route to proving polynomial nonnegativity and hence polynomial inequalities. A candidate decomposition can be checked exactly, but finding one requires choosing among non-unique regroupings and coordinating multiple symbolic transformations. We develop an agent that combines algebraic task training, symbolic tools, and verifier-grounded optimization for this task. Rather than training only on the composite SOS task, we construct 1.35 million synthetic examples covering eight supporting polynomial tasks together with weighted-SOS decomposition. We first apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces, and then use Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-specific symbolic rewards. The SFT corpus contains no native tool-calling messages; at evaluation, the agent uses native SymPy calls for expansion, collection, reordering, and factorization. Every final SOS answer is checked by exact expansion and coefficient comparison. On held-out, same-generator synthetic problems, the full SFT+GRPO+tools system is the strongest of four evaluated configurations, reaching 78.96% verified success on weighted SOS, compared with 44.73% for the base model with the same tools, and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks. Within this controlled setting, our work provides a case study of combining domain-specific skill training, executable tools, and verifier feedback, and may inform the design of tool-calling agents in other domains with exactly checkable outputs.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an LLM-based agent for weighted sum-of-squares (SOS) decomposition that combines synthetic algebraic task training, symbolic tool use (SymPy), and verifier-grounded RL optimization (GRPO), achieving 78.96% verified success versus 44.73% for the base model with tools.
AI.motivation: Tool calling enables LLMs to invoke external computation, but current approaches lack effective integration of domain-specific symbolic reasoning, tool orchestration, and exact verification. Weighted SOS decomposition serves as a well-defined testbed: candidate decompositions can be checked exactly by polynomial expansion, but finding one requires non-unique regroupings and multiple coordinated symbolic transformations — a challenge well-suited to studying how LLMs can learn to call tools for exact mathematical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors construct 1.35M synthetic examples across eight supporting polynomial tasks plus weighted-SOS. Training proceeds in two stages: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on direct algebra problems and simulated symbolic traces, with no native tool-calling messages in the corpus; (2) Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task-specific symbolic rewards. At evaluation, the agent autonomously invokes SymPy for expansion, collection, reordering, and factorization. Every SOS answer is verified by exact expansion and coefficient comparison.
AI.result: The full SFT+GRPO+tools configuration achieves 78.96% verified success on held-out weighted SOS problems (vs. 44.73% for base model with tools) and 91.75% macro accuracy across nine polynomial tasks. Ablation shows each component (SFT, GRPO, tools) contributes to performance gains.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific skill training, executable symbolic tools, and verifier feedback can be effectively combined to build reliable tool-calling agents for exactly checkable mathematical tasks. This case study may generalize to other domains where outputs admit exact verification.

title: Advancing Relevance Measurement with Vision-Language Models for Web-Scale Search
summary: Relevance evaluation plays a crucial role in personalized search systems, serving as a guardrail alongside user engagement metrics to ensure that search results align with user queries and intent. While human annotation is the traditional method for relevance evaluation, its high cost and long turnaround time limit its scalability. In this work, we present a VLM-based automated relevance evaluation pipeline deployed within Pinterest Search for online A/B experiments. We rigorously validate the alignment between VLM-generated judgments and human annotations, demonstrating that VLMs can provide reliable relevance measurement for experiments while greatly improving the evaluation efficiency. Leveraging VLM-based labeling further unlocks opportunities to expand the query set, optimize sampling design, and efficiently assess a wider range of search experiences at scale. This approach leads to higher-quality relevance metrics and significantly reduces the Minimum Detectable Effects (MDEs) in online experiment measurements.

AI.tldr: Pinterest deploys a VLM-based automated relevance evaluation pipeline for online A/B experiments, validating alignment with human annotations, improving efficiency, expanding query coverage, and reducing Minimum Detectable Effects (MDEs).
AI.motivation: Traditional human annotation for relevance evaluation in personalized search is costly, slow, and limits scalability. There is a need for an automated, reliable, and efficient alternative that maintains alignment with human judgment while enabling broader experimentation.
AI.method: A VLM-based (Vision-Language Model) automated relevance evaluation pipeline is deployed within Pinterest Search for online A/B experiments. The approach includes rigorous validation of VLM-human annotation alignment, expansion of query sets, optimization of sampling design, and efficient assessment of diverse search experiences at scale.
AI.result: VLM-generated judgments demonstrate reliable alignment with human annotations. The pipeline improves evaluation efficiency, enables higher-quality relevance metrics, and significantly reduces Minimum Detectable Effects (MDEs) in online experiment measurements.
AI.conclusion: VLMs can serve as a scalable, reliable replacement for human relevance annotation in production search systems, unlocking broader experiment coverage and more sensitive online A/B testing.

title: Safety Invariants for Agents Orchestrating Irreversible State Transitions: A Four-Dimensional Formalism Evaluated on Public Ledgers
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly asked to produce irreversible effects on external systems - transferring funds, writing to durable storage, actuating hardware. Existing agent frameworks (ReAct, Reflexion, MCP) optimize task success on benchmarks and give little attention to the safety of irreversible side-effects. We formalize one such setting, movement of value across public ledgers, as state transitions in a four-dimensional space indexed by (wallet, chain, address, protocol), and use that formalism to state and prove a guarantee we call execution fidelity: under a fault model admitting planner mis-mapping, ambiguous outcomes, retries, at-least-once delivery, and delegated non-human callers, a session's realized effect on the ledger is either nothing at all or exactly the transition that was rendered to the user, exactly once. The theorem deliberately does not claim that the rendered transition matches the user's intent - no runtime layer can decide that - but it confines that unbounded question to a single predicate over a finite object, which is what makes a preview a sufficient control rather than a formality. Seven safety invariants, derived from the fidelity condition rather than enumerated from experience, discharge the guarantee. Empirically, on a controlled N=60 adversarial suite the stack lifts pass rate by ~74 percentage points over a naive-ReAct baseline on two write-aggressive backing models, but by only ~3 points on a write-cautious one - evidence that single-model evaluations of agent safety stacks are close to unfalsifiable. The system is deployed; 108 production write operations across 8 chains back the failure taxonomy. Although the evaluation setting is public ledgers, the formalism and invariants apply to any probabilistic agent acting on irreversible external state.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "execution fidelity" for autonomous agents performing irreversible actions on public ledgers, proving that under a defined fault model, realized ledger effects match exactly what was previewed to the user. Seven safety invariants enforce this guarantee. Empirical evaluation shows the safety stack substantially improves correctness on write-aggressive models but reveals single-model evaluations are near-unfalsifiable.
AI.motivation: Existing agent frameworks (ReAct, Reflexion, MCP) prioritize task success but neglect safety of irreversible side-effects — like fund transfers or durable writes — where mistakes have real-world consequences. There is no formal guarantee ensuring that what an agent actually does matches what was shown to the user for approval.
AI.method: The authors formalize ledger operations as state transitions in a four-dimensional space (wallet, chain, address, protocol), define a fault model (planner mis-mapping, ambiguous outcomes, retries, at-least-once delivery, delegated non-human callers), and prove an "execution fidelity" theorem: realized effects are either null or match the rendered transition exactly once. Seven invariants derived from the fidelity condition enforce this. Evaluation uses an N=60 adversarial suite across two write-aggressive and one write-cautious model, plus 108 production operations across 8 chains.
AI.result: The safety stack lifts pass rate by ~74 percentage points over a naive-ReAct baseline on two write-aggressive models, but only ~3 points on a write-cautious model — indicating single-model safety evaluations are near-unfalsifiable. The system is deployed in production with 108 write operations across 8 chains backing the failure taxonomy.
AI.conclusion: Execution fidelity provides a provable safety boundary for irreversible agent actions by separating the unbounded problem of user intent matching from the finite, verifiable problem of execution matching the preview. The near-zero improvement on write-cautious models demonstrates that evaluating agent safety stacks on a single model is methodologically unsound. The formalism generalizes beyond public ledgers to any probabilistic agent acting on irreversible external state.

title: FedWorld: Scope-Aware Federation of Agent World Models
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents learn world dynamics from local interaction experience to support subsequent planning and action selection. However, the experience available to a single client is often incomplete, which motivates sharing knowledge across clients. Existing federated methods mainly aggregate model parameters, while agent memory-sharing methods commonly pool trajectories, memories, or rules without checking whether they remain valid for each client. This assumption is problematic because the same abstract action may produce different effects under different policies, environments, or exception conditions. Consequently, a rule supported by most clients may overwrite correct knowledge held by a minority client. To address this problem, we propose FEDWORLD, a scope-aware federated world-model protocol that exchanges structured abstract transition rules. Each client converts private transitions into normalized rules, and the server aligns related rules to identify each rule supporting and contradicting evidence across clients. The resulting evidence determines whether a rule is shared, cluster-specific, private, or unresolved. Each target client retains its local rules and accepts federated updates only for uncovered cases whose inferred scope is compatible; ambiguous rules are withheld. Experiments on $τ$-bench and ALFWorld show that FEDWORLD reduces negative transfer under conflicting dynamics while retaining useful cross-client transfer, leading to fewer state regressions, repeated actions, and excess steps, as well as higher task success.

AI.tldr: FEDWORLD is a federated world-model protocol for LLM agents that shares structured abstract transition rules with scope-awareness, preventing negative transfer by only accepting federated updates for uncovered cases with compatible inferred scope, while retaining local rules and withholding ambiguous ones.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in federated settings suffer from negative transfer when sharing knowledge, because the same abstract action can produce different effects under different policies, environments, or exceptions. Existing methods that aggregate model parameters or naively pool trajectories/memories/rules fail to check whether shared knowledge remains valid for each client, causing majority rules to overwrite correct minority knowledge.
AI.method: FEDWORLD operates by having each client convert private transitions into normalized abstract transition rules. A central server aligns related rules across clients and identifies supporting and contradicting evidence for each rule. Based on this evidence, rules are classified into four categories: shared, cluster-specific, private, or unresolved. Each target client retains its local rules and only accepts federated updates for uncovered cases where the inferred scope is compatible; ambiguous rules are withheld to prevent harmful overwrites.
AI.result: Experiments on τ-bench and ALFWorld demonstrate that FEDWORLD reduces negative transfer under conflicting dynamics while preserving beneficial cross-client transfer. This yields fewer state regressions, fewer repeated actions, fewer excess steps, and higher overall task success rates.
AI.conclusion: Scope-aware, evidence-based rule sharing in federated world-model learning effectively mitigates negative transfer caused by conflicting environment dynamics, enabling robust multi-client knowledge collaboration for LLM agents.

title: Less Is More: Tuning Configurable Systems with Imperfect Fidelity
comment: Accepted by the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Configuration tuning is essential for optimizing the performance of highly configurable systems, e.g., throughput or runtime, under a given environment. Yet, this is a challenging process as there can be many options to tune, and configuration measurement is often highly expensive. In this paper, we demonstrate the phenomenon of ``less can be more'': system configuration tuning can be greatly improved with much superior budget utilization by partially tuning under the imperfect-fidelity---an environment that is similar, but cheaper to measure, compared with the concerned perfect-fidelity of environment under which the system should be tuned. We codify a conceptual framework of fidelity for configurable systems, drawing on which allows us to propose MFTune, a tuner that proactively explores in the space of $>10^4$ possible imperfect-fidelity settings to approximate a useful one, which strikes for the wideness of tuning. This creates high-quality seeds for the perfect-fidelity, which in turn ensures the tuning depth. Experiment results against $10$ state-of-the-art tuners, obtained from running diverse real-world systems for $19$ months $24 \times 7$, show that MFTune performs considerably better on $83.33$\% cases with up to $19.34\%$ improvement while achieving hours of budget saving in general.

AI.tldr: MFTune leverages cheaper, imperfect-fidelity environments to generate high-quality seeds for tuning configurable systems in expensive perfect-fidelity environments, achieving up to 19.34% improvement over 10 state-of-the-art tuners across 83.33% of cases while saving hours of measurement budget.
AI.motivation: Configuration tuning of highly configurable systems is challenging due to the vast number of configurable options and the high cost of performance measurement. The authors observe that existing tuners waste budget by exploring suboptimal regions in the expensive perfect-fidelity environment, and they identify an opportunity to exploit cheaper, similar (imperfect-fidelity) environments to improve budget utilization.
AI.method: The authors first codify a conceptual framework of fidelity for configurable systems. They then propose MFTune, a tuner that proactively explores a large space (over 10^4 possible imperfect-fidelity settings) to identify a useful approximation that maximizes tuning wideness. This imperfect-fidelity environment is used to generate high-quality seed configurations, which are then transferred to the perfect-fidelity environment to ensure tuning depth. The approach effectively decouples exploration breadth (in cheap fidelity) from exploitation depth (in expensive fidelity).
AI.result: MFTune was evaluated against 10 state-of-the-art tuners on diverse real-world systems over a 19-month continuous (24/7) experimental campaign. Results show MFTune performs considerably better in 83.33% of cases with up to 19.34% improvement, while generally saving hours of measurement budget.
AI.conclusion: The "less can be more" phenomenon demonstrates that partial tuning under imperfect-fidelity environments can substantially improve both tuning quality and budget efficiency. The fidelity framework and MFTune provide a principled approach for transferring insights from cheap, approximate environments to expensive, target environments in configurable system optimization.

title: Exploring More to Solve More: Boosting Diversity in Text Diffusion Models via Entropy-Based Guidance
summary: Although diffusion models have revolutionized continuous domains like image synthesis through high quality generations and controllable guidance mechanisms, bringing this controllability to the discrete, sequential nature of text remains an open challenge. Meanwhile, current sampling strategies and guidance methods adjust token likelihoods without capturing the broader semantic landscape, leading to a suboptimal balance between fidelity and diversity. In this work, we introduce a novel training-free Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy (SAKE) guidance method. Our method computes the order-2 Rényi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix that captures both cross-token semantic interactions and relative token positions. By linearizing this objective in the embedding space, we derive a tractable guidance signal that dynamically adjusts the sampling distribution, flattening it to encourage exploration during redundancy and sharpening it for fidelity when diverse. Empirical experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves a superior Pareto frontier between fidelity and diversity, and improves multi-sample performance on reasoning-intensive tasks, such as code and mathematics generation, compared to temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines.

AI.tldr: SAKE introduces a training-free guidance method for discrete text generation that uses order-2 Rényi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix to dynamically balance fidelity and diversity, outperforming existing baselines on reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: Current controllable text generation methods adjust token likelihoods without capturing the broader semantic landscape, resulting in suboptimal fidelity-diversity trade-offs. Diffusion-style controllability has not been effectively ported to discrete text domains.
AI.method: SAKE computes order-2 Rényi entropy over a kernel Gram matrix encoding both cross-token semantic interactions and relative token positions. This objective is linearized in embedding space to produce a tractable guidance signal that dynamically flattens or sharpens the sampling distribution depending on whether the context is redundant or diverse.
AI.result: SAKE achieves a superior Pareto frontier between fidelity and diversity compared to temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines, and improves multi-sample performance on reasoning-intensive tasks including code and mathematics generation.
AI.conclusion: SAKE provides an effective, training-free mechanism for controllable discrete text generation by leveraging semantic-aware kernel entropy, successfully bridging the gap between continuous diffusion guidance and discrete text sampling.

title: RMSWeb: Reflection, Failure-Mode Mining, and Salvage-DS for Web Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, and 6 tables. Includes appendices
summary: Compact web agents can reduce deployment cost, but training them poses challenges in both data collection and post-SFT reinforcement learning (RL). Successful trajectories are expensive to collect and often contain inefficient detours. After supervised fine-tuning (SFT), full trajectory corpora are dominated by routine states; moreover, when group-relative RL is applied to web actions, inadequately designed action-level rewards can yield weak or misleading relative updates, while groups rejected as unsuitable for such updates receive no fallback learning signal. We present RMSWeb, a three-part recipe for Qwen3-VL-Instruct at 8B and 32B. Reflection-conditioned retries increase collection yield and shorten successful trajectories; failure-mode mining concentrates offline RL on critical states exposed by the SFT policy; and Salvage-DS combines an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for rejected groups. Policies trained with reflection-collected data use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, RMSWeb improves over SFT by 2.4-7.0 points at 8B and 1.2-7.7 points at 32B. Our 8B model also achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models in our comparison and a leading reported accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench, with the caveat that external evaluation protocols differ.

AI.tldr: RMSWeb is a three-part training recipe (reflection-conditioned retries, failure-mode mining, and Salvage-DS for RL) that improves compact web agents (8B/32B Qwen3-VL-Instruct) by boosting data collection efficiency and designing better RL rewards, yielding 2.4–7.7 point gains across benchmarks with up to 19.7% fewer action steps.
AI.motivation: Compact web agents reduce deployment costs but suffer from two core challenges: (1) collecting successful trajectories is expensive and yields data with inefficient detours, and (2) after SFT, routine states dominate the corpus while group-relative RL with poorly designed action-level rewards provides weak or misleading learning signals, with rejected groups receiving no fallback training.
AI.method: RMSWeb comprises three components applied to Qwen3-VL-Instruct (8B/32B): (1) Reflection-conditioned retries — the agent reflects on failures and retries, increasing collection yield and shortening successful trajectories; (2) Failure-mode mining — concentrates offline RL on critical states where the SFT policy fails; (3) Salvage-DS — a novel RL approach combining an action-semantic polarized reward, contrast-and-competence-gated dynamic sampling, and an action-only anchor for groups rejected by group-relative RL, ensuring all data contributes to learning.
AI.result: Policies trained with reflection-collected data use up to 19.7% fewer action steps on solved tasks. On WebVoyager, Online-Mind2Web, and WebTailBench, RMSWeb improves over SFT baselines by 2.4–7.0 points (8B) and 1.2–7.7 points (32B). The 8B model achieves the strongest reported Online-Mind2Web result among similarly sized open-weight models and a leading accuracy-cost trade-off on WebVoyager and WebTailBench.
AI.conclusion: RMSWeb demonstrates that systematic improvements to data collection (reflection-conditioned retries), targeted RL state selection (failure-mode mining), and robust reward design (Salvage-DS) can significantly boost compact web agent performance, enabling smaller models to approach or exceed larger counterparts while reducing deployment costs.

title: Syntax Meets Semantics: Understanding Scientific Formulae
summary: Scientific formulae are a fundamental component of scholarly communication, yet their dual nature -- as structured syntax and carriers of semantics -- remains underexplored in scholarly information retrieval. Although prior studies show that jointly modeling syntactic and semantic modalities improves retrieval performance, the relationship between their underlying representations has not been systematically investigated. In this work, we empirically study cross-modal correspondence between formula syntax and semantics. We find that their native representation spaces exhibit extremely weak observable correspondence despite strong latent correlation, indicating a substantial representation mismatch between the two modalities. We further evaluate whether this mismatch can be reduced using standard representation learning and alignment techniques. We represent syntactic structure using graph-based encoders and semantic information using text-based encoders, then apply contrastive learning to induce a shared representation space.
