AI.tldr: Textual descriptors from founder narratives alone can predict startup exit success (F1=0.30), with LightGBM achieving F1=0.48 using 850 engineered framing features. A novel "Hyping Score" quantifies how optimized densities of adjectives, jargon, and buzzwords correlate with higher exit probability.
AI.motivation: To determine whether textual/linguistic features of startup narratives alone—without any financial, human capital, or contextual data—can serve as standalone predictive signals for early-stage startup success (Exit) under conditions of high information asymmetry.
AI.method: The authors used VC-curated datasets of 7,419 startups spanning 20 years. They isolated text-based framing variables, engineered 850 features via startup narrative mapping, evaluated statistical significance of data subsets and vector embeddings, and tested six supervised machine learning models, with LightGBM delivering the best performance.
AI.result: LightGBM achieved the highest F1 score of 0.48; textual descriptors alone reached F1=0.30, confirming standalone predictive value. Optimized densities of "hyping markers" (adjectives, jargon, buzzwords) positively correlated with Exit probability, while excessive statement/name length reduced it. A quantifiable Hyping Score was introduced for VC application.
AI.conclusion: Founder narrative framing provides measurable, standalone signals for predicting startup Exit, demonstrating that linguistic hyping—when optimized rather than excessive—can serve as a practical screening tool for venture capital decision-making in high-information-asymmetry settings.

title: SymboUQ: Symbolic Uncertainty Quantification for Spatial Reasoning in LLMs
summary: Although large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent spatial reasoning traces, their intermediate relations may fail to support the final conclusion, making token-level confidence insufficient for final-answer reliability estimation. Existing formal verifiers provide stronger semantic evidence, but their applicability is partial: a parsed claim need not yield a definite semantic verdict. To address this issue, we introduce SymboUQ, a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates final-answer reliability from reasoning traces by distinguishing symbolizability, whether a claim can be represented in the verifier's formal language, from semantic determinacy, whether its execution yields an entailed or contradicted verdict rather than an unknown or not-evaluable outcome. SymboUQ comprises (i) a Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims and extracts feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (ii) a label-free Determinacy Profile that characterizes effective executable coverage; and (iii) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that integrates constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability. Extensive experiments on five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones show that SymboUQ achieves approximately an 8% relative improvement in AUROC and a 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss over the strongest baseline.

AI.tldr: SymboUQ is a symbolic uncertainty quantification framework that estimates LLM final-answer reliability on spatial reasoning by distinguishing symbolizability from semantic determinacy, integrating constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores to achieve significant improvements in AUROC and calibration over baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce fluent spatial reasoning traces, but token-level confidence is unreliable because intermediate relations may not support the final conclusion. Existing formal verifiers offer stronger semantic evidence but have partial applicability — a parsed claim may not yield a definite verdict (entailed/contradicted). There is a gap in reliably estimating answer correctness when verifier coverage is incomplete.
AI.method: SymboUQ introduces three components: (1) a Layout Auditor that executes ordered spatial claims to extract feasibility, conflict, and repair evidence; (2) a label-free Determinacy Profile that characterizes effective executable coverage by distinguishing symbolizability (can the claim be represented?) from semantic determinacy (does execution yield entailed/contradicted rather than unknown/not-evaluable?); and (3) a Determinacy-Aware Reliability Composer that fuses constraint-based, representation-based, and decoding-based scores according to verifier applicability.
AI.result: On five spatial reasoning benchmarks with four frozen LLM backbones, SymboUQ achieves approximately an 8% relative improvement in AUROC and a 7% relative reduction in class-balanced Brier loss compared to the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Disentangling symbolizability from semantic determinacy enables more reliable uncertainty quantification for LLM spatial reasoning. SymboUQ's hybrid scoring approach effectively leverages formal verifiers even when their coverage is partial, yielding better calibration and selective prediction performance than both token-level and purely verification-based methods.

title: Beyond the Final Prompt: Measuring the Effect of Within-Conversation Context on AI Answers
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Companion to arXiv:2607.22392
summary: An isolated final user message is often treated as the query in evaluations of AI systems. In a conversation, however, the actionable request may be distributed across preceding turns. We directly test whether that omitted within-conversation context changes answers. For each of 180 English multi-turn conversations sampled from a governed commercial corpus and the public PRISM dataset, we hold the final user message and requested answer model constant while generating three answers: one from the full role-labelled conversation, one from the final message alone, and one from the final message plus a prefix-only reconstruction capped at 160 words. A separately requested judge model evaluates answers under randomized labels. The prespecified primary endpoint is a material difference that could change what the user does, rather than a difference in style or detail. After inverse-probability weighting to the eligible cohorts, the full-conversation and isolated-final answers differ materially in 44.7% of cases (95% bootstrap CI 33.8% to 56.1%). Full-conversation answers score 0.49 points higher on a 0 to 4 request-satisfaction scale (0.32 to 0.67). Adding the compressed prefix reduces the material-difference rate to 30.8% (20.2% to 42.1%), a 13.9-point reduction (4.9% to 24.1%), and reduces the mean satisfaction gap to 0.01 points (-0.12 to 0.13). Yet compression is not equivalent to the complete dialogue context: almost one third of answers remain materially different. An order-swapped repeat on 48 cases yields 91.7% agreement and kappa = 0.83 for the primary decision. The study concerns preceding turns in the same conversation and does not test persistent memory across separate conversations.

AI.tldr: Removing conversational context before a final user message materially alters AI answers in ~45% of cases; adding a compressed prefix reduces but does not eliminate this gap (~31% remain different), demonstrating that isolated-query evaluation is insufficient for assessing conversational AI performance.
AI.motivation: Standard AI evaluation practices often treat the final user message in isolation as the query, ignoring preceding conversational context. The authors hypothesize that this omitted within-conversation context substantially changes model answers in ways that matter for downstream user actions—not merely stylistic differences.
AI.method: From 180 English multi-turn conversations (sourced from a governed commercial corpus and PRISM), the authors hold the final user message constant and generate three answers per case: (1) full role-labeled conversation, (2) final message alone, (3) final message plus a compressed prefix reconstruction (≤160 words). A blinded judge model evaluates answers on a 0–4 request-satisfaction scale, with the primary endpoint being a material difference that could change user behavior. Inverse-probability weighting adjusts for cohort eligibility. An order-swapped repeat on 48 cases assesses reliability (91.7% agreement, κ=0.83).
AI.result: Full-conversation vs. isolated-final answers differ materially in 44.7% of cases (95% CI: 33.8%–56.1%). Full-conversation answers score 0.49 points higher (0.32–0.67) on the satisfaction scale. Adding compressed prefixes reduces the material-difference rate to 30.8% (20.2%–42.1%), a 13.9-point reduction (4.9%–24.1%), with a residual mean satisfaction gap of 0.01 (−0.12 to 0.13). However, ~31% of answers remain materially different, indicating compression is not equivalent to full context.
AI.conclusion: Isolated final-message evaluation systematically underestimates answer quality and misrepresents model behavior. Compressed prefixes offer partial mitigation but do not substitute for full conversational context. The findings challenge standard single-turn evaluation paradigms and underscore the need for conversation-level assessment frameworks, while noting the study is limited to within-conversation context (not cross-conversation memory).

title: A Decade of Healthcare Cyber Threats: Empirical Analysis, Evidence-Based Prioritisation, and AI Threat Model
summary: Healthcare systems face persistent and evolving cyber threats, yet how adversarial tactics and techniques have shifted over time has not been systematically characterised using empirical, multi-source data. This paper analyses 1,214 threat records drawn from three authoritative sources: the MITRE ATT&CK behavioural framework, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue, and the NIST vulnerability database, covering 44 validated healthcare-targeting threat entities from 2017 to 2024. We show that attacker behaviour has shifted measurably toward stealth-oriented tactics: defense evasion remained the dominant tactic throughout the observation period, consistently accounting for 15-20% of observed technique use from 2017 to 2024, while persistence declined from 11.2% to zero and initial access from 9.0% to zero over the same period. We further demonstrate that existing detection guidance is structurally misaligned with where attacker effort is concentrated, with the least-covered techniques receiving the most adversarial attention. A convergence analysis links 679 confirmed exploited vulnerabilities to a single dominant behavioural technique, identifying a common addressable chokepoint across the vulnerability and behavioural surfaces. Finally, we identify 42 high-priority techniques representing immediate detection opportunities and show that this set of techniques maps directly to emerging threats against AI-integrated clinical systems.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 1,214 threat records (2017–2024) from MITRE ATT&CK, CISA KEV, and NIST NVD reveals a shift toward stealth-oriented attacker tactics in healthcare, with defense evasion dominant (15–20%) while persistence and initial access declined to zero. Detection guidance is structurally misaligned with adversarial effort, and 42 high-priority techniques are identified as chokepoints applicable to emerging AI-clinical system threats.
AI.motivation: Despite persistent cyber threats against healthcare systems, no prior study has systematically characterized how adversarial tactics and techniques have evolved over time using empirical, multi-source data. The authors aim to fill this gap by quantifying behavioural shifts and identifying mismatches between attacker focus and existing detection guidance.
AI.method: The study aggregates and analyzes 1,214 threat records from three authoritative sources — the MITRE ATT&CK framework, the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogue, and the NIST National Vulnerability Database — covering 44 validated healthcare-targeting threat entities from 2017 to 2024. Techniques are mapped and trended over time; detection coverage is compared against adversarial attention; a convergence analysis links 679 confirmed exploited vulnerabilities to a single dominant behavioural technique; and 42 high-priority techniques are identified and mapped to AI-integrated clinical system threats.
AI.result: Defense evasion remained the dominant tactic at 15–20% of observed technique use throughout 2017–2024. Persistence declined from 11.2% to zero, and initial access from 9.0% to zero over the same period. Detection guidance is structurally misaligned: the least-covered techniques receive the most adversarial attention. A convergence analysis links 679 confirmed exploited vulnerabilities to a single dominant behavioural technique, revealing a common chokepoint. Forty-two high-priority techniques are identified as immediate detection opportunities and map directly to emerging threats against AI-integrated clinical systems.
AI.conclusion: Healthcare cyber threats have measurably shifted toward stealth-oriented behaviours, with defense evasion as the persistent dominant tactic. Existing detection frameworks are misaligned with actual adversarial effort, but a concentrated set of 42 techniques — linked to both vulnerability exploitation and AI-system threats — represents actionable, high-impact detection opportunities that can address structural gaps in current defences.

title: Emotional Expression in Persuasion by Quadruped Virtual Agents: Toward Cross-Species Design Patterns
comment: Preprint. 68 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables. Submitted to Frontiers in AI
summary:
Persuasive technologies increasingly use virtual agents to influence attitudes and behavior, but research has focused mainly on humanoid agents. The persuasive design of non-humanoid, quadruped agents remains underexplored, and it is unclear whether emotional expression works consistently across animal species or whether species-specific motion is necessary.
  We developed virtual dog, cat, and horse agents and compared three behavioral conditions: species-specific behavior, shared behavior across species, and a bark-only baseline. Participants completed everyday tasks involving trash disposal, feeding, and refraining from smartphone use. We evaluated intention understanding, behavioral intention, actual behavior, psychological reactance, discomfort, familiarity, and agent acceptance.
  In several task contexts, the bark-only baseline produced lower intention-understanding and behavioral scores than the expressive conditions. Emotional expression and attention-guiding cues therefore appear to improve interpretation of agent intention and support behavior change. However, no consistent significant differences emerged between species-specific and shared behavior, suggesting that faithful reproduction of animal-specific motion is not the main determinant of persuasive effectiveness. Psychological reactance and discomfort remained low, while familiarity with an animal species was associated with actual behavior in some conditions.
  These findings indicate that persuasion by quadruped virtual agents depends more on functional cues, including emotional expression, attention guidance, and intention readability, than on accurate species-specific behavior. The results support cross-species generalizability and provide a basis for reusable design patterns in persuasive technology and human-AI interaction.

AI.tldr: Quadruped virtual agents (dog, cat, horse) can persuade through emotional expression and attention-guiding cues; faithful species-specific motion is not necessary for effectiveness. Functional cues matter more than biological accuracy.
AI.motivation: Persuasive technology research has focused on humanoid virtual agents, leaving non-humanoid quadruped agents underexplored. It is unknown whether emotional expression works consistently across animal species or whether species-specific motion is required for persuasive effectiveness.
AI.method: Developed virtual dog, cat, and horse agents with three behavioral conditions: species-specific behavior, shared behavior across species, and a bark-only baseline. Participants performed everyday tasks (trash disposal, feeding, refraining from smartphone use). Evaluated intention understanding, behavioral intention, actual behavior, psychological reactance, discomfort, familiarity, and agent acceptance.
AI.result: The bark-only baseline yielded lower intention understanding and behavioral scores than expressive conditions. Emotional expression and attention-guiding cues improved interpretation of agent intention and supported behavior change. No consistent significant differences emerged between species-specific and shared behavior. Psychological reactance and discomfort remained low; familiarity with an animal species correlated with actual behavior in some conditions.
AI.conclusion: Persuasion by quadruped virtual agents depends more on functional cues (emotional expression, attention guidance, intention readability) than on accurate species-specific behavior. Results support cross-species generalizability and provide a basis for reusable design patterns in persuasive technology and human-AI interaction.

title: RefactorAssist: Agentic Refinement for Reliable Code Refactoring
comment: 27 pages, 10 figures, submitting to ACM TOSEM
summary: Code refactoring aims to enhance the internal structure of source code without affecting its functional behavior. The recent advancements of Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated potential for automating software engineering tasks, such as code refactoring. However, the refactorings produced by LLMs often introduce subtle errors, leading to functional behavior changes and failed unit tests, which limit their practical adoption. To address the limitations of LLM-generated refactorings, we analyze the root causes of their failures and develop the RefactorAssist agent to improve the functional correctness of LLM-generated refactorings. To this end, we use 10 open-source Java projects with their native test suites and manually evaluate why LLM-generated refactorings fail unit tests. We then design an agentic approach that leverages unit-test logs, error explanations, project context retrieval, and code diffs to guide the iterative refactoring. Our findings show that the main reasons for failure are context misunderstanding/hallucination (24.3%), incorrect or inconsistent renaming (15.3%), adding new functionality or variables (13.7%), code incompleteness (11.3%), syntax and structural errors (9.7%), edge cases not handled (9%), improper type handling (8.7%), and variables outside scope (8%). To make our approach cost-effective, RefactorAssist first applies a static repair step for missing imports, unbalanced brackets, and compilation errors without LLMs. For remaining failures, RefactorAssist incorporates error logs and code diffs, achieving up to a 70.8% repair rate on the remaining failures and a 94.2% cumulative pass rate under the best-performing configuration. These results indicate that static checks and test-guided, context-aware agentic repair can increase the reliability of LLM-generated refactorings, bringing them closer to practical integration within developer workflows.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated code refactorings often fail unit tests due to context misunderstanding, renaming errors, and other issues. The authors analyze these root causes and propose RefactorAssist, an agentic approach combining static repair with test-guided, context-aware iterative refinement, achieving up to 94.2% cumulative pass rate on 10 Java projects.
AI.motivation: LLMs show promise for automated code refactoring but frequently introduce subtle functional errors that cause unit test failures, hindering practical adoption. Understanding why these failures occur and developing a mechanism to correct them is essential for reliable LLM-based refactoring.
AI.method: The authors manually analyzed refactoring failures on 10 open-source Java projects with native test suites, categorizing root causes (context misunderstanding, renaming errors, etc.). They then built RefactorAssist, a two-phase agent: (1) a static repair step that fixes missing imports, unbalanced brackets, and compilation errors without LLM invocation; (2) an LLM-based iterative repair step that leverages unit-test error logs, error explanations, project context retrieval, and code diffs to guide corrections.
AI.result: Root cause distribution: context misunderstanding/hallucination (24.3%), incorrect/inconsistent renaming (15.3%), adding new functionality/variables (13.7%), code incompleteness (11.3%), syntax/structural errors (9.7%), unhandled edge cases (9%), improper type handling (8.7%), and out-of-scope variables (8%). RefactorAssist achieved up to 70.8% repair rate on remaining failures and a 94.2% cumulative pass rate in the best configuration.
AI.conclusion: Static checks combined with test-guided, context-aware agentic repair significantly improve the functional correctness of LLM-generated refactorings, bringing them closer to practical use in developer workflows.

title: Neural Circuit Function Inference with LLMs
summary: The success of connectome mapping now shifts the challenge of understanding the nervous system to the interpretation of neural circuits. Here, we devise a new automated method, LLantia (LLM automated neural circuit inference and analysis), to systematically infer neural circuit function and the role of its component neural cell types. Our approach distills descriptions of cell type function from the literature and, in combination with the connectome, then infers the function for all other cell types, which serves as a basis for subsequent neural circuit function inference. Results are structured hierarchically, with different possible circuit functions organised under multiple possible behavioural and physiological contexts, and each circuit function composed of subcircuit descriptions alongside relevant cell types to facilitate both backtracking to known, published information and support further experimental research. We illustrate our method by inferring cell type function for all cell types of the adult fruit fly brain and for select broader circuits within, and validate our findings, including by cross-checking with literature published after the release date of our analysis.

AI.tldr: LLantia is an automated method that combines literature-derived cell-type functional descriptions with connectome data to systematically infer the function of all neural cell types and circuits in the adult fruit fly brain, with hierarchical organization enabling both validation against published work and guidance for future experiments.
AI.motivation: Connectome mapping has succeeded in producing wiring diagrams, but interpreting what these neural circuits actually do remains a major bottleneck. Manual inference of circuit function from connectomes and literature is labor-intensive and non-scalable, motivating the need for automated, systematic approaches.
AI.method: LLantia employs a large language model (LLM)-based pipeline that: (1) distills functional descriptions of known cell types from the published literature; (2) leverages the connectome's wiring graph to propagate and infer functions for all remaining cell types; (3) structures outputs hierarchically under behavioral/physiological contexts, with each circuit function decomposed into subcircuit descriptions and associated cell types.
AI.result: The method was applied to infer functions for all cell types in the adult Drosophila melanogaster brain and for selected broader circuits. Validation included cross-checking predictions against literature published after the analysis cutoff date, confirming the accuracy of the automated inferences.
AI.conclusion: LLantia demonstrates that combining LLM-based literature mining with connectomic data enables scalable, systematic, and verifiable inference of neural circuit function, providing a structured foundation for both retrospective validation and prospective experimental design.

title: Mask-Based Priors Are More Persistent than Query-Key Initializations
summary: Transformers do not merely lack data on some Boolean extrapolation tasks; they generalize in a systematically wrong way. Recent work on generalization on the unseen has shown that, despite fitting the observed domain, Transformers often extrapolate according to a simpler minimum-degree interpolator rather than the true target function. These Boolean tasks are not practical applications, but controlled stress tests for understanding Transformer inductive bias. We ask whether this failure mode can be corrected by injecting explicit structural priors into attention. Existing structured-initialization methods alter Transformer inductive bias indirectly, by choosing query and key projections whose similarity scores approximate a desired attention pattern. However, we find that when applied to Boolean extrapolation, these QK-based priors can be rapidly overwritten during training and fail to change the learned extrapolation rule. We propose a simpler alternative: initialize the additive attention mask directly. Unlike standard hard masks used for causality or locality attention, our mask is a finite, learnable attention-logit bias initialized from task-level interaction structure. This separates the structural prior from content-dependent attention scores, allowing it to persist throughout optimization. On Boolean reasoning tasks, mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation where vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers remain trapped by the default inductive bias. The same mechanism also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks. These results show that attention masks can serve not only as architectural constraints, but as a simple substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers.

AI.tldr: Transformers fail on Boolean extrapolation tasks due to a systematic inductive bias toward minimum-degree interpolators. The authors propose initializing learnable additive attention masks directly from task-level interaction structure, rather than manipulating QK projections, achieving near-perfect extrapolation where existing methods fail.
AI.motivation: Transformers exhibit a systematic failure mode on Boolean extrapolation tasks: they generalize according to a simpler minimum-degree interpolator rather than the true target function. Existing structured-initialization methods that inject priors via QK projections are rapidly overwritten during training and fail to correct this bias. This motivates a need for a more persistent mechanism to encode structural inductive priors.
AI.method: The authors propose mask-based initialization: directly initializing the additive, learnable attention-logit bias (mask) from task-level interaction structure, rather than indirectly through query/key projections. This mask separates the structural prior from content-dependent attention scores, allowing it to persist throughout optimization. The mask is finite, learnable, and distinct from standard hard masks used for causality or locality.
AI.result: On Boolean reasoning tasks, mask-based initialization achieves near-perfect extrapolation, while vanilla and QK-initialized Transformers remain trapped by the default minimum-degree inductive bias. The method also improves low-data arithmetic performance and remains competitive on vision and language benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Attention masks can serve not only as architectural constraints (e.g., causality, locality) but as a simple and effective substrate for encoding persistent inductive bias in Transformers, correcting systematic generalization failures that QK-based structural priors cannot fix.

title: Unleashing the Potential of Large Language Models: A Blueprint for Real-Time, Enterprise-Ready Deployments
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Authors' accepted version of an article published in IEEE Computer. The version of record is available at the DOI below
summary: Large language models deployed in real-time, regulated settings face knowledge staleness, catastrophic forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback loops. We present a unified, pattern-driven LLMOps architecture integrating real-time data ingestion, continual learning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and human-in-the-loop feedback into a single operational pipeline. Four contributions map to established software design patterns: an adaptive ingestion pattern orchestrator (AIPO) evaluated with FreshStreamBench; STAR+FAR continual learning with sparse temporal adapter routing and freshness-aware replay; SAGE, an SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy predicting a per-query passage budget to meet tail-latency targets; and an automated feedback-driven convergence stage with RLHF triggers. The result reduces latency-cost-accuracy trade-offs while supporting auditability and rollback for high-risk sectors such as health care and finance.

AI.tldr: A unified LLMOps architecture combining real-time data ingestion, continual learning (STAR+FAR), adaptive retrieval (SAGE), and RLHF-driven feedback loops to reduce latency-cost-accuracy trade-offs in regulated, high-risk domains.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLMs suffer from knowledge staleness, catastrophic forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback loops — failures that are unacceptable in regulated sectors like healthcare and finance. Existing solutions address these problems in isolation, lacking a unified operational pipeline that simultaneously handles freshness, adaptability, and auditability.
AI.method: The architecture comprises four pattern-driven components: (1) AIPO — an adaptive ingestion pattern orchestrator benchmarked on FreshStreamBench; (2) STAR+FAR — continual learning via sparse temporal adapter routing with freshness-aware replay to mitigate forgetting; (3) SAGE — an SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that predicts per-query passage budgets to satisfy tail-latency constraints; (4) an automated feedback convergence stage with RLHF triggers, supporting auditability and rollback.
AI.result: The unified pipeline reduces latency-cost-accuracy trade-offs while maintaining compliance-grade auditability and rollback capabilities, making it viable for high-stakes deployment in healthcare and finance.
AI.conclusion: A pattern-driven, unified LLMOps architecture can holistically address staleness, forgetting, hallucination, and weak feedback in production LLM systems. The four design patterns — AIPO, STAR+FAR, SAGE, and RLHF-triggered feedback — provide a blueprint for deploying safe, adaptive LLMs in regulated environments.

title: 3D Gaussian Splatting and Mesh-Based Digital Twins: An Exploratory Study for Virtual Reality Tourism
comment: Accepted to the 1st Workshop on Hyperrealism in XR at ISMAR 2026
summary: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly used for immersive experiences in virtual tourism. Virtual Reality (VR) enables remote visits to replicated locations for promotional purposes or access to fragile and rural cultural heritage sites. However, developing high-fidelity DTs of tourist destinations is costly, due to the manual creation of 3D environments. Novel 3D rendering techniques, such as 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS), pose a promising approach to creating immersive experiences. This study investigates the user experience (UX) of a 3D-mesh-based scene and a 3DGS-based scene within a VR tourism application. In a laboratory study, 20 participants engaged with both versions and rated UX, cybersickness, presence and affect through standardized questionnaires. A custom questionnaire was created to measure the perception of the DTs. The collected data suggests that both versions were enjoyed and induced positive affect, with the Mesh version receiving good UX ratings. While the 3DGS version scored higher in terms of experienced realism, it showed clear weaknesses in pragmatic quality. Further, the results suggest that the feeling of presence could be enhanced and cybersickness reduced in both versions. Overall, the study contributes to the understanding of UX in VR tourism applications by implementing mesh-based and 3DGS-based DTs and raising important questions about the perception of realism.

AI.tldr: This study compares user experience (UX) between 3D-mesh-based and 3D Gaussian Splatting-based digital twins in a VR tourism application. Twenty participants tested both versions; results show the 3DGS version scored higher on realism but weaker on pragmatic quality, while both induced positive affect and enjoyment.
AI.motivation: Digital twins for virtual tourism rely on costly manual 3D environment creation. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offers a promising alternative for immersive experiences, but its UX in VR tourism applications remains unexplored compared to traditional mesh-based approaches.
AI.method: A within-subjects laboratory study with 20 participants who engaged with both a 3D-mesh-based scene and a 3DGS-based scene in a VR tourism application. UX, cybersickness, presence, and affect were measured via standardized questionnaires, supplemented by a custom questionnaire on digital twin perception.
AI.result: Both versions were enjoyed and induced positive affect. The Mesh version received good UX ratings. The 3DGS version scored higher on experienced realism but showed clear weaknesses in pragmatic quality. Presence could be enhanced and cybersickness reduced in both versions.
AI.conclusion: The study advances understanding of UX in VR tourism by implementing and comparing both mesh-based and 3DGS-based digital twins, highlighting a realism–pragmatic quality trade-off and raising important questions about how realism is perceived in immersive virtual environments.

title: Claim Plane: Reliability Gains and the Limits of Selective Concurrency for Parallel Coding Agents: A 30-Pair, Three-Seed Confirmatory Study of Deterministic Pre-Write Admission
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, 6 main-text tables. Confirmatory follow-up to arXiv:2607.21909. Code: https://github.com/SkeinRank/claim-plane. Data and artifacts: https://huggingface.co/datasets/skeinrank/claim-plane-confirmatory-30x3
summary: Parallel coding agents can produce locally valid changes that fail when combined. Claim Plane addresses this failure mode as deterministic pre-write admission over versioned change intents. This paper reports a confirmatory study on 30 frozen CooperBench feature pairs, balanced between 15 conflict and 15 clean labels, with three coder seeds, four coordination arms, and 360 completed executions. DeepSeek V4 Pro generated 60 feature-level planner declarations once; the declarations were frozen across all arms and coder seeds, while DeepSeek V4 Flash performed the coding work. Static Claim Plane raised pair pass from 23.3% under unconstrained parallel execution to 50.0%, a paired task-cluster difference of +26.7 percentage points (95% bootstrap CI 9.6 to 60.0), and raised integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%. On conflict-labeled pairs, pair pass rose from 6.7% to 60.0%. However, static admission serialized 96.7% of executions, including 93.3% of clean cases, and therefore recovered reliability largely by collapsing toward serial execution. Dynamic admission was more selective, serializing 66.7% of conflict cases and 13.3% of clean cases, but 46 of 90 executions failed closed on undeclared scope, reducing pair pass to 22.2%. Forty-five of those 46 blocks targeted files already present in the frozen declarations, indicating region undercoverage and insufficient amendment handling rather than wholly unknown files. The results support pre-write admission as a reliability mechanism, but they do not establish useful wall-clock parallel speedup: provider calls were physically sequential, and the conservative policy largely serialized the workload. The complete study artifacts, hashes, and clustered bootstrap analysis are publicly released for reproduction.

AI.tldr: Claim Plane uses deterministic pre-write admission control over versioned change intents to prevent integration failures when parallel coding agents produce locally valid but mutually incompatible changes. A confirmatory study on 30 CooperBench feature pairs shows static admission raises pair pass from 23.3% to 50.0% and integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%, but largely by serializing execution. Dynamic admission is more selective but suffers from declaration undercoverage.
AI.motivation: Parallel coding agents independently produce locally valid code changes that can conflict when merged, causing integration failures. Existing unconstrained parallel execution yields low reliability (23.3% pair pass). The work explores whether a pre-write admission control mechanism — Claim Plane — can deterministically prevent these merge conflicts before they occur, thereby improving multi-agent coding reliability without relying on post-hoc conflict resolution.
AI.method: A confirmatory study using 30 frozen CooperBench feature pairs (15 conflict-labeled, 15 clean-labeled) with three coder seeds, four coordination arms, and 360 total executions. DeepSeek V4 Pro generated 60 feature-level planner declarations once and froze them across all arms. DeepSeek V4 Flash performed the actual coding. Four arms were compared: (1) unconstrained parallel execution, (2) static Claim Plane admission, (3) dynamic Claim Plane admission, with clustered bootstrap analysis for statistical inference.
AI.result: Static Claim Plane raised pair pass from 23.3% (unconstrained) to 50.0% (+26.7 pp, 95% CI 9.6–60.0) and integration success from 65.6% to 96.7%. On conflict pairs, pair pass rose from 6.7% to 60.0%. However, static admission serialized 96.7% of all executions (93.3% of clean cases), collapsing toward serial execution. Dynamic admission serialized only 66.7% of conflict cases and 13.3% of clean cases, but 46/90 executions failed closed due to undeclared scope, yielding only 22.2% pair pass. Of those 46 blocks, 45 targeted files already in declarations, indicating region undercoverage rather than unknown files.
AI.conclusion: Pre-write admission control is supported as a reliability mechanism for multi-agent coding, but the study does not demonstrate useful wall-clock parallel speedup, since provider calls were physically sequential and the conservative policy largely serialized workload. The approach shows promise for correctness but requires further work on declaration coverage, dynamic amendment handling, and true parallel execution to achieve both reliability and speedup.

title: LLM-OSDA: An Optimal-Stopping Dynamic Auction for Native Advertising in Multi-Turn LLM Conversations
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to the 41st AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence (AAAI 2027)
summary: LLM-native advertising embeds sponsored content directly into model-generated responses, shifting the unit of sale from a fixed slot to a moment within an evolving conversation. Existing LLM ad-auction mechanisms primarily operate within a single response, settling the winner but not the timing. The extension is nontrivial: with one native insertion opportunity per session, the stopping time depends on bids, coupling timing with allocation, so static truthfulness arguments no longer apply. We propose the LLM-based Optimal Stopping Dynamic Auction (LLM-OSDA), a dynamic cost-per-click auction that integrates Bellman optimal stopping, winner allocation, and envelope pricing. A bid-independent LLM layer estimates contextual click quality and seamlessly renders the winning ad, while bids enter only the committed auction mechanism. Under an exact Bellman oracle, the expected discounted-click allocation is monotone in each advertiser's bid, and the corresponding envelope payment makes truthful bidding weakly dominant in expectation. For practical deployment, a learned StopNet approximates the Bellman action values. We show that its decisions differ from the optimal policy only near the stopping boundary and bound the resulting incentive loss in terms of its approximation error. Experiments on a simulated conversational advertising corpus show that LLM-OSDA improves net revenue by 11 percent over the strongest fixed-timing baseline while maintaining comparable user retention. Code is at https://github.com/2025Fang2025/llm-osda.

AI.tldr: LLM-OSDA is a dynamic auction for embedding native ads in LLM conversations. It jointly optimizes when to insert an ad (optimal stopping) and which ad to show (allocation/pricing), using a learned StopNet to approximate the Bellman optimal policy. The mechanism is approximately truthful and improves revenue by 11% over fixed-timing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM ad auctions only handle allocation within a single response but ignore the timing decision. In session-based LLM conversations with one native insertion opportunity, when to insert the ad and which ad to show are coupled — static truthfulness arguments fail because bids influence the stopping time.
AI.method: The authors propose LLM-OSDA, which separates concerns: (1) a bid-independent LLM layer estimates click quality and renders ads, (2) a dynamic auction layer uses Bellman optimal stopping to decide when to insert, allocates to the highest bid, and charges the second-price envelope payment. A learned StopNet approximates the Bellman oracle for deployment, with theoretical bounds on incentive loss from approximation error.
AI.result: Under an exact Bellman oracle, truthful bidding is weakly dominant in expectation. StopNet's decisions differ from optimal only near the stopping boundary. On simulated conversational advertising data, LLM-OSDA yields 11% higher net revenue than the best fixed-timing baseline while maintaining comparable user retention.
AI.conclusion: LLM-OSDA demonstrates that jointly optimizing timing and allocation in LLM-native advertising is both theoretically sound and practically beneficial, with the modular StopNet architecture enabling real-world deployment with bounded incentive losses.

title: TrAC: Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency for Efficient Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent reasoning traces that nevertheless lead to incorrect answers, making response-level uncertainty estimation important for abstention, human review, and adaptive compute allocation. Existing approaches generally fall into three categories: passive single-trace methods use token-level confidence signals, sampling-based methods compare multiple complete traces at higher generation cost, and active prefix-based methods probe partial traces to study answer stabilization or preference transitions. However, none actively re-elicits an answer from a completed reasoning trace to measure its consistency with and support for the original answer. To address this gap, we introduce Trace-Conditioned Answer Consistency (TrAC), a correctness-supervised uncertainty quantification framework that combines active and passive signals anchored to one completed reasoning trace. Its active component, Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed trace and represents both its consistency with the original answer and its token-level probabilistic support. Its passive component, Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), summarizes how token-level uncertainty evolves throughout the original generation without additional decoding. A lightweight head then integrates the two representations into a response-correctness score. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% relative to eight-sample self-consistency, while using one complete reasoning trace and a short cached answer probe. When eight samples are already available, augmenting sample consensus with re-elicitation further improves macro AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3%, without additional full-trace generation.

AI.tldr: TrAC is a two-component uncertainty quantification framework that re-elicits answers from completed reasoning traces (active) and analyzes token-level uncertainty evolution (passive), outperforming eight-sample self-consistency while using only one trace and a cached probe.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM uncertainty methods either passively use token-level signals from a single trace, compare multiple complete traces (expensive), or probe partial traces for answer stabilization — but none actively re-elicit an answer from a completed reasoning trace to measure self-consistency and support. This gap limits efficient and accurate response-level uncertainty estimation.
AI.method: TrAC combines two components: (1) Prefix-Conditioned Elicitation (PCE), which re-elicits a short answer conditioned on the completed trace and measures both answer consistency and token-level probabilistic support; (2) Trace Uncertainty Profile (TUP), which summarizes token-level uncertainty evolution throughout the original generation without extra decoding. A lightweight head integrates both representations into a correctness score, supervised by ground-truth correctness labels.
AI.result: Across five math reasoning benchmarks and three LLM families, TrAC improves macro AUROC by 1.8% and reduces AURC by 3.4% relative to eight-sample self-consistency, while using only one complete trace and a short cached answer probe. When eight samples are already available, augmenting consensus with re-elicitation further improves macro AUROC by 4.3% and reduces AURC by 8.3%.
AI.conclusion: Active re-elicitation from completed traces provides a strong correctness signal. TrAC offers a cost-effective and extensible framework that outperforms multi-sample self-consistency in uncertainty estimation and can further enhance existing sample-based methods without additional full-trace generation.

title: Verification Without Sufficiency: Per-Chunk Filtering Fails on Multi-Hop RAG, and Decomposition Repairs It
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables, 1 algorithm. Code, per-question traces and analysis scripts: https://github.com/iamhero2709/verification-without-sufficiency
summary: Verification for retrieval-augmented generation usually scores each retrieved chunk and drops the ones that fail. We show this cannot work for multi-hop questions, and show what does. Per-chunk scoring assumes one chunk is a sufficient premise for the answer. Multi-hop questions are built so that none is, and the paragraph carrying the answer is the one the question does not name. Entailment scoring reaches 0.643, 0.523 and 0.560 AUC on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue, against 0.951 on single-hop SQuAD. Seven controls rule out model capacity, premise length, hypothesis template, decision threshold, retriever, answer-matching criterion and prompt. End to end across three datasets, three generator sizes and two prompts, per-chunk gating is significantly worse than not filtering at all in every cell, and its penalty grows with generator capability. The repair is to condition verification on the decomposed sub-question rather than the original query. Using MuSiQue's gold decomposition, entailment on a later hop rises from 0.546, which is chance, to 0.840, a paired lift of +0.355 with a bootstrap interval of [0.331, 0.382]. An off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-7B decomposer, given the question and the top retrieved paragraph, reaches 0.637 and captures 31% of that ceiling; decomposing without retrieval reaches 0.533, below the original question. Iterative retrieval systems already produce such decompositions and discard them before verifying.

AI.tldr: Per-chunk entailment verification fails catastrophically on multi-hop QA because no single chunk alone entails the answer. The fix is to condition verification on decomposed sub-questions rather than the original query, recovering most of the lost performance.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems commonly use per-chunk verification — scoring each retrieved chunk and discarding those that fail an entailment check. The authors argue this approach is fundamentally flawed for multi-hop questions, where the answer depends on synthesizing information across multiple chunks, none of which individually entails the answer. The paper aims to diagnose this failure and propose a principled repair.
AI.method: The authors benchmark entailment-based chunk verification across three multi-hop datasets (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue) and one single-hop dataset (SQuAD). They conduct seven ablation controls to isolate the cause (ruling out model capacity, premise length, hypothesis template, decision threshold, retriever quality, answer-matching criteria, and prompt design). The proposed repair conditions verification on decomposed sub-questions: each chunk is scored against the sub-question it is meant to address, rather than against the original composite query. Experiments test both gold sub-question decompositions (from MuSiQue) and automatic decomposition using an off-the-shelf Qwen2.5-7B model.
AI.result: Per-chunk entailment achieves 0.643, 0.523, and 0.560 AUC on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue respectively, versus 0.951 on single-hop SQuAD. End-to-end, per-chunk gating is significantly worse than no filtering across all three datasets, three generator sizes, and two prompts; the penalty increases with generator capability. Using gold sub-question decomposition on MuSiQue, entailment AUC on a later hop rises from 0.546 (chance-level) to 0.840, a paired lift of +0.355 (bootstrap 95% CI: [0.331, 0.382]). The Qwen2.5-7B decomposer given the question and top retrieved paragraph reaches 0.637 (31% of the ceiling gain); decomposing without retrieval reaches only 0.533.
AI.conclusion: Per-chunk verification is structurally unsuitable for multi-hop RAG and actively harms performance relative to no filtering. The correct approach is sub-question–conditioned verification. The authors note that iterative retrieval systems already produce sub-question decompositions but discard them before verification, representing a missed opportunity for straightforward integration.

title: NoisePQC++: A Unified NIST-Compliant PQC and Hybrid-PQC Implementation of the Noise Protocol
comment: 11 pages. Accepted to be presented and published at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering
summary: The threat of quantum computers to classical public-key cryptography has created an urgent need to evolve secure communication protocols with post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) primitives. The Noise Protocol Framework, widely used in systems such as WireGuard and WhatsApp, traditionally relies on the Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) public-key exchange scheme, which is vulnerable to quantum threats. In this paper, we present NoisePQC++, a unified C++23 implementation of the Noise Protocol framework augmented with post-quantum Key Encapsulation Mechanisms and Hybrid Forward Secrecy. Our design integrates the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) standardized ML-KEM algorithm alongside classical ECDH, enabling full PQC, hybrid ECDH+PQC handshakes, and unified support for all 57 classical Noise handshake pattern variants, 13 post-quantum Noise handshakes, and their hybrid variants. Compared with prior work, NoisePQC++ offers broader protocol coverage, more complete implementation support, and greater flexibility. Our evaluation shows minimal overhead under normal network conditions and acceptable overhead in adverse cases, while significantly improving resistance against quantum adversaries. These results indicate that NIST-standardized post-quantum and hybrid Noise handshakes are practical and provide a credible basis for future deployment.

AI.tldr: NoisePQC++ is a C++23 implementation of the Noise Protocol Framework that integrates NIST-standardized ML-KEM post-quantum cryptography alongside classical ECDH, supporting all 57 classical, 13 post-quantum, and hybrid handshake variants with minimal performance overhead.
AI.motivation: Quantum computers threaten classical public-key cryptography (specifically ECDH used in Noise-based protocols like WireGuard and WhatsApp), creating an urgent need to augment the Noise Protocol Framework with post-quantum cryptographic primitives to ensure long-term security.
AI.method: The authors developed NoisePQC++, a unified C++23 framework that integrates NIST-standardized ML-KEM (Kyber) with classical ECDH, supporting three handshake modes: full PQC, hybrid ECDH+PQC (Hybrid Forward Secrecy), and classical-only. The implementation covers all 57 classical Noise handshake patterns, extends to 13 post-quantum patterns, and their hybrid variants. Performance was evaluated under normal and adverse network conditions.
AI.result: NoisePQC++ offers broader protocol coverage and more complete implementation than prior work. Performance evaluation shows minimal overhead under normal network conditions and acceptable overhead under adverse conditions, while significantly improving quantum resistance.
AI.conclusion: NIST-standardized post-quantum and hybrid Noise handshakes are practical and provide a credible foundation for future deployment in real-world secure communication systems.

title: HaptoFlow: High-Fidelity Real-Time Vibrotactile Generation via Flow Matching for Virtual Reality
summary: Haptic feedback is widely employed to enhance immersion in Virtual Reality (VR) environments. However, designing haptic stimuli that cover diverse interaction conditions remains a significant scalability challenge. Data-driven haptic generation has emerged as a promising approach, yet existing models face an inherent trade-off between waveform expressiveness and inference responsiveness, which becomes increasingly critical as training data grow in scale and diversity. To address this challenge, we propose HaptoFlow, a vibrotactile generative model based on Flow Matching, designed for interactive real-time haptic rendering in VR. Flow Matching learns a continuous vector field that transforms a base distribution into the target data distribution, enabling efficient representation of complex haptic data distributions and thereby facilitating both high-quality generation and computational efficiency. We train HaptoFlow conditioned on material labels and interaction parameters (stroking velocity and applied force), and integrate it into a VR system. Technical evaluation demonstrates that HaptoFlow outperforms all baseline methods in both waveform reproduction accuracy and inference latency. Furthermore, user studies confirm that the system latency falls well within the perceptual threshold of visual-haptic delay, and statistically significant improvements in perceived haptic quality are observed for a subset of materials. These findings establish a practical foundation for scalable, data-driven haptic content creation in VR, and provide latency benchmarks that inform the design of future real-time haptic rendering systems. Project page: https://tamago117.github.io/HaptoFlow/.

AI.tldr: HaptoFlow is a Flow Matching-based vibrotactile generative model that enables real-time, high-quality haptic rendering in VR, outperforming baselines in both waveform accuracy and inference latency while staying within perceptual thresholds for visual-haptic synchrony.
AI.motivation: Existing data-driven haptic generation models suffer from a fundamental trade-off between waveform expressiveness and inference responsiveness, a problem that worsens as training datasets scale up. There is a need for a model that can simultaneously achieve high-fidelity haptic waveform generation and real-time inference for interactive VR applications.
AI.method: HaptoFlow employs Flow Matching to learn a continuous vector field that transforms a simple base distribution into the complex target vibrotactile data distribution. The model is conditioned on material labels and interaction parameters (stroking velocity and applied force) and is integrated into an end-to-end VR system for real-time rendering.
AI.result: Technical evaluation shows HaptoFlow surpasses all baseline methods in both waveform reproduction accuracy and inference latency. User studies confirm system latency remains below the perceptual threshold for visual-haptic delay, and statistically significant improvements in perceived haptic quality were observed for a subset of materials.
AI.conclusion: HaptoFlow establishes a practical foundation for scalable, data-driven haptic content creation in VR and provides latency benchmarks to guide the design of future real-time haptic rendering systems.

title: AgenTag: Attribution of AI Coding Agents from Behavioral Fingerprints
summary: AI coding agents increasingly author pull requests (PRs), often under developers' own accounts, obscuring who actually produced a change. Reliable attribution is important for repository governance, empirical studies of AI-assisted software development, and measuring the impact of AI coding agents. Existing work focuses on closed-set identification of known agents, leaving the practical limits of open-world AI coding agent attribution largely unexplored. In this paper, we present AgenTag, a multimodal framework for open-world AI coding agent attribution, evaluated on AIDev, comprising 33,580 PRs from five AI coding agents and 6,618 human-authored PRs. We represent each PR using textual, behavioral, and code-based modalities, and compare conventional classification with supervised contrastive learning for open-set recognition and few-shot enrollment of previously unseen agents. AgenTag identifies authoring agents with a weighted F1 of 0.96 (macro F1 of 0.84), distinguishes AI- from human-authored PRs with a balanced F1 of 0.89, and detects previously unseen agents with an AUC of 0.84. We further show that PR descriptions and commit messages provide nearly all of the attribution signal, whereas code diffs contribute little across multiple representations, indicating that coding agents are distinguished primarily by how they communicate changes rather than by the code they generate. Moreover, these behavioral fingerprints persist after removing explicit self-disclosed markers, demonstrating that attribution relies largely on latent stylistic characteristics. These findings show that reliable attribution of AI coding agents is feasible and clarify the practical trade-offs between attribution accuracy and the information required to achieve it.

AI.tldr: AgenTag is a multimodal framework for open-world AI coding agent attribution that identifies which AI agent authored a PR, distinguishes AI- from human-authored PRs, and detects previously unseen agents. Evaluated on 33,580 AI-authored and 6,618 human-authored PRs, it achieves strong performance using primarily textual/behavioral features from PR descriptions and commit messages, while code diffs contribute little — showing agents are distinguished by communication style, not code patterns.
AI.motivation: AI coding agents increasingly author pull requests under developers' accounts, obscuring true authorship. Reliable attribution is critical for repository governance, empirical studies of AI-assisted development, and measuring AI's impact. However, existing approaches only handle closed-set identification of known agents, leaving open-world attribution — including detecting novel, previously unseen agents — largely unexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose AgenTag, a multimodal framework using textual (PR descriptions, commit messages), behavioral (temporal patterns, interaction metadata), and code-based (diffs) modalities. They compare conventional classification with supervised contrastive learning for open-set recognition and few-shot enrollment of unseen agents. Evaluation uses the AIDev dataset: 33,580 PRs from five AI coding agents plus 6,618 human-authored PRs.
AI.result: AgenTag identifies authoring agents with weighted F1 of 0.96 (macro F1 of 0.84), distinguishes AI- from human-authored PRs with balanced F1 of 0.89, and detects unseen agents with AUC of 0.84. PR descriptions and commit messages provide nearly all attribution signal; code diffs contribute little. Behavioral fingerprints persist after removing explicit self-disclosed markers, indicating attribution relies on latent stylistic characteristics rather than overt signals.
AI.conclusion: Reliable open-world attribution of AI coding agents is feasible. The key finding is that agents are distinguished primarily by how they communicate changes (PR descriptions, commit messages) rather than by the code they generate. This reveals practical trade-offs between attribution accuracy and the information required, and shows that latent stylistic fingerprints survive even when explicit markers are removed.

title: DiffusionGemma Technical Report
summary: We introduce DiffusionGemma, an experimental open-weight language model that uses discrete diffusion to generate text at exceptionally high speed. Rather than decoding one token at a time, DiffusionGemma iteratively refines blocks of 256 tokens in parallel, avoiding the sequential decoding bottleneck of conventional autoregressive (AR) large language models. Instead of training from scratch, we obtain DiffusionGemma by fine-tuning the mixture-of-experts Gemma 4 model with 3.8B activated and 25.2B total parameters. Our compute-efficient two-stage training pipeline uses fewer than 10% of the starting AR model's total training token budget. The first stage uses supervised fine-tuning to teach bidirectional denoising, while the second stage combines reinforcement learning with sampler distillation to jointly improve generation quality and inference efficiency. DiffusionGemma establishes a new Pareto frontier for the trade-off between generation speed and model capability. Averaged across our full evaluation suite, it generates around 20 tokens per forward pass and achieves roughly 1,500 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, which is substantially faster than AR models even with state-of-the-art speculative decoding. DiffusionGemma also retains the starting model's support for thinking mode, multimodal inputs, and long contexts. Despite diffusion fine-tuning, it remains capable of AR generation with only minor performance degradation, suggesting a path toward hybrid diffusion-AR decoding.

AI.tldr: DiffusionGemma is a fine-tuned language model that uses discrete diffusion for parallel text generation, achieving ~1500 tokens/sec on an H100 by refining 256-token blocks simultaneously, establishing a new speed-capability Pareto frontier while retaining multimodal and thinking capabilities.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive (AR) LMs suffer from a sequential decoding bottleneck — generating one token at a time limits throughput. The authors aim to overcome this via discrete diffusion, which enables parallel token generation across blocks, dramatically accelerating inference without training a model from scratch.
AI.method: DiffusionGemma is obtained by fine-tuning Gemma 4 (MoE, 3.8B active/25.2B total parameters) using a two-stage pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning for bidirectional denoising, (2) reinforcement learning with sampler distillation to jointly optimize generation quality and inference efficiency. The pipeline uses <10% of the original AR model's training tokens. The model generates ~20 tokens per forward pass in blocks of 256 tokens.
AI.result: DiffusionGemma achieves ~1,500 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU, substantially faster than AR models even with state-of-the-art speculative decoding. It establishes a new Pareto frontier for the speed-capability trade-off. It retains thinking mode, multimodal input support, and long-context capabilities, and can still perform AR generation with only minor degradation.
AI.conclusion: Discrete diffusion fine-tuning offers a compute-efficient path to high-speed text generation without sacrificing core model capabilities. The retained AR capability suggests a promising hybrid diffusion-AR decoding paradigm for future models.

title: Diagnose Before You Compress: Prediction-Independent Bottleneck Witness Refinement for LLM Serving Traces
summary: Production LLM serving generates millions of diverse requests, making full-trace replay across serving configurations increasingly expensive. Existing trace reduction methods mainly preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads may be rare and non-representative. Moreover, evidence for one component cannot compensate for missing evidence in another, while using predicted bottlenecks as target truth creates circular evaluation. These limitations make it necessary to preserve evidence for every bottleneck component rather than rely on workload representativeness alone. We propose Bottleneck-Preserving Witnessing (BPW), a quality-constrained framework for compact and diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites. BPW first performs Workload Candidate Nomination using response-blind workload features and closed source-side measurements. This stage identifies workloads that may expose scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks. Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction then organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges and prioritizes weak and uncovered dimensions. Finally, Bottleneck Truth Verification derives prediction-independent labels solely from direct target-system measurements. The verified results determine the earliest prefix satisfying the direct two-witness requirement for every component. Experiments on BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake show that BPW reaches the verified gate with a compact workload set and outperforms 16 policies, achieving relative improvements of 2.3% and 16.3% in Mean prefix Macro-F1 and WBRC-AUC, respectively. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm the distinct contributions and local stability of its three stages. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/llmllmllm/BPW

AI.tldr: BPW is a framework for constructing compact, diagnostically reliable LLM serving replay suites that preserve bottleneck evidence across all components (scheduler, prefill, decode, KV-cache), outperforming 16 policies on key metrics.
AI.motivation: Production LLM serving generates massive, diverse request traces. Existing trace reduction methods preserve workload distributions or representative requests, but bottleneck-revealing workloads can be rare and non-representative. Evidence for one bottleneck component cannot compensate for another, and using predicted bottlenecks as ground truth creates circular evaluation. Hence, there is a need to preserve direct measurement-based evidence for every bottleneck component.
AI.method: BPW operates in three stages: (1) Workload Candidate Nomination uses response-blind workload features and closed-source-side measurements to identify workloads potentially exposing scheduler, prefill, decode, or KV-cache bottlenecks; (2) Coverage-Priority Sequence Construction organizes multi-component proposals as reusable hyperedges, prioritizing weak and uncovered dimensions; (3) Bottleneck Truth Verification derives prediction-independent labels from direct target-system measurements, determining the earliest prefix satisfying a direct two-witness requirement for every component.
AI.result: On BurstGPT, ServeGen, and Mooncake benchmarks, BPW achieves a compact workload set meeting verified gate criteria and outperforms 16 baseline policies with relative improvements of 2.3% in Mean Prefix Macro-F1 and 16.3% in WBRC-AUC. Stage-resolved and sensitivity analyses confirm distinct contributions and local stability of each stage.
AI.conclusion: BPW provides a quality-constrained, bottleneck-preserving framework for LLM serving replay that avoids circular evaluation by using direct target-system measurements as verification labels, producing compact and diagnostically reliable replay suites.

title: What Syntax Cannot See: The Dynamic Syntactic Invariance Principle and Several Instances of the Same Hidden Assumption, and a Contradiction
summary: This paper develops a single method, find what an accepted result silently assumed, make it a variable, and prove what follows once it is dropped, and shows it keeps working across domains with nothing in common. Its formal core is the Dynamic Syntactic Invariance Principle: a known static inaccessibility result survives when a system's rules evolve in time, under one sharp necessary condition. A direct cryptographic payoff follows: the secrecy of a rolling-key scheme persists across sessions under a structural update, strengthening a static guarantee from earlier work. The same move is then carried into settings far from each other, special relativity, the reach of a formal theory of physical law, and computable output that is fully meaningful yet indistinguishable from noise to every observer, each established on its own terms, so the recurring structure beneath them is found, not imposed: a distinction real at a full level of description can be invisible at a restricted one. Applied to \textsc{SAT}, this yields a contradiction from which coherence forces $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$, derived from what standard theory already admits rather than assumed,offered with one reservation, about the proof, not the answer.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a general method: identify a silently assumed condition in an accepted result, treat it as a variable, drop it, and derive what follows. Applying this across domains reveals a recurring structure — a distinction visible at a full description level but invisible at a restricted one. The formal core is the Dynamic Syntactic Invariance Principle. The method yields a cryptographic payoff (rolling-key secrecy under structural updates), applications in relativity and formal theories of physical law, and a claimed derivation of P≠NP from standard theory, offered with a reservation about the proof.
AI.motivation: The author seeks a unified method that operates across apparently unrelated domains — cryptography, special relativity, formal theories of physical law, and computational indistinguishability — to reveal a common underlying structure rather than imposing one. The deeper motivation appears to be demonstrating that a single structural move (making a hidden assumption variable and dropping it) yields substantive results in each domain, ultimately culminating in a claimed resolution of the P vs NP problem.
AI.method: The method consists of: (1) identifying an accepted result and the assumption it silently relies upon; (2) making that assumption an explicit variable; (3) dropping it and proving what follows. The formal core is the "Dynamic Syntactic Invariance Principle," which states that a known static inaccessibility result survives when system rules evolve over time, subject to one sharp necessary condition. This principle is applied across domains: to rolling-key secrecy (cryptography), to special relativity, to the reach of formal theories of physical law, to computable output indistinguishable from noise, and to SAT, where it allegedly forces P≠NP.
AI.result: 1. Cryptographic: secrecy of a rolling-key scheme persists across sessions under structural update. 2. The same structural pattern is found (not imposed) in special relativity, formal theories of physical law, and computable output meaningful yet indistinguishable from noise. 3. Applied to SAT, the method yields a contradiction from which P≠NP follows, derived from what standard theory already admits. The author adds a reservation about the proof (though not about the answer P≠NP).
AI.conclusion: A single method — surfacing and dropping hidden assumptions — works across domains with nothing in common, revealing a recurring structure: distinctions real at a full level of description can be invisible at a restricted one. This recurring structure is found, not imposed. The method yields P≠NP as a consequence of standard theory, with a caveat about the proof but not the conclusion.

title: From Information to Delegation: Mapping Human-AI Financial Decision Making
summary: As AI increasingly participates in human decision making, understanding how decision-making authority is distributed between humans and AI has become a fundamental behavioural question. We introduce a behavioural measurement framework combining intent and delegated decision authority to quantify what consumers seek from AI and how much decision-making authority they assign to it. Applied to 1.5 million real-world ChatGPT and Gemini interactions from 6,304 users in the United States and India, we find that financial services are already a substantial AI use case. Consumers overwhelmingly use AI to retrieve information and shape financial judgement, while delegation of financial execution remains rare. By shifting attention from conversation topics to delegated decision authority, this work establishes a behavioural baseline for measuring the transition to increasingly agentic AI.

AI.tldr: Using 1.5M real-world AI interactions, the paper introduces a framework that distinguishes between using AI for information/judgement versus delegating actual decision authority, finding that consumers predominantly use AI for financial information and judgement while rarely delegating execution.
AI.motivation: As AI becomes embedded in human decision-making, there is a lack of behavioural measurement frameworks to quantify how decision authority is distributed between humans and AI. The authors seek to move beyond simply tracking conversation topics to understanding the degree of delegated decision-making authority.
AI.method: The authors develop a behavioural measurement framework based on two dimensions: intent (what consumers seek) and delegated decision authority (how much authority they assign). This framework is applied to 1.5 million real-world interactions with ChatGPT and Gemini from 6,304 users across the United States and India, focusing on financial services as a consequential domain.
AI.result: Financial services emerged as a substantial AI use case. Consumers overwhelmingly use AI for information retrieval and shaping financial judgement, whereas delegation of financial execution (actual decision-making authority) remains rare. The framework reveals a clear gap between informational reliance and authoritative delegation.
AI.conclusion: Shifting analytical focus from conversation topics to delegated decision authority establishes a behavioural baseline for tracking the transition toward increasingly agentic AI. The framework enables systematic measurement of how human-AI decision-making boundaries evolve over time.

title: Registry Descriptions Go Stale Unevenly: An 89-Day Measurement of Model Context Protocol Drift, and Why Drift-Ranked Re-Auditing Under-Covers It
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Dataset and code: Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21709945 (CC-BY-4.0)
summary: Security studies of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem share a design: each audits a registry at a single point in time. None reports how long the registry descriptions those audits judged stay current - a necessary condition for any description-level finding to still apply, though not a sufficient one: we measure the shelf-life of the audited text, not the validity of a security finding itself (Sec. 7.1). We reconstruct 120 observations of the official MCP registry over 88.6 days, covering 19,099 distinct servers as it grew from 3,510 to 18,966. Our central result is a policy one: you cannot keep description-level findings current by re-auditing the servers that drift most. At a top-5% re-audit budget, ranking by prior drift catches only ~20% of the previously-seen servers whose description changes in a held-out window - versus ~27% for descriptor drift overall - and only ~10% of all description changers. The limit is not unpredictability: the ranking still buys ~4x lift. It is that the description surface is sparse - 8.6% of servers ever rewrite one, against 24.8% for descriptors - and that roughly half of all description changes land on new arrivals a history ranking cannot reach, so the same lift buys far less coverage. The control that fits is content-binding - revalidate the moment a description's hash moves - plus a sized periodic full-catalog sweep; a drift-history ranking is at best a partial, blind-to-new-arrivals control. This is scanner hygiene for a description-level auditor, not a runtime trust signal. Of servers observed across at least ten intervals, three-quarters never change, the most active 5% generate 61% of all change events, and only 11.9% of a cohort's descriptors change within 30 days; naive compounding predicts 35.8% at 30 days (73% at 89), a heavy-tail overestimate we use only as a diagnostic. We release the panel, figure generator, and analysis code.

AI.tldr: This paper measures how long MCP registry descriptions remain current, finding that description changes are sparse and concentrated among new arrivals, making drift-history-based re-auditing strategies ineffective. Content-binding (hash-triggered revalidation) plus periodic full sweeps is the recommended control.
AI.motivation: Prior security audits of the MCP ecosystem sample registries at a single point in time, but none measures how long audited descriptions stay current. A finding based on a description is only applicable while that description remains unchanged, motivating a longitudinal study of description drift.
AI.method: The authors reconstruct 120 observations of the official MCP registry over 88.6 days, tracking 19,099 distinct servers as the registry grew from 3,510 to 18,966. They measure description and descriptor change rates, evaluate a drift-history-based re-audit ranking against held-out windows, and compare it to content-binding and periodic full-catalog sweeps.
AI.result: At a top-5% re-audit budget, ranking by prior drift catches only ~20% of previously-seen servers whose descriptions change (vs. ~27% for descriptors overall) and ~10% of all description changers. Only 8.6% of servers ever rewrite a description (vs. 24.8% for descriptors). Half of all description changes come from new arrivals unreachable by history ranking. Three-quarters of servers observed across ≥10 intervals never change; the top 5% generate 61% of all change events. Only 11.9% of a cohort's descriptors change within 30 days, far below the 35.8% naive compounding predicts.
AI.conclusion: Description-level findings cannot be kept current by re-auditing the servers that drift most. The recommended control is content-binding (revalidate when a description's hash changes) plus a sized periodic full sweep. Drift-history ranking is at best a partial, blind-to-new-arrivals control and represents scanner hygiene rather than a runtime trust signal.

title: A Constitution-Grid Instrument for Data-Efficient RL Alignment (C-Guard)
summary: Conflicting objectives are general in RL alignment, and training on them data-efficiently is hard. Training a safety guard with RL means optimizing two objectives that conflict: catch real harm, and do not refuse benign prompts. Our finding is that over-refusal improves 22.4% to 12.8%, while under-refusal on adversarial attacks silently worsens 0.27 to 0.33. We present C-Guard, a constitution-grid instrument that generates the RL training data, and C-LIM, a per-cell learnability score that decides each cell's move: prune, densify, amend, expand. C-LIM flags the dead-weight data region before any training budget is spent: 187 untargeted rows had bought zero gain, and our method lifts the same region's learning impact 0.733 to 0.80.
